en: The Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kāśmīra during the Song Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Introduction to the Bodhisattva-bhūmi. The First Chapter: The Introduction to the Bodhisattva-bhūmi.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Monastery, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus and one thousand bodhisattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the immeasurable bodhisattvas, saying:
"Who among you is able to receive, uphold, and protect the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* during this future age of evil?"
"Who is able to protect the Dharma?
Who is able to teach and transform all sentient beings?
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In the evil age to come, I am able to receive, uphold, and protect Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; I can protect the True Dharma and transform sentient beings.”
The Bodhisattva Siṃha further spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
I, too, am able to gather and sustain sentient beings through various skillful means.”
Vajrasattva said: “World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who are about to fall into the three evil realms, I am able to restrain and support them so that they do not fall.”
Mañjuśrī spoke again: “World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who seek anything at all, I am able to cause them to have everything fully provided.”
The Bodhisattva Jñānaketu further spoke these words:
"I am able to bestow great wisdom upon sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Dharmaketu further spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
I am able to universally bestow the Dharma upon all sentient beings.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to bestow peace and happiness upon sentient beings.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Candraprabha.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to teach and transform all sentient beings, causing them to cultivate merit and virtue.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Suvārakṣita.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to teach and transform all sentient beings so that they do not become negligent.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to transform and guide all sentient beings, causing them all to know and see the meaning of the inexhaustible realm.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Moon-Child (Candraprabha).
“World-Honored One!
I am able to bestow unsurpassed peace and happiness upon all sentient beings.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Sādhumati.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to bestow upon all sentient beings the causes of peace and happiness.
Thus spoke Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to rescue and protect sentient beings from fear.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to cause those who have not yet crossed over to cross over.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Zhongshan.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to bring those who are undisciplined to discipline.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Subhāṣita.
“World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who have fallen into the realm of animals, I am able to teach and transform them so that they become subdued.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Anabhirati.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to bestow wisdom upon the foolish.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Prabhākūṭa.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to cause those of inferior faculties to attain superior faculties.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Adṛḍha.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to show that madman the correct path.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Ruciraketu.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to bestow immeasurable peace and happiness upon immeasurable sentient beings.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Śakradhvaja.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to cause those sentient beings who undergo suffering to constantly remember their painful experiences.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva of Inconceivable Liberation.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to cause those sentient beings who are hungry ghosts to be far removed from the suffering of hunger.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Noble Light.
"World-Honored One!
I am able to bring those who are undisciplined to discipline.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to destroy the doubts of those sentient beings.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to block the gates of the three evil realms.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Vajraguṇa.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to cause those sentient beings of divergent understandings to all attain a single understanding.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Immeasurable Practice.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to bestow upon those sentient beings the path free from outflows.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Fearless.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to destroy those various fears.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Ratnaguṇa.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to manifest the treasury of merit and virtue of all sentient beings.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Good Will.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to tame sentient beings with these subtle and gentle words.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Pure Light.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to discipline all sentient beings through affection.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Ratnabhadra.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to cause all those sentient beings to remember their past lives.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Noble Virtuous Radiance (Kalyāṇaprabhāsa).
“World-Honored One!
I am able to cause him to cultivate diligence with vigor.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Śubhaguṇa.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to cause all those suffering sentient beings to attain complete liberation.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to bestow upon those immeasurable sentient beings various kinds of jewels.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Cintāmaṇi.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to destroy the poverty of those sentient beings.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Destroyer of Knots.
“World-Honored One,
I am able to destroy the afflictions of those sentient beings.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Golden Light.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to show those deluded and false sentient beings the path of true reality.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Guṇavarṇarūpa.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to cause all those sentient beings of the various vehicles to abide in the Single Vehicle.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Dharmamati.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to cause them all to attain the Dharma-eye.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Vajrīputra.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to destroy the evil karma of those sentient beings.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Dharmavardhana.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to gather and sustain sentient beings in accordance with the Dharma.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Anāman.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to cause all those sentient beings to be far removed from the three poisons.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Candravijaya.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to show those sentient beings skillful means.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Siṃhamati.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to bestow the Dharma as a gift upon sentient beings.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to destroy the net of doubts of sentient beings.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Gandhahastirāja.
“World-Honored One!
In the future evil age, I am able to manifest dreams for sentient beings so that they may destroy their afflictions.
At that time, Śāriputra had this thought:
"How truly marvelous and extraordinary! The affairs of the bodhisattvas are inconceivable.
He then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If there are bodhisattvas who diligently cultivate vigor and are fully endowed with skillful means, thereby able to benefit sentient beings in various ways—
World-Honored One,
how is it that sentient beings come to beg from such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas for their heads, eyes, marrow, brains, blood, flesh, and all other necessities?"
“World-Honored One!
I now know for certain that such a beggar is indeed a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!
It is truly as you have said.”
Only Bodhisattvas truly know a Bodhisattva; this is certainly not something that Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas can attain.
Śāriputra, although a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva may manifest various kinds of supernatural powers (ṛddhi) like those of a Buddha, they never abandon the mind of a Bodhisattva.
Śāriputra! If there is a householder who gives rise to a mind of arrogance, the Bodhisattva manifests in the form of a householder in order to shatter that pride.
If there are those among Nārāyaṇas or handsome men who possess arrogance, he manifests his body before them all to destroy their arrogance.
If one attains the noble Dharma, it is shown through the Mahāyāna.
Why is this? Because apart from the single liberation, there is no other liberation; for this reason, he is called the Tathāgata.
Śāriputra! A householder bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates two kinds of giving: the first is the gift of the Dharma;
[the second is the gift of material things].

Śāriputra, once a renunciant bodhisattva has fully accomplished these four kinds of giving, they are able to discipline their mind, destroy arrogance, and cultivate and accumulate patience. Śāriputra!
A renunciant bodhisattva who is fully endowed with patience is able to receive and uphold the bodhisattva precepts.

Furthermore, one must be fully endowed with the three kinds of giving in order to receive and uphold the bodhisattva precepts: first, the giving of material things; [second, the giving of fearlessness; and third, the giving of the Dharma].
Second is great giving;
third is unsurpassed giving.
As for giving, one does not begrudge even the four continents, let alone minor objects; this is what is called giving.
Great giving consists of being able to renounce one's wife and children.
Supreme giving consists of one's head, eyes, marrow, brain, bones, flesh, skin, and blood.
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these three kinds of giving, they are then endowed with patience.
Having perfected this patience, one is then able to receive and uphold the bodhisattva precepts. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva wishes to receive the bodhisattva precepts, they should first discipline and soften their faculties: they should not give rise to thoughts of desire toward objects that provoke desire; they should not give rise to thoughts of anger toward objects that provoke anger; they should not give rise to thoughts of delusion toward objects that provoke delusion; and they should not give rise to thoughts of fear toward objects that provoke fear.

If one knows for oneself that they possess these four matters, then they will be known by the Buddhas of the ten directions, and that person will also be able to know the Buddhas of the ten directions. Śāriputra!

If one knows that they do not possess these four things yet receive the Bodhisattva precepts, such a person likewise does not obtain the Bodhisattva precepts and deceives the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas currently residing throughout the ten directions.
“Śāriputra, there are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
the first arises from the causal conditions of anger;”
The second arises from the causal conditions of delusion. Śāriputra!
Anger can create the causal conditions for the eight great hells, while delusion can serve as the causal condition for all evil afflictions.
Because of these two causes and conditions—anger and ignorance—one is able to destroy the bodhisattva precepts. Śāriputra!

If one wishes to receive and uphold the bodhisattva precepts, one should first distance oneself from desire, ignorance, anger, and fear, and for six months, day and night, dwell alone in a quiet and secluded place to repent of all transgressions.

"I, [name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, take refuge in the Saṅgha; I take refuge in all the Buddhas and the Saṅgha of Bodhisattvas currently residing in the ten directions, and I take refuge in the Tathāgata Śākyamuni."
Homage to the Buddha, homage to the Dharma, homage to the Saṅgha; homage to the Buddhas and the assembly of Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha; homage to the Indestructible Vajra Body;
homage to Ratnaprabha; homage to Amitavikrāmin; homage to Anuttaravana-rāja; homage to the Unsurpassed.
With joy, I take refuge in Ratnāgni, I take refuge in Ratnacandraprabha,
I take refuge in Viśuddha, I take refuge in Vīryapāṇi, I take refuge in Brahmaguṇa, I take refuge in Sugata,
I take refuge in Candanaguṇa, I take refuge in Prabhāguṇa, I take refuge in Aśokaguṇa, and I take refuge in...
Nārāyaṇa-strength, Homage to Flower-Virtue, Homage to Lotus, Homage to Wealth-Virtue, Homage to Mindfulness-Virtue, Homage to Good Renown, Homage to Śākya King,
Homage to Unconquerable, Homage to Boundless Body-Radiance, Homage to Boundless Body, Homage to No...
Movement, I take refuge in the Great Mountain King.
In this manner, there are immeasurable Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the world who eternally abide in the world, proclaiming the Dharma and transforming beings through their teachings.

I pray that you will have compassion for me, turn your attention toward me, and keep me in mind. Whatever various sins, unwholesome deeds, and evil karmas I have committed throughout immeasurable past lives as well as in the present life—whether committed by myself, witnessed being committed by others, or having given rise to a mind of rejoicing therein;

If one takes property belonging to the Buddha, property belonging to the Dharma, property belonging to the Sangha, property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, or property belonging to the present Saṃgha; or if one takes it oneself, or seeing others take it, gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy;
or if one commits the five heinous crimes oneself, or seeing others commit them, gives rise to a heart of delight;
or if one commits the ten unwholesome karmas oneself, or seeing others do so, gives rise to a heart of delight.

Due to these causes and conditions of unwholesome karma, they shall be born among animals, hungry ghosts, or in the hells; or they shall take birth as humans in borderlands, or as long-lived devas; their faculties will be incomplete, they will associate with wrong views, and they will not encounter the era of a Buddha.
I now, with a sincere heart, seek mercy and repent for all such transgressions as these.

Just as before the present Śākyamuni Buddha, the Tathāgata, World-Honored One—who possesses true knowledge and vision, whose wisdom is unimpeded, whose pure eyes are free from obstruction, and who constantly acts as a witness for all sentient beings—so do I confess.
I only pray that you will observe my sincere repentance; from this day forward, I shall never dare to commit such acts again.
Furthermore, may all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions listen with a sincere and attentive mind!

Whatever merit I have cultivated through practicing generosity—from the past immeasurable eons until the present—even down to giving a single handful to an animal, and whatever merit I have from observing the precepts, even for a single thought-moment, I dedicate it all toward unexcelled bodhi.

Just as the Buddhas of the past and all Bodhisattvas have made vows and dedicated their merit, just as the Buddhas of the future and all Bodhisattvas will make vows and dedicate their merit, and just as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas currently residing throughout the ten directions make vows and dedicate their merit.

"Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva has thus paid homage with a sincere heart and revered all the Buddhas for six months, whether walking, standing, moving, or sitting, the Buddhas of the ten directions will manifest their bodies and faces to them, fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics."
Although he manifests such marks and signs of a bodhisattva, he never wavers from the dharma-realm at all. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata truly knows their minds.

The Buddhas of the ten directions know with certainty that this person is capable of receiving and upholding the bodhisattva precepts and cultivating compassion; they are able to destroy the hosts of Māra, turn the wheel of the true Dharma, and tame sentient beings by proclaiming the Dharma-realm.
For this reason, the Buddhas of the ten directions manifest their bodies for the sake of these bodhisattvas.
Śāriputra, can a wildcat or a mongoose produce the lion’s roar? No.
"No, World-Honored One!
If there were one who had not planted the roots of all virtues under immeasurable Buddhas throughout immeasurable lifetimes, would they be able to receive and uphold the Bodhisattva precepts?"
"No, World-Honored One. "Śāriputra!"
"Could a donkey carry the burden that a king of fragrant elephants carries? "No,
World-Honored One."
“Śāriputra! Is the light of the sun and moon like that of a firefly? “No, it is not.”
“World-Honored One!
[The Buddha replied: “Śāriputra!
Is the wealth and treasure possessed by Vaiśravaṇa equal to that of the poor?”
"No, World-Honored One. "Śāriputra!"
“When a garuḍa flies, can a crow keep up with it? “No,
World-Honored One.”

“Śāriputra! If there are those who, throughout immeasurable lifetimes and in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, have deeply planted the roots of virtue, such persons are able to receive the bodhisattva precepts and clearly behold the Buddhas of the ten directions.”

Śāriputra! Having received the bodhisattva precepts, if one should transgress a rule that can be confessed due to the causes and conditions of adventitious afflictions, one should confess it before all the Buddhas.
A bodhisattva shall never commit the five heinous crimes.

If greed does not cease even unto the birth of a child, one should, before the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions, fulfill two full days and nights by constantly seeking compassionate repentance with a most earnest mind.
If, out of a greedy mind, one takes property belonging to the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha, one must repent before the Buddha for two years as prescribed.
Śāriputra! It is impossible for a bodhisattva to violate the prohibitions and precepts on account of anger.
"It is likewise impossible for one who has violated the precepts due to the cause of anger to obtain purification through repentance.

At that time, Upāli arose from meditative concentration in the early morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As it is said in the *Śīla-sūtra*: "If my disciples possess faith, they shall never violate the precepts they have received, even at the cost of their lives.

Now that the World-Honored One is present, or should he enter parinirvāṇa, how am I to distinguish and fully understand the prohibitive precepts of the śrāvakas, the prohibitive precepts of the pratyekabuddhas, and the prohibitive precepts of the bodhisattvas?
The World-Honored One has declared me to be the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya; yet I do not now know the skillful means of the Vinaya—how then should I speak?
Here now are many great bhikṣu-saṃghas and bodhisattva-saṃghas; I only pray that the Tathāgata will fully demonstrate and explain it in detail.
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent, Upāli!”
Listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it for you.
Upāli! The causal conditions for the precepts of the śrāvakas are distinct, and the causal conditions for the precepts of the bodhisattvas are distinct.
The precept-mind of the śrāvaka is different, and the precept-mind of the bodhisattva is different.
The adornment of the śrāvaka’s precepts is different, and the adornment of the bodhisattva’s precepts is different.
The skillful means of the śrāvaka’s precepts are different, and the skillful means of the bodhisattva’s precepts are different.
Upāli! The purity of the śrāvaka precepts is not the purity of the bodhisattva precepts, and the purity of the bodhisattva precepts is not the purity of the śrāvaka precepts.
When a śrāvaka does not seek existence for even a single thought-moment, this is called the purity of the śrāvaka precepts.
If a bodhisattva does not seek existence, this is called great violation of the precepts and impure precepts.
For a śrāvaka to seek existence is called a violation of the precepts and impure precepts.

Upāli! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells constantly within existence throughout immeasurable kalpas without the mind giving rise to regret, this is called the purity of the bodhisattva precepts, not the purity of the śrāvaka precepts.
For this reason, Upāli! You should proclaim that the śrāvaka precepts are strict while the bodhisattva precepts are lenient;
the śrāvaka precepts are restrictive while the bodhisattva precepts are open.
In the precepts of the śrāvakas, one should explain the causes and conditions, but in the precepts of the bodhisattvas, one should not. Upāli!
A bodhisattva accords with the minds of sentient beings, unlike a śrāvaka; therefore, the bodhisattva is somewhat lax regarding the precepts, whereas the śrāvaka is strict in his protection of them.

Upāli! If a bodhisattva should violate the precepts in the morning, they must nevertheless continue to keep Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in mind and recognize their own transgressions; they should do so during the three periods of the day and night. This is called the bodhisattva precept.
Upāli! If a bodhisattva commits an offense from time to time, it is not called a breach of the precepts;

however, if a śrāvaka commits an offense from time to time, this is called a breach of the precepts, this is called the loss of the precepts, and this is called failing to attain the fruits of the śramaṇa path.
Why is this? Śrāvakas practice diligence with the intent of destroying afflictions; they must not violate the precepts. Upāli!

If a bodhisattva were to experience the pleasures of the five desires for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, they would still not lose their bodhisattva precepts; they would not be called one who has broken the precepts, nor one who has lost the precepts, nor one who fails to attain the fruit of bodhi.
Upāli! A bodhisattva cannot exhaust all afflictions within a single lifetime; rather, they should cause them to be exhausted gradually through skillful means. Upāli!
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi must be attained through the power of supreme and great adornment before it can be realized; it is not attained in a single lifetime.
For this reason, the Tathāgata does not say that a bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of regret within saṃsāra, nor does he proclaim the permanent severance of craving and attachment.
Instead, he teaches the Dharma of joy, the profound Dharma, the Dharma free from doubt, and the Dharma of emptiness; having heard these teachings, they take delight in saṃsāra.
Upāli said: “World-Honored One!
There are three kinds of offenses:”
First is greed; second is hatred;
third is delusion.
"Regarding the transgressions committed by a bodhisattva,
which are grave and which are light?
The Buddha said:
“Upāli! If a bodhisattva commits as many instances of greed as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, such a bodhisattva is not said to have violated the precepts.
However, if one violates the precepts through a single instance of anger, this is called a breach of the precepts.”
Why is this? Upāli!
A mind of anger can abandon sentient beings, whereas a mind of craving and attachment can protect them.
If one feels attachment toward sentient beings, it is not called an affliction;
if one feels aversion or indifference toward sentient beings, it is called a grave affliction. Upāli!
Therefore, the Tathāgata has said in the sūtras: "The fetter of greed is difficult to sever but is not called heavy; hatred is easy to sever and is thus called heavy. Upāli!
That which is difficult to sever but not grave is constantly present in Bodhisattvas;
that which is easy to sever but grave, they do not commit even in their dreams. Upāli!
Ignorant bodhisattvas lack skillful means and thus fear committing offenses of attachment;
wise bodhisattvas, being well-versed in skillful means, fear committing offenses of anger more than they fear committing offenses of attachment.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Vinaya is called ‘subduing,’ yet the nature of all dharmas is ultimately already subdued.”
"For what reason does the Tathāgata proclaim the Vinaya?
"Mañjuśrī! If ordinary persons were able to know that all dharmas are ultimately disciplined, the Tathāgata would never proclaim the Vinaya."
Because ordinary people do not know and do not understand this, the Tathāgata has preached the Vinaya for them. Mañjuśrī!
For what reason do you not now preach the Vinaya?
"Upāli wishes to hear it. Then Mañjuśrī said to Upāli: "Upāli!"

All dharmas are ultimately subdued; the nature of all dharmas cannot be defiled; the nature of all dharmas is non-perverted; the nature of all dharmas is pure; all dharmas are ineffable; all dharmas are without grasping or attachment; all dharmas neither go nor come; all dharmas are inconceivable; all dharmas are without obstruction; all dharmas are fundamentally without self-nature; all dharmas are without activity; all dharmas neither arise nor cease; all dharmas do not exist within the three periods of time; and all dharmas are free from the net of doubt.
"The Buddha has fully awakened to and known all such dharmas as these. Upāli said,
"World-Honored One!"
"What Mañjuśrī has spoken is not a definitive explanation. The Buddha said, "Upāli!"
“Mañjuśrī always delights in proclaiming such liberation. Upāli said,
“World-Honored One!”
"What is called pride?
It is when a bodhisattva says:
'I possess the bodhicitta.'"
I practice the six pāramitās for the sake of bodhi;
I cultivate all practices through prajñā.
The practice of bodhi is profound, while the practice of the śrāvakas is shallow.
"Bodhisattva conduct is pure; śrāvaka conduct is impure.
Bodhisattva conduct is ultimate; śrāvaka conduct is not ultimate.

If one further discriminates, saying, "This is the Dharma of śrāvakas, this is the Dharma of pratyekabuddhas, this is the Dharma of bodhisattvas, and these are the Dharmas of the Buddhas," or "this is called pure and that is called impure," or "this is called the Path and that is called not the Path," this is called the pride of a bodhisattva.

Chapter 2: The Nature of Good Conduct, from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*. Chapter Two: The Nature of Good Conduct. "The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates and accumulates the noble practices and acts in accordance with their wholesome fruits."
The path to enlightenment consists of ten dharmas, by which one can encompass all wholesome dharmas. What are these ten?
The first is the limb (aṅga).
Second is assistance;
third is a pure mind;
fourth is practice.
Fifth is existence;
sixth is cause;
seventh is the vessel.
Eighth, the stages;
ninth, the skillful means;
tenth, the abidings.
What are the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa)?
They are the nature of a bodhisattva.
The nature of a bodhisattva refers to the initial generation of the mind of awakening and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Why is this? Because the bodhicitta generated by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is the root of all wholesome dharmas; therefore, it is called a "limb" (aṅga).
Because one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of generating this mind, it is called a "cause" (hetu).
Because one who has first resolved their mind will certainly and inevitably attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is called "nature" (*gotra*).

Due to this initial resolution of the mind, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to practice the *dāna-pāramitā*, *śīla-pāramitā*, *kṣānti-pāramitā*, *vīrya-pāramitā*, *dhyāna-pāramitā*, and *prajñā-pāramitā*.

Because one practices the six pāramitās, one attains the cultivation of the adornment of wisdom and the adornment of merit, and cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; therefore, the bodhisattva’s arousal of the bodhicitta is called its "limb."
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas fulfill their conduct according to the arousal of the mind, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; therefore, these are called "limbs.

If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas lacked the bodhisattva-nature (*gotra*), then even if they were to arouse the mind and diligently cultivate vigor, they would ultimately be unable to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Therefore, one should know that it is not because of the arousal of the mind and the diligent cultivation of vigor that there is the nature of a bodhisattva; for this reason, the nature of a bodhisattva is termed a "limb" (aṅga).
Although a bodhisattva possesses the nature of a bodhisattva, if they do not resolve their mind and diligently cultivate vigor, they will be unable to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Because there is the nature of a bodhisattva, and by generating the bodhicitta and diligently practicing with vigor, one is able to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; for this reason, the nature of a bodhisattva is termed a "limb" (aṅga).
Furthermore, "limb" (aṅga) is called a cause; it is also called a ladder, a growth, an adornment, a reliance, a sequence, a progression, and a dwelling.
For this reason, nature (*prakṛti*) is called a "limb" (*aṅga*).
What is meant by "nature"?
There are two kinds of nature:
The first is the intrinsic nature;
the second is the adventitious nature.

Regarding the intrinsic nature: the aggregates, elements, and six sense bases continue in succession without beginning or end, and this dharmic nature is naturally so; this is called the intrinsic nature.
Regarding the term "adventitious nature" (*āgantuka-svabhāva*): it refers to attaining the bodhisattva-nature through the cultivation and accumulation of all wholesome dharmas;
this is called the adventitious nature. In this sutra, these two kinds are designated as "nature," and these two natures are termed "limbs" (*aṅga*).
Furthermore, "nature" (prakṛti) is also called the "son" (putra), also called the "element" (dhātu), and also called "nature.
It is further of two kinds:
first, the subtle; second, the coarse.
That which is called "subtle" is obtained without cause;
because it obtains its fruit without a cause, it is termed subtle.
That which is called "gross" is obtained with a cause.
Because one attains the fruit from the cause, it is termed "coarse.
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who is fully endowed with these two kinds of natures surpasses all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, let alone the various non-Buddhists.
For this reason, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is named "Victorious.
Why is he named "Victorious"? Because he is pure.
Purity is twofold: first, purity from the hindrance of knowledge;
second, purity from the hindrance of the fetters.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are called "pure" because they have purified the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), but not the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are endowed with both purities, for this reason the nature of a bodhisattva is termed "supreme."
“Furthermore, there are four matters in which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva excels over śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others: first, excellence of faculties;
second, excellence of practice; [third, excellence of wisdom; fourth, excellence of liberation.]”
Third is the excellence of skillful means;
fourth is the excellence of attaining the fruit.

Regarding the excellence of faculties (*indriya-viśeṣa*): the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is by nature sharp and acute, whereas those of the pratyekabuddha-nature and śrāvaka-nature are dull; this is called the excellence of faculties.

Regarding the superiority of conduct: while Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cultivate and accumulate wholesome dharmas for the sake of their own liberation, Bodhisattvas do not act for their own sake, but rather cultivate and accumulate wholesome dharmas solely for the sake of sentient beings, bestowing peace and happiness upon them with great compassion and pity; this is called the superiority of conduct.

Regarding the superiority of skillful means (*upāya*): Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are only able to understand the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), but they cannot understand the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) or what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*).
The skillful means of a Bodhisattva, however, enables them to thoroughly know all phenomena; this is called the superiority of skillful means.

Regarding the superiority of the fruit: the śrāvaka attains for himself the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha attains for himself the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, and the bodhisattva attains for himself the enlightenment of a bodhisattva; this is called the superiority of the fruit.
"The nature of a bodhisattva possesses six seals; by means of these seals, all sentient beings can recognize and know:
'This is a bodhisattva. What are the six? "
These are the so-called *dānapāramitā* through to the *prajñāpāramitā*. For what reason is the *dānapāramitā* called the "Seal of the Bodhisattva Nature"?

It is because the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to attain such a mind of renunciation (*tyāga-citta*). Regarding all material goods, whether they be many or few, their mind is free from greedy attachment. When they desire to give, while giving, and after having given, they experience joy in every instance. Regardless of whether the object given is much or little, their mind is free from doubt or regret. Even when giving little, they feel no shame; and when they have no wealth, they always praise the act of giving.
Seeing those who are stingy, one can break through their hearts; seeing those who practice giving, one’s mind gives rise to joy and celebration, leaping with delight as if seeing one's own parents.

Seeing those who come to seek [something], one feels deep personal庆幸 (gratitude/fortune). If one lacks material wealth, one should provide for elders, parents, and teachers through physical actions. One should employ words of joy, gentle words, words of Dharma, truthful words, and correct words to eliminate the false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and senseless chatter of sentient beings. Even when asked by others, one does not speak of another’s long or short faults or transgressions, much less speak of them unsolicited on one’s own accord.

If there are sentient beings who fear the calamities of kings, bandits, water, or fire, he is able to rescue and liberate them; he recognizes kindness, remembers kindness, accepts kindness, and is able to repay it.
When entrusted with another's deposits, he does not cause them doubt, and even if they be precious treasures, his mind harbors no greed or attachment toward them.
Regarding one's own possessions, one has no sense of stinginess in the heart; being able to provide food and clothing, one bestows them as gifts upon others.

One is able to subdue the mind of desire, the mind of attachment, the mind of frivolity and the like, and the mind that craves music and entertainment, and cultivates a collection of shame and remorse (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*).
To not give rise to greed or joy even upon obtaining great treasures is called the Bodhisattva-nature seal of *dānapāramitā*.
"What is the Bodhisattva-nature seal of *śīlapāramitā*?"
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s actions of body, speech, and mind are by nature pure and supple; among sentient beings, they do not give rise to evil thoughts or thoughts of malice and harm.

If, due to adventitious afflictions and the like, they commit various transgressions, once having committed them, they feel remorse in their hearts, deeply engender shame and dread, and openly confess and repent.
He gives rise to a heart of compassion for all sentient beings, regarding them as his only child, and never inflicts harm upon any being with his hand, a staff, or a stone.
His mind constantly seeks out true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), and he is devoted to making offerings to his parents, teachers, elders, and those of long-standing virtue.
He destroys arrogance and inquires after others with kindness; he recognizes and remembers the kindness of others.
If there are those who beg, he consoles them with gentle words.
He does not deceive sentient beings with illusory arts, nor does he ever delight in sustaining his life through unrighteous means.
He constantly delights in cultivating and accumulating all merits, and teaches all sentient beings to extensively cultivate meritorious deeds.

Seeing sentient beings undergoing various sufferings—such as having their life-force severed, being beaten, bound, imprisoned, or afflicted by hunger, thirst, cold, and heat—the Bodhisattva at that time contemplates those who suffer as no different from himself.
He upholds the Buddha’s precepts, not intentionally violating even the most minor ones, much less those that are grave.
He is able to transform all beings through the ten wholesome paths of action, and takes no pleasure in seeing or hearing of sentient beings who engage in strife, contention, or verbal abuse.
All three types of karma are always performed for the sake of sentient beings and never for oneself.
If there are sentient beings who possess precepts, patience, and wisdom, one should joyfully practice together with them and attain a supple mind.
He harbors no harmful intent and no lack of forbearance; his mind always reveres all the precepts.
He does not deceive sentient beings, nor does he engage in divisive speech or idle chatter.
Even when no one asks, one still praises the goodness of others; how much more so when someone does ask—how could one fail to speak?
To revere and honor words that are correct and true is called the Bodhisattva-nature seal of the *śīlapāramitā*.
"What is the seal of the bodhisattva-nature regarding the perfection of patience?
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva observes sentient beings, if there should be one who comes to strike this body of mine, I ought not to retaliate with evil."
Why is this? My body is not a body; that which is called a "body" is what is termed the "true body," and the true body cannot be struck.

This body of mine, however, is a composite body, and a composite body is what is called impure. Within this composite, even if one part is struck, for the most part there is no harm. Since there is no harm for the most part, why should I not be joyful?
One who is angry has only a small portion of anger and a large portion of non-anger; since non-anger predominates, how can such a person be called "angry"?
If it is a composite that strikes and a composite that receives the blow, then who is it that strikes and who is it that receives?
For example, when two objects strike one another, sound is produced.
If it were "I" who was angry, then I should be angry with myself. Why is this?
It is by the conditions of karma that this body is obtained; because of this body, one undergoes such bitter suffering.
It is like a target upon which an arrow strikes.
If I were to increase this mind of anger, I would be unable to contemplate dharmas such as good and evil.
If one is unable to discern between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, one will certainly fall into the three evil realms.
For this reason, whether struck or reviled, one should not give rise to a mind of anger or resentment toward others.
Having observed in this way, it is called the Bodhisattva-nature seal of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

Furthermore, if one sees someone who strikes or reviles them, they should conceive of that person as their own only son and harbor no resentment; this is called the Bodhisattva-nature seal of the perfection of patience.
"What is the Bodhisattva-nature seal of the *vīryapāramitā*?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva diligently cultivates vigor; rising at dawn and retiring at night, they take no pleasure in sleep or reclining. They never dwell upon cold or heat, hunger or thirst, fear or joy."

Whatever one undertakes, whether it be worldly affairs or supramundane matters, one must ensure they are brought to ultimate completion without interruption; if a task is not yet finished, one shall never regret it midway.
Although one receives the respect and offerings of others, one does not cease or rest in the practice one has undertaken.

One does not give rise to a sense of self-contempt regarding one's own person by saying that one cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor does one ever shrink back, even when seeing things in the world that are difficult to accomplish.
This is called the Bodhisattva-nature Seal of Vīryapāramitā.
What is the Bodhisattva-nature Seal of Dhyānapāramitā?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva wholeheartedly delights in contemplating the true meaning of all phenomena; he delights in dwelling in tranquility and in solitary places; he delights in distancing himself from evil people and increasing wholesome dharmas; and upon seeing those who delight in stillness, he rejoices and pays them respect.

Although their afflictions are by nature slight, all their wholesome minds are never destroyed by evil thoughts and reflections; they cultivate and accumulate a mind of loving-kindness, regarding enemies as their own children.

If one sees sentient beings undergoing great suffering and affliction, one gives rise to a heart of compassion and, according to one's own strength, works to eliminate it, vowing that all sentient beings may be made entirely secure and at peace.

Even when the body undergoes suffering, one does not give rise to distress; whether one loses life or property, or is imprisoned, bound, beaten, or exiled, one is able to admonish oneself and, without losing right mindfulness, does not give rise to sorrow and pain.

To listen to the Dharma with single-minded devotion, to transcribe, receive, uphold, recite, and explain it, and to provide instruction when others have forgotten it—through such causes and conditions of sincere mind, one does not forget the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) in future lives; this is called the Bodhisattva-nature-seal of the dhyāna-pāramitā.
“What is the seal of the bodhisattva-nature in the perfection of wisdom?
It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva thoroughly understands all worldly affairs, knows all arts and crafts, and understands all the speech of sentient beings.”

Although one knows this matter, the mind is neither deluded nor errant, nor is it negligent; one is not deceived by non-Buddhists, nor does one follow the doctrines and principles expounded by those with false views. This is called the Bodhisattva-nature Seal of Prajñāpāramitā.
I have now briefly described the characteristics of the coarse seals; the characteristics of the subtle seals are known only by the Buddhas.
"The nature of a bodhisattva is inconceivable; it is the fulfillment and perfection of all meritorious deeds, pure and true, and fully endowed with pure dharmas."
For this reason, it is called "Supreme," and it is also called "Immovable," and it is also called the "Seal of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not perceive the faults and afflictions of unwholesome dharmas, they will be unable to cultivate all wholesome dharmas.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates supreme goodness, even if they should fall into the three evil realms due to the causes and conditions of adventitious afflictions, they still remain superior to the sentient beings of those evil realms.
Why is this? Because of their bodhisattva nature.
If, due to the conditions of adventitious afflictions, they should fall into the evil realms, they are able to swiftly destroy those conditions and quickly attain liberation.
If he does not emerge [from his meditative state], he will not undergo heavy suffering in the evil realms.

Even when experiencing such suffering, he still gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all sentient beings; it is by virtue of the causal conditions of his nature that he attains this compassionate mind.
Therefore, the bodhisattva surpasses all sentient beings of the three evil realms.
"The bodhisattva-mahāsattva destroys pure dharmas due to the causal conditions of the four afflictions."
What are the four? First, they are heavy, constant, and perpetual;
second, by means of these two fetters, one draws near to evil friends.
Third, if one feels fear toward one's teacher, a sovereign, or enemies and bandits, thereby losing the wholesome mind and giving rise to afflictions;
fourth, performing various unwholesome deeds for the sake of one's body and life.
By means of these four dharmas, although one possesses the nature of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, one will ultimately be unable to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, there are four other matters by which, although one possesses the nature of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, one likewise cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are the four? First, not encountering virtuous friends—namely Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who do not misinterpret the meaning of the teachings;
second, although encountering virtuous friends—namely Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—one misunderstands the meaning and fails to train in all the precepts of a Bodhisattva.
Third, although they encounter virtuous friends—Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—and follow their teachings to understand the meaning, they are unable to study and uphold the bodhisattva precepts;

fourth, although they encounter virtuous friends—Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—and follow their teachings to understand the meaning and study the bodhisattva precepts, their roots of goodness are not yet mature and they have not attained the full adornment of bodhi; for these reasons, they do not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Although a bodhisattva possesses the nature of a bodhisattva, if they do not fulfill these four matters, they will ultimately be unable to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Even if one were fully endowed with these four things, it is impossible that one who lacks the nature of a bodhisattva could attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Chapter Three: The Chapter on Generating the Bodhicitta in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* "When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first generates the bodhicitta, he establishes a great, correct vow and speaks these words:

'When I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall bring great benefit to all sentient beings; I must certainly establish all sentient beings within Great Nirvāṇa, and furthermore, I shall teach and transform all sentient beings so that they are fully endowed with the great wisdom of Prajñā. This is what is called benefiting oneself and benefiting others.'"

Therefore, those who first resolve upon Bodhicitta are said to possess the causal conditions for Bodhi: the causal condition of sentient beings, the causal condition of the true meaning, and the causal condition of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. They grasp the root of all wholesome dharmas; thus, the Bodhisattva is called "wholesome" and "greatly wholesome," "real" and "truly real," and is also called the "wholesome root of all sentient beings. He is able to destroy all evils of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind.
Among all the vows belonging to the mundane world as well as those of the supramundane, none can surpass *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; such a vow is unsurpassed and supreme.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva first gives rise to the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are five things.
What are these five? The first is their nature (*gotra*).
Second, practice;
third, the objective sphere; fourth, merit.
Fifth is growth; these are the five.
If a bodhisattva is able to give rise to the bodhicitta, they are then called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, and will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi while practicing the Mahāyāna path.
Therefore, the initial arousal of the bodhicitta enables one to encompass all wholesome dharmas.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva arouses the bodhicitta, they gradually attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through their practice; if they do not arouse this mind, they will ultimately never attain it. Thus, the arousal of the mind is the root of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas see suffering sentient beings, they give rise to a heart of compassion; therefore, by means of this mind of loving-kindness and compassion, they resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. By means of this bodhicitta, they cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and by means of these thirty-seven factors, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, the arousal of the mind is called a "limb.
Because one practices the bodhisattva precepts by virtue of arousing the bodhicitta, this arousal of the mind is a limb of the bodhisattva precepts.
For this reason, the arousal of the mind is called the root, the cause, the gathering, the fruit, and is also called the seed.
The bodhisattva’s production of the thought of enlightenment is further of two kinds:
first, ultimate; second, non-ultimate.
"Ultimate" means that until one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is never any falling back or loss; "non-ultimate" means that there is falling back and loss.
There are two kinds of falling back: first, ultimate falling back; [the second being non-ultimate falling back]."
Second, there is no ultimate regression.
One who regresses ultimately will never again resolve their mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor will they be able to seek out, cultivate, or accumulate its dharmas.
Regarding those who are not yet ultimate, they seek the bodhicitta and cultivate its dharmas.
This bodhicitta has four kinds of causes. What are these four?
First, if a son or daughter of good family sees or hears of the inconceivable [powers] of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they will then give rise to a mind of faith and reverence, thinking:
"The deeds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are inconceivable."
"If the inconceivable deeds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas were attainable, I too would have resolved my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, with a sincere heart, one should contemplate enlightenment and resolve upon the bodhicitta."

Second, there are those who do not behold the inconceivable deeds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, but merely hear of the secret treasury of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; having heard it, they immediately give rise to a mind of reverence and faith.
Because they have attained faith, they resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of supreme enlightenment and great wisdom.
Thirdly, there are those who do not witness the inconceivable deeds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, nor hear the Dharma, but see the time when the Dharma is perishing; they then form this thought:

"The unsurpassed Buddha-Dharma can extinguish the immeasurable suffering and affliction of sentient beings and bring about great benefit; only the Bodhisattvas can cause the Buddha-Dharma to abide long and not perish."

I too shall now resolve to attain bodhicitta, so that all sentient beings may be led far away from the great suffering of afflictions, and the Buddha-dharma may be protected and maintained for long in the world.
They resolve their minds on Bodhicitta for the sake of remaining in the world.

Fourth, there are those who do not see the time when the Buddha-dharma is extinguished, but see only the sentient beings of this degenerate age, who are possessed of heavy afflictions such as greed, anger, and delusion; who lack shame and remorse; and who are stingy, envious, sorrowful, distressed, faithless, and indolent.
Having seen this, he immediately thought:

"In this age of great evil, sentient beings are so wicked that they cannot cultivate goodness; even in such a degenerate age, they cannot give rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles, let alone the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
I shall now resolve to attain bodhicitta; having resolved this mind, I shall then teach and transform all sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"For this reason, a bodhisattva resolves upon bodhicitta amidst these evil beings in this degenerate age.
Furthermore, there are four causes for resolving upon bodhicitta. What are the four?"
First, the perfection of nature;
second, the perfection of virtuous friends;
third, the perfection of a compassionate mind.
Fourth, by contemplating the suffering of birth and death, one fulfills the noble practices and does not fear the difficult practices for the sake of enlightenment.
Regarding the fulfillment of nature, there are four matters by which the Bodhisattva’s nature is naturally fulfilled and fulfilled through spiritual friends.
What are the four?

First, having virtuous friends who possess all their faculties intact and are endowed with great wisdom, who can demonstrate what is wholesome and unwholesome and prevent one from following wrong paths—this is called being fully endowed with virtuous friends.
Second, his mind is not negligent; he is able to destroy negligence and close off the evil realms.
Third, he is himself able to fulfill the bodhisattva precepts and further teaches them to others.

Fourth, one does not cause others to turn from the higher path to a lower path, does not cause others to turn from the Mahāyāna to the Hīnayāna, and does not cause others to turn from meditative concentration and wisdom to the cultivation of merit.
There are four further matters for fully possessing a mind of loving-kindness.
What are the four?

First, there may be worlds where there are places of suffering and affliction, or there may be worlds where there are no such places of suffering and affliction; the Bodhisattva makes a vow to be reborn therein, and whether seeing others undergoing suffering or experiencing it himself, he gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in order to destroy that suffering.
Second, when born among those in the hells, whether seeing them undergoing suffering or experiencing it oneself, one likewise gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness to destroy their suffering.
Third, when born among the hungry ghosts, whether seeing them undergoing suffering or experiencing it oneself, one likewise gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness to destroy their suffering.

Fourth, when one is born among animals, whether seeing them undergoing suffering or experiencing it oneself, one likewise gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in order to sever that suffering.
This perfection of the mind of loving-kindness further possesses three grades: namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior [practice] further consists of four matters:
first, contemplating the suffering of birth and death;
second, cultivating a mind of compassion that is without beginning or end.
Third is a mind that is courageous and robust by nature;
fourth is a mind that has attained wisdom.
Furthermore, there are four other matters.
What are the four? First, heedfulness;
second, the fulfillment of the precepts.
Third, being able to endure with patience;
fourth, single-mindedly and with a sincere heart recollecting *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, there are four other matters.
What are the four? First, regarding all sentient beings with equality as if they were one's only child;
second, making no distinction between enemies and kin.
Third, attaining firm faith;
fourth, practicing the noble conduct. These are the four.
“There are four kinds of power for cultivating and gathering the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). What are these four?
The first is internal power;”
Second is the power of external conditions;
third is the power of causes;
fourth is the power of adornment.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva single-mindedly and with focused intent contemplates anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this is called internal power.
When they resolve their mind upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of transforming and delivering all sentient beings, this is called external power.
To have cultivated and accumulated virtuous conduct throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, serving as attendants to all Buddhas and bodhisattvas—this is called the power of causes (*hetubala*).

For a bodhisattva mahāsattva to delight in associating with virtuous friends, to listen to and receive the true Dharma, to contemplate its meaning, and to practice according to the teachings—this is called the power of adornment (*vyūhabala*).

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by means of these two powers, gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this is called the right mind, the unshakable mind, the non-retrogressive mind, and the non-reversing mind; namely, the power of internal strength and the power of causes.
If one arouses the bodhicitta through external forces or the power of adornments, this is called an improper mind, a wavering mind, a regressive mind, and a shifting mind.
There are four causes and conditions for a bodhisattva’s shifting mind.
What are the four?
First, the lack of inherent endowment;
second, association with evil friends.
Third, they lack compassion for all sentient beings;
fourth, they are unable to discern the faults and sufferings of birth and death.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas first give rise to the bodhicitta, there are two matters that are inconceivable.
What are these two? First, regarding all sentient beings, one forms the perception of them as kinsmen;
second, one has no perception of sentient beings.
A bodhisattva constantly observes with wisdom: "Who is a sentient being? To whom do sentient beings belong?
These are called the two causes.
These two mental states enable a bodhisattva to be without regression.
The initial arousal of bodhicitta consists of two kinds of mind. What are these two?
First, that which acts to bestow peace and security upon sentient beings; [the second is that which seeks unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment].
The second is to bestow happiness upon sentient beings.
To transform sentient beings through various wholesome dharmas so that they may leave behind unwholesome dharmas is called "peace and security.
To be able to provide sentient beings with material goods to relieve their poverty—namely, clothing, food, housing, bedding, and medicine for the sick—is called "happiness."
Non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas possess two kinds of mind. What are these two?
The first is the adornment of nature;
Second is the adornment of single-minded upholding.
Constantly mindful of the desire to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, this is called the adornment of nature.
Never retreating from the bodhicitta, and by virtue of this sincere mind being able to bestow peace and happiness upon all sentient beings, this is called the adornment of upholding.
There are two sources from which the merit produced by non-regressive bodhisattvas arises. What are these two?
The first is the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
Second, sentient beings undergo suffering.
These two matters are called the great accumulation of wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who has first resolved with a firm mind possesses two matters that surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
What are these two? First, the excellence of the cause;
second, the excellence of the fruit.
The wholesome dharmas cultivated by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has resolved upon bodhicitta are called the cause.
Attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through the practice of these wholesome dharmas as the cause is called the fruit.
Such causes and effects surpass those of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
A non-retrogressive bodhisattva has two great matters. What are these two?

First, having generated this mind, one immediately becomes a field of merit for all immeasurable sentient beings; one acts as their parent, elder, teacher, and preceptor, giving rise to great compassion. Because of this compassion, whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, or awake, one is constantly protected by the devas, just as a wheel-turning monarch is constantly protected by five hundred blue-clad spirits.
The non-retrogressive bodhisattva is also like this: out of compassion, even if they take on another body, they will have no suffering from illness.

Second, the bodhisattva who has resolved their mind is always one whom sentient beings delight to see, just as they do for their own parents; all sentient beings, in the presence of such a bodhisattva, find their physical, verbal, and mental actions to be gentle and free from evil.

These are called the two. When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has resolved upon the Bodhi-mind, they do not lose right mindfulness; they harbor no intent to harm toward sentient beings, they do not eat meat, and they do not deceive. They constantly teach and transform sentient beings through wholesome dharmas, such that these beings do not reject, abandon, or feel distress. Being able to discipline themselves, they are also able to discipline others; wherever they transform sentient beings, they are able to cause their meritorious karma to flourish and increase.
If, due to the causes and conditions of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*), they fall into the three evil realms, they are able to emerge from them swiftly.
Although they undergo suffering together with others, they do not give rise to feelings of bitterness or agony; rather, seeing those who suffer, their hearts give rise to compassion and pity.
A bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening (*bodhicitta*) accomplishes such immeasurable merit.
Chapter Four: On Benefiting Oneself and Others within the Bodhisattva-bhūmi. "When a bodhisattva mahāsattva resolves upon awakening, what is called the practice of awakening?"

If a bodhisattva, whether in this place or that, whether studying or teaching, does so for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—namely, through precepts, hearing, and reflection—this is called the practice of bodhi.
In what does a bodhisattva mahāsattva train?
There are seven points of training. What are these seven?
First, the internal meaning;
second, the external meaning;
third, the meaning of ultimate reality.
Fourth is the meaning of the inconceivable;
fifth is the meaning of disciplining sentient beings;
sixth is the meaning of maturing the Buddha-dharma within oneself.
Seventh is the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
These are called the seven.
What is their internal meaning?
The internal meaning consists of ten aspects. What are these ten?
The first is the meaning of reality;
Second is the meaning of benefiting others;
third is the meaning of subduing;
fourth is the meaning of peace and security.
Fifth is the meaning of happiness;
sixth is the meaning of cause;
seventh is the meaning of fruit.
Eighth is the meaning of the present;
ninth is the meaning of future lives;
tenth is the meaning of the ultimate.
That a bodhisattva-mahāsattva acts for the sake of others is called the internal meaning. As for the true meaning:

it is to know the nature of afflictions and their antidotes; to bestow one’s own means of happiness upon sentient beings; to constantly and resolutely cultivate and accumulate the unsurpassed right path;

and in whatever one seeks, to do so for the peace of sentient beings—once having obtained wealth and goods, to have no greed or stinginess, and to be able to make offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, parents, and teachers.

They seek the Buddha’s scriptures and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka across thousands of myriads of li; having obtained these teachings, they cause them to be widely disseminated without harboring any secretiveness or stinginess.

Although they understand profound meanings, they do not give rise to arrogance. To those seeking rebirth in the heavens, they speak of the benefits of observing the precepts; to those seeking to become wheel-turning kings, they speak of the virtue of giving; to those on the paths of the two vehicles, they speak of cultivating samādhi. For the sake of attaining great worldly rewards, they instruct others to make offerings to the Triple Gem and extensively cultivate meritorious deeds. To those with greedy minds, they speak of matters concerning greed; to those who are deceitful, they speak of matters concerning deception; and for those who act contrary to the Dharma, they serve as their servants.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has performed these deeds, this is called the meaning of reality.
Whatever benefit for oneself a bodhisattva-mahāsattva possesses, they dedicate it entirely to sentient beings; this is called the meaning of others.

Whatever the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva expounds is entirely for the purpose of destroying various heterodox and deviant views. Because those who lack cause and effect and violate the precepts do not perceive their own transgressions, he expounds upon the various faults of breaking the prohibitions; he expounds the Dharma in order to destroy the three evil realms.
If there are those who regress from dhyāna or wholesome dharmas, he expounds the Dharma so that they may not regress, and he expounds the Dharma in order to increase all wholesome dharmas.

He expounds the Dharma because he wishes to enable sentient beings to attain mastery, and he expounds the Dharma because he wishes to enable the sentient beings of the worlds of the ten directions to attain excellent spiritual powers (ṛddhipāda); this is called the meaning of "subduing" (vinaya).
The meaning of the internal is called the meaning of the external, and the meaning of the external is also called the meaning of the internal;
the meaning of both the internal and external is called the meaning of discipline, and the meaning of discipline is also called the meaning of both the internal and external.
The Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, eighteen unique qualities, great compassion, three foundations of mindfulness, five knowledges, and samādhis—these are called the meaning of reality.
The meaning of reality is called the meaning of the internal and external.
There are two kinds of the meaning of the internal and external. What are these two?
First is self-discipline;
second is disciplining others.
That Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas skillfully know the means (upāya) is what is meant by the meaning of "subduing" (vinaya).
All virtuous practices performed by a bodhisattva are termed the meaning of "subduing.
Furthermore, what is meant by the "internal and external meanings"?
There are five matters regarding the internal and external meanings.
What are the five?
First, purifying the bodies of others;
second, increasing the wholesome dharmas of others.
Third, benefit in the present life;
fourth, benefit in future lives;
fifth, destroying the afflictions of others.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, according to the amount of wholesome roots they have cultivated—whether much or little—teaches sentient beings so that they likewise attain what he has attained, this is called the meaning of "subduing" (vinaya).

Once the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has established himself in peace and security, he further bestows that peace and security upon sentient beings—whether it be the supramundane or the mundane, whether it be the realm of desire or meditative concentration; this is called the meaning of "peace and security."
The meaning of "peaceful security" (*kṣema*) is also called the meaning of "internal and external," the meaning of "subduing," and the meaning of "reality.

For a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the meaning of internal and external, there is that which is happiness in the present but not in future lives; there is that which is happiness in future lives but not in the present; there is that which is happiness both in the present and in future lives; and there is that which is neither happiness in the present nor in future lives.

Furthermore, there are four types of meaning regarding the internal and external: there are those who, having received the Dharma, experience happiness in the present life but suffering in future lives; there are those who, having received the Dharma, experience suffering in the present life but happiness in future lives; there are those who, having received the Dharma, experience happiness in the present life and also happiness in future lives; and there are those who, having received the Dharma, experience suffering in the present life and also suffering in future lives.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva speaks of nirvāṇa and mahāparinirvāṇa, the eightfold noble path, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the mundane and supramundane paths, this is called the meaning of peace and security.

The meaning of "peaceful security" (kṣema) is called the meaning of "internal and external"; the meaning of "internal and external" is called the meaning of "correctness" (samyaktva); the meaning of "correctness" is called the meaning of "unsurpassed," the meaning of "unconquerable," the meaning of "peaceful security," and the meaning of "eternal bliss."

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas experience constant bliss, they are able to bring about the meaning of the internal and external, the meaning of correctness, the meaning of harmony, and the meaning of peace and security.
What is meant by the meaning of happiness?
There are five kinds of the meaning of happiness. What are the five?
The first is the happiness of the cause.
Second, the pleasure of sensation;
third, the pleasure of the cessation of sensation;
fourth, the pleasure of seclusion.
Fifth is the bliss of awakening.

What is causal bliss? It is the bliss of sensation that arises dependent on internal and external contact; because contact serves as the causal condition, there is the experience of bliss, which is called causal bliss.
Practicing wholesome dharmas as a cause results in happiness in future lives; this is called "happiness as a cause.
What is "experienced happiness"?
Through causes and conditions, the body attains growth and the mind achieves tranquility; this is called "experienced happiness."
There are two kinds of those who experience pleasure. What are the two?
The first is that which is with outflows (sāsrava).
The second is the untainted (anāsrava).
There are two kinds of the untainted: first, the stage of training (śaikṣabhūmi); [and second, the stage beyond training].
The second is the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
There are three types of outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) states:
those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Because the three realms of existence possess internal and external sense bases, there are six types of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśa*).
These six contacts are twofold:
first, physical pleasure; [and second, mental pleasure].
The second is mental pleasure (*citta-sukha*).

That which functions together with the five consciousnesses is called bodily pleasure (*kāya-sukha*); that which functions together with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called mental pleasure.

Because one cultivates and accumulates the Noble Path to sever all sensations (*vedanā*), the qualities of the Path increase until no sensations remain; this is called the "pleasure of the cessation of sensation" (*vedanā-prahāṇa-sukha*).
Being eternally free from afflictions and having no physical or mental suffering is called the bliss of seclusion.
Because one experiences constant bliss, it is called the bliss of bodhi. Some say:
To claim that the state of non-ideation is called the "cessation of pleasure" is incorrect. Why is this so?
Because of the non-interruption of sensation.
There are four kinds of the renunciation of pleasure:
first, the pleasure of leaving the household life;
Second is the bliss of tranquility;
third is the bliss of cessation;
fourth is the bliss of awakening.
People of the world have much sorrow and suffering; to sever this suffering forever is called the joy of renunciation.

To sever craving in the desire realm is called the joy of tranquility. To sever afflictions forever is called the joy of abandonment. Because one experiences eternal bliss, it is called the joy of Bodhi.
That Bodhisattvas are always able to bestow happiness upon sentient beings is called the joy of bodhi.
That Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas themselves receive constant bliss and then transfer it to sentient beings is called the joy of bodhi.
Why is it called "causal happiness" (*hetusukha*)?
Because it is the cause of happiness, it is called causal happiness; it is not called the happiness of feeling (*veditasukha*).
That which is the happiness of feeling is not called causal happiness, but is called essential happiness (*prakṛtisukha*).
The "joy of abandonment" (prahāṇa-sukha) is not called the joy of cause, nor is it called the joy of feeling; it is called the joy of abandonment because many forms of pleasure have been abandoned.

The "joy of seclusion" (viveka-sukha) is not called the joy of cause, nor the joy of feeling, nor the joy of abandonment; because it contemplates the manifold faults and afflictions of birth and death, it is called the joy of wisdom (prajñā-sukha).

The bliss of bodhi is not called the bliss of causes, nor the bliss of sensation, nor the bliss of cessation, nor the bliss of detachment; because it is infinite and eternal, it is called the bliss of bodhi, the unsurpassed bliss, the boundless bliss, and the supreme bliss; it is also called the bliss of permanence and the bliss of tranquility.
That a bodhisattva mahāsattva can bestow these five kinds of happiness upon sentient beings is called the meaning of cause.

That a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly destroys the various evil karmas of sentient beings and demonstrates right action to them, and because of this right action they attain the unsurpassed path, is called the meaning of cause.

For the sake of sentient beings, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas undergo great suffering; because they undergo this suffering, they are able to discipline sentient beings—this is called the meaning of cause (*hetu*).

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas observe good and evil and are able to demonstrate to sentient beings matters of good and evil; because they reveal these things, they attain great wisdom, and because they attain wisdom, they are able to destroy great evils—this is called the meaning of cause.
“Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās by means of wisdom, until they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this is called the meaning of the fruit.”

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by destroying the mind of greed, is able to bestow upon sentient beings five kinds of happiness because of that destruction of greed; and because sentient beings obtain this happiness, it is termed the "meaning of fruit."
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, out of compassion for sentient beings, desires to cause all to experience happiness equal to his own; this is called the meaning of the internal and external.
There are three kinds of internal and external meanings, with three kinds of causes and three kinds of fruits:
the retributive cause and the retributive fruit.
The cause of merit is the fruit of merit;
the cause of wisdom is the fruit of wisdom.
What is meant by "retribution"?
There are eight kinds of retribution. What are the eight?
The first is long life;
Second, receiving a complete and perfect body;
third, attaining a noble lineage;
fourth, attaining mastery.
Fifth, his speech is subtle and refined;
sixth, he obtains a male body;
seventh, he obtains great strength.
Eighth is being invincible; these are the eight.
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate and accumulate a mind of loving-kindness, they attain long life; this is called the retribution of causes.
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas delight in giving clothing, food, dwellings, bedding, and medicinal requisites for the sick to sentient beings, they obtain a complete and perfect body.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas shatter their hearts of pride and offer worship and respect to their parents, teachers, elders, and those of virtuous character, they thereby attain birth into a noble lineage.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva acts in accordance with the Dharma and destroys what is contrary to the Dharma; therefore, he attains sovereign non-obstruction.
The Bodhisattva is truthful and does not deceive sentient beings; therefore, he attains exquisite eloquence.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly revile the five desires; for this reason, they obtain a male body.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas always delight in making offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; for this reason, their bodies obtain great power.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are constantly able to teach and transform all sentient beings and make offerings to the Triple Gem; therefore, they are able to attain that which none can surpass—this is called the karmic retribution.
Not harming sentient beings causes one’s life-span to increase; this is called the cause of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*).
By joyfully bestowing food, clothing, dwellings, bedding, and medicine for the sick upon sentient beings, the Bodhisattva thereby attains a complete body.
Because he can destroy all the arrogance of sentient beings, he attains a noble lineage.
Because he can eliminate the poverty and suffering of sentient beings, he attains sovereignty.
Because he can destroy the false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter of sentient beings, he attains exquisite speech.
By praising the male body and censuring the female body, one obtains birth among humans with a male body due to these two causes.
Furthermore, by remaining far removed from unrighteous desire, one obtains a male body.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas bestow pure food upon sentient beings and are able to provide rescue and relief to those who are in peril or fear, they therefore attain great strength for their bodies.
By upholding, reciting, and explaining the True Dharma, one is able to become invincible.
These constitute the eight kinds of retribution.
Furthermore, these eight kinds increase due to three causes.
What are the three?
First, purity of mind;
second, purity of adornment.
Third is the purity of the field of merit.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva seeks Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi with a sincere and single-minded heart, this is called purity of mind.
To make offerings to those who share one's studies, the same Dharma, and the same teacher is called purity of mind.
To feel joy in one's heart upon seeing or hearing of those who share one's studies and the same Dharma is called purity of mind.

One cultivates and accumulates the practices that assist the path to enlightenment, constantly delighting in receiving, upholding, copying, and reciting the Dharma-treasury of enlightenment, and further transforming sentient beings through this Dharma;
if there are those who do not accept it, one feels no sorrow or regret, nor does one cease one's efforts—this is called the adornment of purity.
These two purities are called the purity of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
What is the bodhisattva’s fruit of retribution?
The bodhisattva’s long life is called the fruit of retribution.
For what reason does a bodhisattva seek long life?
