This is called "impure things which are not to be given as alms."
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees a beggar coming and seeking something, he gives immediately; he never uses giving as a means to compel others to serve him.

He does not practice giving for the sake of celestial pleasures, nor does he practice giving for the sake of reputation, nor does he practice giving in order to seek a reward of gratitude. He does not practice giving for the sake of becoming a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), nor does he practice giving for the sake of becoming a Māra, a Deva, or a Brahmā. He does not practice giving for the sake of being honored, venerated, or respected by kings, elders, or householders.
One gives even a small amount, let alone a great deal.

One practices giving not for the sake of deception, nor for the purpose of destroying the retinue of others to establish one’s own retinue, nor even for the sake of villages, cities, towns, or kingdoms.

When a bodhisattva practices giving, he offers with his own hands to those from the senior monks down to the novices, whether they uphold the precepts or violate them, without ever feeling weary or disheartened.
When a bodhisattva gives, he never reviles or disparages the beggars, nor does he practice generosity out of pride.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva always gives rise to a mind of renunciation toward all things; whatever items he possesses are always for the sake of sentient beings.
If there is someone who knows with certainty that the bodhisattva has already relinquished them, and they take what belongs to themselves as their own portion, there is no fault in doing so.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees a seeker, his heart gives rise to joy, like a gravely ill person seeing a great and skilled physician. He allows them to take whatever they require as they please, rejoicing at three times: namely, before giving, while giving, and after having given. When the Bodhisattva practices giving, he always generates this mind.
If there are both the poor and the wealthy who come to beg, one should reflect:
"If I have many goods, I shall give equally to all; if they are few, I shall first relieve those in poverty and suffering."
"One who makes such a vow possesses the very cause for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
There are three types of stinginess: namely, inferior, middling, and superior."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first destroys inferior stinginess; by destroying inferior stinginess, he is able to destroy both middling and superior stinginess. Having himself destroyed stinginess, he further preaches the Dharma for destroying stinginess to sentient beings, thereby benefiting them through his teaching of the Dharma.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva may forcibly bestow material goods upon those who do not ask for them; if he lacks material wealth, he should employ skillful means to labor and seek it out before practicing such giving.
If there is no material gift to give, one should transform sentient beings by practicing the gift of the Dharma, asking:
"For what reason do you not practice giving?
If the person before one follows this by practicing generosity, one should feel deep joy, assist them with physical strength, and act as their deputy in managing the task.
Furthermore, for those who possess no material wealth, one should use wisdom to reveal the distinction between good and evil to all sentient beings.

Moreover, a bodhisattva does not bestow the authentic scriptures upon those with wrong views, nor does he peddle the sutras and vinaya for the sake of a livelihood; however, if there are those who can recite them, he should bestow them upon them. To be stingy and refuse to give them away is called "dharma-avarice."
If one is able to preach the Dharma but does not do so, this is also called stinginess regarding the Dharma.
If I am unable to bestow the Dharma upon others, how can I destroy the afflictions of sentient beings?
A bodhisattva never says such things as,
"I have no wealth now and cannot practice giving," nor does he become angry or vexed and burn his own mind with distress.
Using skillful means, he consoled the seeker, saying:
"I do not yet possess this; it does not accord with your purpose. Why is this?"
"At the time of first generating the mind of enlightenment, he vowed, 'I shall give to all sentient beings.

Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva hears that a seeker has arrived, he immediately goes out to welcome them and provides a seat; having met them, he speaks first with a kind intention, greeting them with gentle words, and provides whatever items they require, supplying each thing according to their needs."
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva first resolves to attain enlightenment, he says to himself:
"Whatever I now possess, I shall give as a gift to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions, as well as to all sentient beings."
"It is, for example, like a disciple who offers his robes, bowl, and possessions to a teacher; although the teacher does not accept them, this disciple gains immeasurable merit.

It is the same for a Bodhisattva: whatever objects he offers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, even though the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not accept them, they cause the donor to obtain immeasurable merit that constantly follows the Bodhisattva as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates his own wealth and possessions as being like those entrusted to him by the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions, he knows that the Buddhas and bodhisattvas have no mind of stinginess regarding these things; therefore, the bodhisattva freely bestows them upon sentient beings according to their wishes.
Furthermore, one should deeply contemplate those to whom one ought not to give, and should admonish and instruct them thus:
"Such objects truly do not belong to me; they are the property of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
By using gentle speech to instruct and console those who seek [his help], he does not cause them to feel resentment.
Therefore, the bodhisattva achieves and fulfills both the giving of material wealth and the giving of the Dharma.
Having fulfilled these two types of giving, he understands nature, understands causes, understands results, and understands distinctions.
If a bodhisattva gives to those who are hostile or hateful, it is due to the causal condition of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
If he gives to those who are suffering, it is due to the causal condition of compassion (*karuṇā*).
If he gives to those who possess virtue, it is due to the causal condition of sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
If one gives to one's retinue, brothers, servants, and employees, it is because of the causal conditions of relinquishment;
this is called the bodhisattva’s giving through wisdom.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva understands that which harms the mind of giving.
There are four types of those who harbor thoughts that obstruct giving:
first, because they have not practiced giving for immeasurable lifetimes;
second, because their wealth and possessions are meager.
Third, because of being greedily attached to fine things;
fourth, because of not seeking the wholesome retribution of future lives.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees a seeker who possesses abundant wealth and does not immediately give rise to the mind of giving, this indicates that the Bodhisattva has not practiced the mind of giving throughout immeasurable lifetimes.
At that time, the bodhisattva should reflect within himself by means of the power of wisdom:
"It is because I have not practiced giving since immeasurable ages past that I have not yet brought forth the resolve."

At this time, I possess abundant wealth and there are those who seek it; if I do not bestow it as a gift, my stinginess will increase further in future lives, and I shall never be compliant with or cultivate a mind of generosity.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva sees that the wealth of a petitioner is meager and thus does not immediately give rise to the intention to give, the bodhisattva should further reflect with the power of wisdom:

"Due to the causes and conditions of my immeasurable evil karma, throughout immeasurable lifetimes my body has belonged to others, and I have endured great suffering—hunger, thirst, cold, and heat—without being able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings. It is because of these karmic conditions that my body possesses so little wealth."
If I do not practice giving now, my poverty and suffering in future lives will only increase further.
By giving these few items to others now, although I shall endure poverty and hardship, I will ultimately never fall into the sufferings of the three evil realms.
Reflecting in this way, one can destroy the stingy mind that clings to even the slightest thing.

Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva sees a supplicant and, out of attachment to a fine object, does not immediately give rise to the intention to give, the Bodhisattva should at that time reflect with wisdom:
"I perceive what is impermanent as permanent; I perceive what is without 'mine' as being 'mine'."
"If I do not practice giving, my greed and attachment will increase; this would be my perversion.
For this reason, the bodhisattva is able to destroy the mind that clings to desirable things.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva does not practice giving for the sake of seeking a karmic reward; at that time, the bodhisattva should reflect as follows:
"All dharmas are impermanent and lack fixedness; if they were permanent and fixed, there would be no need for giving.
Why is this? Because there would be no cause and effect."
"Because all things are impermanent, there is cause and effect.
If one does not practice giving now, how could one ever attain the fruit of the path to Bodhi?
For this reason, the Bodhisattva is able to destroy the mind that seeks a result and practices the gift of generosity.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva understands the four inversions; since phenomena have no fixed nature and possess no characteristic of permanence, he is thus able to destroy the four malicious and evil minds.
Furthermore, with his inner body in tranquility, the Bodhisattva reflects with focused thought, constantly forming this thought:
"If I possess wealth, I shall use it to make offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or give it as alms to the Dharma and the Sangha."
This is called the bodhisattva’s gift of wisdom.
Whether possessing wealth or lacking it, one should always maintain such focused reflection; the same applies to the gift of Dharma. This is called the "gift of all."
"What is meant by 'the bodhisattva’s ability to give what is difficult to give'?
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva possesses even a small amount of goods and constantly bestows them as gifts, this is called giving what is difficult to give."

To give to others those things which one holds dear and to which one is deeply attached—things acquired through diligent seeking over immeasurable lifetimes, or obtained through great skillful means and the expenditure of physical labor—is called "difficult giving."
What is meant by "giving everything oneself"?

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva either practices giving himself or instructs his parents, brothers, wife, children, kinsmen, servants, and slaves to practice giving, this is called "giving everything oneself."
What is the giving of a virtuous person?

If a son of good family gives with a virtuous mind, with a mind of faith, with a sincere mind, with his own hand, at the proper time, and having acquired wealth in accordance with the Dharma—this is called the giving of a virtuous person.
What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing all-encompassing giving?
Because they do not seek karmic retribution, it is called practicing all-encompassing giving.
Because they give constantly, it is called practicing all-encompassing giving.
Because it is given as a field of merit, it is called "giving in all practices.
Because it is given without regard for whether the recipient is a field of merit or not a field of merit, it is called "giving in all practices.
Because it is given without regard for whether the time is appropriate or inappropriate, it is called "giving in all practices."
Not considering whether wealth and goods are suitable for giving or unsuitable for giving is called "giving in all circumstances.
What is the bodhisattva’s giving for the sake of removal?

If there are sentient beings suffering from hunger and thirst, one practices giving to remove these conditions: giving clothing to those who are cold, giving vehicles to those seeking vehicles, giving necklaces to those seeking necklaces, and likewise providing ointments, powdered incense, various flowers, lamps, dwellings, bedding, and medicine for the sick—this is called giving for the sake of removal.
What is the giving that benefits both oneself and others?
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva bestows material goods or the Dharma upon others, they are able to bring about happiness for both themselves and sentient beings in two worlds.

To constantly bestow upon sentient beings the joy of fearlessness—namely, to provide rescue and relief from tigers, wolves, lions, water, fire, kings, calamities, and hostile bandits—is called the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*).
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the gift of Dharma, whatever they teach is from the outset free of error; this is called the gift of Dharma.
Being well able to instruct and admonish all sentient beings, this is called the pure gift of Dharma.
The material gift (*āmiṣadāna*) of a bodhisattva benefits the present life; however, one who practices the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*) is able to benefit both the present and future lives.

Furthermore, there are cases where a material gift may cause suffering for sentient beings in the present life, whereas the gift of Dharma is not like this, as it can bring about happiness in both the present and future lives.
The gift of material wealth is impure; the gift of the Dharma is pure.
One who practices the gift of material wealth is not said to be boundless; the gift of the Dharma is called the boundless gift.
Material gifts are easy to obtain; the gift of the Dharma is difficult to encounter.
This is called giving for the benefit of oneself and others.
What is meant by "tranquil giving"?
There are ten kinds of tranquil giving.
What are the ten? First, unimpeded giving;
second, giving free from error.
Third, giving that is not for the sake of adornment;
fourth, giving without a haughty mind;
fifth, giving without an attached mind.
Sixth is giving without shame;
seventh is giving without sorrow;
eighth is giving without a frowning face.
Ninth is giving without seeking a reward for one's kindness;
tenth is unimpeded giving that does not seek karmic retribution.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices giving, he is not obstructed by any worldly affairs or busy engagements. Although he knows the mind of the seeker, he feels no distress or delay; rather, he is able to relinquish his possessions swiftly according to what is requested. This is called unimpeded giving.
Regarding the giving that is free from error, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva never thinks:
"Giving has no retribution; there is no retribution for good or evil. Nor does he think:

"To practice giving by killing living beings and thereby obtain a virtuous retribution, as Vāsava has taught"—because one does not become greedily attached to the causes and conditions of such giving, one attains worldly happiness as well as the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is called "unerring giving."

Regarding non-ornamental giving: a bodhisattva mahāsattva never gathers objects for the sake of fine adornment before practicing generosity; rather, they give immediately upon obtaining anything and never hoards or accumulates.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva deeply understands that the two dharmas of wealth and life are impermanent and difficult to preserve.
When someone comes to seek [something], he gives it to them immediately upon meeting them, never saying:
"I shall give it to you only after I have adorned it. Why is this?
One who gives for the sake of adornment cannot be said to adorn *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If a bodhisattva practices giving while waiting for adornment, it causes sentient beings to undergo great suffering;
this is called "unadorned giving.

Regarding "giving without a haughty mind": when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees a petitioner, they give rise to a humble mind and do not praise themselves, saying, "I am a donor. They do not seek gratitude or recompense, nor do they practice giving for the sake of a reputation for surpassing others; this is called "giving without a haughty mind."
Regarding giving with an unattached mind: a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not cling to reputation.

A Bodhisattva skillfully contemplates this reputation as being like space, like the wind, or like the fibers within a lotus root. [He reflects: "If I were to seek fame when practicing giving, I would not attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, a Bodhisattva seeking Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi does not seek reputation; this is called giving with an unattached mind.
Regarding "generosity without shame": when practicing generosity, one feels joy at the three times [of preparation, execution, and completion];

this is called generosity without shame. Regarding "generosity without sorrow": when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives away that which is most cherished, they feel no regret; for this reason there is no sorrow, and it is called generosity without sorrow.

Regarding "giving without a frowning face": the Bodhisattva universally observes all sentient beings with a mind of equanimity, never failing to look upon them with joy; this is called giving without a frowning face.

Giving without seeking a reward for one's kindness means giving out of compassion, cultivating loving-kindness, bestowing peace and happiness, and without seeking any recompense; this is called giving without seeking a reward for one's kindness.

Regarding giving without seeking karmic retribution: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices giving, they do not seek the body of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, nor the realms of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Māra Heaven, or the Brahmā Heaven, nor mastery over wealth and possessions.

Why is this? Because the bodhisattva deeply contemplates conditioned phenomena as being like a plantain tree; therefore, when giving, they do not seek a karmic reward. For this reason, it is called "giving without seeking a reward."
These ten matters enable a bodhisattva to fully accomplish the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) and attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Chapter Eleven: The Chapter on Ethics (*Śīla*) within the Bodhisattvabhūmi. "What is called the ethical discipline (*śīla*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
There are nine kinds of precepts:
first, the precept of essential nature;
second, the precept of all-encompassing conduct; [and so forth].
Third is the difficult precept;
fourth is the precept of all self-restraint;
fifth is the precept of virtuous persons.
Sixth is the precept of all practices;
seventh is the precept of elimination;
eighth is the precept of benefiting oneself and others.
Ninth is the precept of tranquility.
Regarding the precept of intrinsic nature, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with the precept of intrinsic nature, there are four merits:
first, receiving it from another with a pure mind;

Second, if one’s mind is impure and one violates the precepts one has received, one should, with a sincere heart, feel shame and remorse and perform repentance; having repented, one should focus the mind and never dare to transgress again.

When a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva receives the precepts from another, they give rise to a sense of shame and remorse; because of this shame and remorse in their heart, they protect and uphold them without violation.
If the mind is impure and one violates the precepts one has received, because of shame and remorse in the heart, one does not dare to conceal them even for a single night.

If a Bodhisattva violates the precepts and a single night has passed, should they wish to repent, they should not simply perform repentance for a single transgression; rather, they should perform repentance for immeasurable transgressions occurring at every moment of thought.
Why is this? If one were to repent for multiple transgressions as if they were a single transgression, it could not be called repentance, and the recipient would incur an offense.
When a Bodhisattva receives and upholds the precepts from another, there are four matters:
First, shame and remorse;
second, maintaining with a sincere mind—wherein the bodhisattva-mahāsattva maintains the precepts with a sincere mind and never gives rise to a thought of violation;
third, having received them, guarding and upholding them with a single-minded focus.
Fourth is upholding with a pure mind.
When a bodhisattva is endowed with these four meritorious precepts, they are able to perform four tasks.
What are these four?
First, not committing offenses;
second, immediately repenting should one commit them;
third, giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse.
Fourth is the absence of regret;
this is called the natural precept (*prakṛti-śīla*).

The Bodhisattva of natural precepts is said to possess the true precept, the precept for the benefit of oneself and others, the precept for the welfare of sentient beings, the precept for the purpose of benefiting sentient beings, the precept for increasing the ranks of humans and devas, and the precept of immeasurable merit.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes such precepts, they give rise to a mind of compassion and are thus able to teach and transform immeasurable sentient beings.

If a bodhisattva does not repent for adventitious afflictions, they should constantly praise the observance of precepts and censure the breaking of them for others, explaining the faults and transgressions incurred by those who violate the prohibitions.
If one can act in this way, although they may be said to have committed an offense, the transgression is slight; furthermore, they will ultimately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is called the morality of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śīla).
"Regarding 'all precepts' (sarva-śīla): those undertaken and maintained by both householders and renunciants are called all precepts.
There are three kinds of precepts for householders and renunciants:
first, the precepts (śīla);..."
Second is the precept of receiving wholesome dharmas;
third is the precept of practicing for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
What is meant by "precept"?
The so-called sevenfold assembly of precepts consists of:
bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to receive and uphold the bodhisattva precepts, they should first purify their mind and receive the seven kinds of precepts.
These seven kinds of precepts are precisely the purification of the mind that leads toward the bodhisattva precepts.
Just as people of the world who wish to invite a great king must first thoroughly clean and maintain their residence,
these seven types of precepts are all received by both laypeople and monastics.
The Bodhisattva precepts are likewise thus: they are received by both those who have left the household life and those who remain within it, and are therefore called "precepts.
What is meant by receiving the "precepts for wholesome dharmas"?

Regarding the precept of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-śīla*): when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having distanced themselves from the seven types of precepts, cultivates the ten kinds of wholesome dharmas of body, speech, and mind for the sake of awakening, this is called undertaking the precept of wholesome dharmas.

Regarding body, speech, and mind: when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has established themselves in the stage of ethical discipline (*śīla-bhūmi*), they engage in reading, reciting, copying, analyzing, and explaining [the teachings]; they cultivate and develop *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* through contemplation; they reverently serve, honor, respect, and praise their teachers, preceptors, elders, and those of virtuous merit; they provide for them from time to time by attending to their needs, performing errands, and carrying their robes and bowls on their behalf when they are ill, aged, or exhausted from travel; when they see those preaching the Dharma or chanting the scriptures, they exclaim "Excellent! in praise; and upon seeing those who uphold the precepts, they protect them with all their might, praise such discipline, and make the vow that all sentient beings may likewise maintain pure ethical conduct.
Seeing those who violate the precepts, they give rise to deep compassion, reprimanding them with skillful words and instructing them to repent.
Regarding all the wholesome deeds performed through their actions of body, speech, and mind, they universally make vows to dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

While one possesses strength of body, speech, and mind, one should diligently make offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; one should practice with diligent vigor in order to increase wholesome dharmas, and cultivate heedfulness in order to attain all wholesome dharmas.

One should always, with a sincere mind, recollect the precepts and guard them, subduing the sense faculties; be moderate in eating and drinking, take no pleasure in sleep, and engage in the reading and recitation of the scriptures during the first and last watches of the night. One should keep the Triple Gem in mind, draw near to virtuous friends, delight in hearing their teachings, and examine one’s own faults. Having recognized them, one should repent and give rise to deep shame and remorse. With a sincere heart, one should recollect [the precepts] and not transgress them again, confessing and repenting before the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—those who share the same teacher, the same Dharma, the same precepts, and the same study. This is called receiving the precept of wholesome dharmas.
There are eleven kinds of those who practice precepts for the benefit of sentient beings.
If there are sentient beings who wish to cultivate goodness, one immediately goes to exhort and encourage them, acting as their companion and performing wholesome deeds together with them.
If there are those who tend to the sick, he also goes to encourage and exhort them to become their companions.
If there are sentient beings who wish to understand the meaning of worldly and world-transcending dharmas, he uses skillful means to explain them for them.
Wherever there is one who has received kindness, one should remember it and desire to repay it.

To repay it means to firmly uphold the prohibitive precepts, to read, recite, and transcribe the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and to contemplate their true meaning, analyzing and explaining them.

They are able to rescue sentient beings from various fears—namely, those caused by lions, tigers, wolves, water, fire, kings, and bandits—and protect sentient beings so that they may remain far removed from such terrors.

If there are sentient beings who have lost their kin, abandoned their wealth, or experience sorrow and grief due to separation from those they love, he is able to preach the Dharma for them so that they may be freed from suffering and affliction.
If there are sentient beings who are impoverished and suffering, he is able to bestow upon them whatever they require.
He accepts and maintains disciples for the sake of upholding the Dharma, not for the sake of fame or profit.
For the sake of upholding the Dharma, they frequent the fourfold assembly and engage in discussion with them, not for the sake of gain or sustenance.
For the sake of upholding the Dharma, they associate with kings, ministers, and elders, not for the sake of gain or sustenance.
One should not, for the sake of a donor, comply with worldly sentiments to perform unrighteous actions of body, speech, or mind; nor should one visit other households at improper times.
There are improper times for both those living at home and those who have gone forth.

"Inappropriate times" refers to the time of greed, the time of anger, and the time of delusion; the time of great winds, the time of heavy rain, the time of weddings, the time of festive gatherings, and the time of setting out on a journey. Excluding these aforementioned inappropriate times is what is called "the appropriate time."
According to the merits of the wholesome dharmas they have attained, they teach them all to sentient beings with a mind free from greed or envy.
Seeing those who violate the precepts, they give rise to deep compassion and instruct them with pure hearts and kind words, just as parents instruct their children:
"That which you have transgressed should be confessed and repented according to the Dharma."

If they do not accept [the invitation], it is improper to provide them with their former supplies or compel them to perform manual labor; instead, they should be censured and penalized according to the specific circumstances.
If they still refuse to accept, they should be expelled from the monastery in order to cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish.

If one cannot be taught, rebuked, punished, or expelled, and thus continues to dwell together [with the community], this is called breaking the precepts; such a person is neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
Within the Buddha-dharma, they are called a stench, a caṇḍāla, and a butcher.
Even those such as caṇḍālas and butchers, though they perform evil deeds, cannot destroy the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, nor will they necessarily fall into the three evil realms.
If a teacher is unable to instruct and admonish their disciples, they destroy the Buddha-dharma and will certainly fall into hell.
To gather and accumulate a following for the sake of reputation is called wrong view; such a person is called a disciple of Māra.

One who does not keep disciples cannot destroy the True Dharma of the Tathāgata; however, one who keeps evil disciples destroys the Buddha-Dharma, and because they destroy the Buddha-Dharma, they are called disciples of Māra.
To gather and maintain a following for the sake of gain and offerings is called wrong view.

Only if one possesses supernormal powers, knowledge of the minds of others, and knowledge of past lives can one then use the Bodhisattva precepts to transform others; such a person is then able to maintain evil disciples.
Why is this? Because they know skillful means; because they know skillful means, they destroy unwholesome dharmas and reveal wholesome dharmas.

If there is a bhikṣu who does not possess these three kinds of wisdom, yet claims, "I possess these three kinds of wisdom and am capable of accepting and maintaining evil disciples," it should be known that such a person commits a grave offense. To be free from such matters is called the precept for benefiting others.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas accomplish such precepts—the precepts of goodness, the precepts of benefiting others, and the precepts of benefiting others—they are called the "excellent precepts" which encompass all precepts; they are called the "precepts that reach the other shore"; they are called the "precepts of liberation"; they are called the "unsurpassed precepts"; they are called the "precepts without cause or effect"; they are called the "precepts of permanence, bliss, self, and purity"; they are called the "ultimately boundless precepts"; and they are called the "precepts of all skillful means."
If a bodhisattva can sincerely recollect the bodhisattva precepts, they surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
If they can fully possess the bodhisattva precepts, they also surpass bodhisattvas of the sixth stage.

If there is a bodhisattva who renounces the position of a wheel-turning monarch, leaves the household life to study the Way and receive the precepts of liberation, casting aside the five desires as if discarding snot or spittle, neither thinking of them, nor seeking them, nor giving rise to regret or attachment—even regarding the pleasures of the five desires in the heavens, it is likewise so.

One does not observe the prohibitive precepts for the sake of experiencing pleasure as a human or deva; rather, one contemplates the pleasures of the five desires as being like a poisonous snake or the three evil realms, and when receiving offerings from others, one views them as vomited food, with a mind free from craving or attachment.
If worldly people who receive the pleasures, gains, and reputations of humans and devas observe the prohibitive precepts, you should know that such persons are not said to have attained the precepts.
One who has perfected the precepts—whether dwelling among the Sangha or in a secluded place—is called "serene."

Because one cannot transform and guide sentient beings, one cannot protect the Dharma; because one cherishes body and life, one cannot protect the Dharma; because one craves gain and offerings, one cannot protect the Dharma; because of enmity and resentment, one cannot protect the Dharma; because of fear, one cannot protect the Dharma; because of arrogance, one cannot protect the Dharma; because one does not receive the Dharma, one cannot protect the Dharma; because of a heart of pity and compassion, one cannot protect the Dharma; and because of dread, shame, and embarrassment, one cannot protect the Dharma. These are called breaking the precepts and are termed lack of tranquility.
If there are those who become complacent regarding the precepts, it should be known that such persons do not truly uphold the precepts.

One should know that because of the precepts, one attains the immeasurable samādhis of all bodhisattvas; if one lacks the precepts, then immeasurable samādhis will not increase. Therefore, for the sake of samādhi, one should guard and maintain the prohibitive precepts.

A bodhisattva who upholds the bodhisattva precepts would rather lose their body and life than ever listen to or employ unrighteous speech; they do not dwell with evil persons nor give rise to or entertain any evil thoughts or observations, and should such thoughts arise, they feel shame and remorse in their hearts, reproaching themselves and repenting.
If one is sitting among the assembly and hears evil words, evil matters, evil teachings, evil sounds, or evil meanings, one should immediately rise and leave.
If one has the power to restrain them, yet remains indifferent, fails to instruct or rebuke them, and departs, this is called an offense.
If one is unable to restrain oneself by force yet remains listening, this is also called a transgression.
If one attains the intention not to listen, this is called upholding the precepts; if one forms the intention to listen, this is called breaking the precepts.
If one delights in listening [to the Dharma], this is called breaking the precepts; if one does not delight in listening, this is called upholding the precepts.
One who gives rise to a mind of regret is called one who upholds the precepts; one whose mind feels no regret is called one who breaks the precepts.

A bodhisattva who upholds the bodhisattva precepts never thinks to himself, "The precepts I have received were obtained solely from my preceptor or teacher"; rather, he reflects that they were received from the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
If I were to receive the precepts from a teacher or a preceptor, it would not be called the Bodhisattva precept;
only that which is received from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions is called the Bodhisattva precept.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva discriminates among the eighteen schools of the Saṃgha, they are not said to have obtained the bodhisattva precepts;
if they can regard them all equally as disciples of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions, they are said to have obtained the bodhisattva precepts.

If one contemplates that all beings are disciples of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions dwelling upon the Great Ground, then by virtue of the causes and conditions of dwelling upon the Great Ground, they shall all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The realm of sentient beings is inconceivable; the dharma-realm of sentient beings is inconceivable; the nature of sentient beings is inconceivable; the precepts of sentient beings are inconceivable. Since I have not yet attained all-knowledge, how can I differentiate these eighteen schools?
If I were to engage in conceptual discrimination, I would be unable to attain all-encompassing precepts, unimpeded precepts, and unsurpassed precepts.
Because I am able to contemplate in this manner, I attain the bodhisattva precepts.

Just as the precepts attained by Bodhisattvas of the past, if a Bodhisattva can contemplate in this way, they will obtain immeasurable and boundless merit; they will be able to know the minds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, and they will also know that those who fully possess the Bodhisattva precepts attain the Unsurpassed Way.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate the Buddhas of the past and the bodhisattvas who, before they had attained the accomplishment of the unsurpassed path, were fully possessed of afflictions while training in the bodhisattva precepts, and having fully accomplished them, attained the unsurpassed path.

This body of mine is also a sentient being; it likewise possesses the five aggregates and is endowed with afflictions. It also receives the bodhisattva precepts and cultivates the accumulation of bodhi; it must also attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. I am also able to discipline the evils of body, speech, and mind, and I shall certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

A bodhisattva who upholds the bodhisattva precepts maintains a sincere and focused mind, reflecting upon his own faults rather than proclaiming the shortcomings of others; seeing those who commit evil deeds, he feels no resentment, and seeing those who violate the precepts, he gives rise to compassion rather than anger or vexation.

When a bodhisattva who upholds the bodhisattva precepts is struck or pelted by an evil person, or is subjected to harsh words and verbal abuse with fists, knives, or staves, they do not give rise to an evil mind or respond with coarse speech toward that person.
If a bodhisattva studies the bodhisattva precepts, there are five forms of non-negligence:
first, observing one's past transgressions and repenting according to the Dharma;
second, observing potential future transgressions and repenting according to the Dharma.
Third, observing present transgressions and repenting according to the Dharma;
fourth, maintaining a sincere mind and firmly upholding the precepts without thoughts of violation;
fifth, having committed a transgression, repenting with a sincere mind.
These are called the five forms of non-negligence.

A bodhisattva who upholds the bodhisattva precepts should conceal all their merits, confess all committed offenses, have few desires and be content, endure all sufferings, always delight in tranquility with a mind free from regret, not be self-exalting or frivolous, and cultivate the practice of cessation as well as subtle conduct to destroy wrong livelihoods.
A bodhisattva who accomplishes such dharmas is said to abide in the bodhisattva precepts.

A bodhisattva who receives and studies the bodhisattva precepts does not dwell on the pleasures of the five desires of the past, does not seek the pleasures of the five desires of the future, and does not give rise to attachment toward the five desires of the present. They always delight in tranquility, destroy evil thoughts and observations, and achieve the full perfection of heedful conduct.
All sentient beings dare not treat them with contempt; they have accomplished patience and possess a pure mind.

Those who study the pure precepts do not spare their own bodies or lives, nor do they begrudge their wealth; they skillfully understand the causes and conditions of breaking the precepts and afflictions, and are well able to subdue the afflictions of breaking the precepts, to subdue anger, and to subdue the hearts of sentient beings that cause harm. They thoroughly understand perversion and know the causes and effects of the wholesome; because they know the causes and effects of the wholesome, they seek them with a diligent mind.

It destroys the inversion of faithlessness regarding the causes and effects of good, and contemplates all phenomena as being impermanent and lacking the characteristics of self; it destroys sentient beings' inversions of perceiving the impermanent as permanent, the miserable as pleasant, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure.
They cultivate and train in virtuous precepts, accumulating the causes of generosity, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

Because Bodhisattvas uphold the precepts for the benefit of others, they teach and transform sentient beings to cause them to practice wholesome deeds; they act as companions to those who cultivate goodness together with them, and they constantly instruct sentient beings to make offerings to the Triple Gem.
If they see those who are separated, they use skillful means to bring them back together.
Seeing those afflicted by illness and suffering, they personally attend to their needs.
Seeing the blind and sightless, they provide them with necessary clothing and food, guide them along the path, and skillfully preach the Dharma for them.
Seeing those who were deaf, he drew figures on the ground to demonstrate the meaning.
Seeing those who were lame, he provided them with vehicles; if there were no vehicles, he would carry them himself.
Seeing those who were greedy and suffered because of their greed, he was able to preach the Dharma for them so that they might eliminate the suffering of greed.
The same applies to anger, ignorance, doubt, and so forth.

When they are weary from traveling on the road, one carries their burdens for them, provides them with water, grain, bedding, and other necessities, and attends to them by massaging their bodies to restore their well-being.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who delight in committing sinful deeds; when a bodhisattva perceives them, he should skillfully expound the Dharma with excellent phrasing and excellent meaning, where the phrasing and sentences are well-joined, and where the sequence of words and meanings increases wholesome dharmas until the exposition of the meaning is complete and perfect. For the sake of adorning the path to Bodhi, he employs skillful means to teach them how to destroy their evil karma.
For those who are stingy and greedy, he preaches the Dharma for breaking through stinginess, so that their wholesome dharmas and material wealth may increase.

If there are sentient beings who do not believe in the Buddha-dharma, he skillfully preaches the Dharma to inspire faith in them. He preaches the Dharma in order to destroy the afflictions and evil karma of sentient beings and enable them to attain the Eightfold Noble Path.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva trains in the bodhisattva precepts and makes great vows, they act to destroy the various evil and false views of sentient beings; they recognize kindness and repay it; they practice patience, speak gentle words, and greet others with courtesy before they speak; they make offerings to teachers, elders, and those of virtue; and they are able to dispel sorrow and fear—namely, those caused by lions, tigers, wolves, water, fire, kings, calamities, and hostile bandits.

If there are sentient beings who have lost their parents, brothers, kinsmen, wives, children, or servants; who have been forced to abandon their wealth and property; or who suffer from the pain of separation from those they love—[the Bodhisattva] is able to employ skillful means to preach the Dharma to them as appropriate, thereby eliminating their suffering and distress.

He constantly bestows upon sentient beings whatever they require, namely: clothing, food and drink, housing, bedding, medicine for the sick and the emaciated, as well as incense, flowers, necklaces, lamps, candles, and other such items.

If a bodhisattva who has received and maintains the bodhisattva precepts keeps disciples but cannot skillfully teach them the Dharma or provide guidance to subdue their greed, anger, and ignorance; if they cannot provide them with clothing, food and drink, housing, and medicine; if they cannot seek out virtuous and generous donors on their behalf; or if, having obtained wealth through skillful preaching of the essential Dharma for the sake of a donor, they cannot share it equally—then one should know that such a person keeps disciples for the sake of reputation, and this is not called practicing according to the Dharma.

If one can, according to the occasion, teach and instruct through the Dharma—acting as their nature, their strength, and their Bodhisattva-piṭaka; desiring to bring them to fulfillment in the Bodhisattva precepts, to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, and to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—this is called a Bodhisattva truly taking on disciples, and not for the sake of reputation.
When a bodhisattva undertakes the training in the bodhisattva precepts, they should first observe and understand the nature and dispositions (*dhātu*) of sentient beings before dwelling with them.

To transform their nature and dispositions, they should preach the Dharma as appropriate and act in accordance with their inclinations, thereby subduing them so that they cease to commit various evils. They should be able to destroy unwholesome dharmas and increase wholesome dharmas; they should be able to bestow whatever material things are required. Upon seeing those who commit evil, they should give rise to deep compassion; upon encountering those who do not accept their words, they should feel profound sorrow and distress. Regarding the various evil karmas they themselves have committed, they should not give rise to grief in their mind, but rather, when seeing others committing such acts, they should especially give rise to compassionate pity.

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva is able to swiftly subdue their own evil of body, speech, and mind, opening the heart to repent; this is due to the power of the causal conditions of their great wisdom.
A bodhisattva may also perform unwholesome deeds of body and speech for the sake of others, in order to subdue the unwholesome karma of others and to accord with their minds.
At times, a bodhisattva manifests the experience of pleasure and joy for the purpose of disciplining others.
For the sake of others, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not prematurely attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Although the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva follows along with sentient beings, he does not slight them, nor laugh at them, nor strike them, nor revile them; he does not speak of their faults, nor praise his own virtues to exalt himself above others. He does not associate with people in an improper manner, yet it is not that he does not associate with them at all; even when he does associate, he does not do so at an inappropriate time. He does not speak of the failings of those whom others love and cherish, nor does he praise those whom they do not love. He does not speak of profound meanings to those whose spiritual faculties he does not yet know. He does not solicit gifts from others, and even if others give much, he should give rise to contentment; his heart finds no pleasure in receiving offerings from others, but always delights in giving away wealth to provide for others, and always delights in praising the good deeds of others.

One does not preach the precepts to those who see transgressions; one does not praise faith to those who lack it; one does not praise giving to those with greedy hearts; one does not praise extensive learning to those who do not delight in recitation; and one does not praise wisdom to those who are mired in the darkness of ignorance.

If one praises the precepts to those who have violated the prohibitions, they will feel neither joy nor pleasure, but will instead give rise to anger and a sense of shame. Because of that anger, they will conceive a great evil mind toward the Buddha’s Dharma and its teacher; and because of that evil mind, their rebirth in hell will increase.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva were to act in such a manner, they would be providing sentient beings with the causes and conditions for hell, and thus cannot be called a bodhisattva.
It is likewise when one preaches the Dharma according to one's own whims, even praising wisdom to those who are deluded.
If there is a bodhisattva who possesses great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), only such a person is able to preach the bodhisattva precepts to those who lack faith. Why is this?
This person, by means of their supernormal powers, manifests to them the hot hells, the cold hells, the great hells,
and the minor hells, and further says:
"Why do you now not believe my words?"
Observe these evil fruits: what is created among human beings is made to be experienced in hell.
If you now still do not believe in such Bodhisattva precepts, you shall again obtain such evil fruits.
When those who lacked faith saw this, their hearts were struck with alarm and fear, and they immediately conceived faith.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, for the sake of those without faith, manifest the form of a rākṣasa through their supernormal powers and say:
"I am now seeking out all those who lack faith, intending to take their lives; as for those who have faith, I shall protect and cherish them."
When those who lack faith see or hear this, they immediately give rise to fear; because of that fear, they come to believe in the Bodhisattva precepts.
Furthermore, by means of supernatural power, he manifests the form of Guhyapada (Vajrapāṇi) holding a vajra-pestle and speaks these words:
"If there be anyone who does not believe in the Bodhisattva precepts, I shall shatter their head into seven pieces."
Those who did not believe, upon seeing and hearing this, immediately gave rise to fear; because of that fear, they then came to believe him.

Furthermore, by means of supernormal powers, he manifested various bodies—sometimes a single body, sometimes many bodies; he manifested bodies as trees, mountains, rivers, and so forth, as well as unobstructed bodies, large bodies, and small bodies, with water and fire issuing from his body.
When those who lacked faith saw this, they immediately asked:
"What are the fruits of such deeds as these? He replied:
"All these are the fruits of the bodhisattva precepts.
Upon hearing this, that person conceived great faith in the bodhisattva precepts.
If one lacks supernormal powers and yet preaches the bodhisattva precepts to such a person who lacks faith, one incurs immeasurable sin.
"Immeasurable sins" refers to those experienced over immeasurable lifetimes; hence they are called "immeasurable.
Even the five heinous crimes are insufficient as a comparison. Why is this so?
The five heinous crimes can be transferred, as was the case with King Ajātaśatru;
however, for those who lack faith, their offenses cannot be transferred.
The retribution for the five heinous crimes lasts for at most one lifetime, whereas the offense of one who lacks faith is to be suffered for immeasurable lifetimes.
Therefore, I say that it cannot be used as an analogy.

Even if one were to take property belonging to the Buddha, property belonging to the Dharma, property belonging to the Sangha, or property belonging to the present Sangha, the retribution for such a sin could not be illustrated by any analogy.
Why is this? While such retribution for [this] offense lasts for at most one lifetime, the offense of one who does not believe reaches immeasurable lifetimes.

Suppose as many sentient beings as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers were to resolve upon bodhicitta; if someone were able to cause these beings, numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to retreat from bodhicitta and instruct them in false views, the retribution for such an offense would be equal to, and no different from, the offense of one who does not believe.

Furthermore, suppose as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River were all established in the fifth stage, and someone were to rob them all of their eyes; the retribution for such a sin would be the same for one who does not believe.

Furthermore, if there were someone who could destroy all the stūpas and temples of the Buddhas, kill all the disciples of the Buddhas, and burn all the sūtras of the Buddhas—the retribution for such a sin would be exactly the same as the retribution for one who, out of lack of faith, receives the Bodhisattva precepts.
Why is this? Because of causes one is born in hell; because of causes one enters nirvana.
Due to the speaker, immeasurable suffering is incurred; therefore, the speaker incurs immeasurable demerit.

Although one knows that immeasurable sentient beings within the great assembly are capable of performing wholesome karma for humans and devas and can give rise to faith, if there is even a single person among them whose mind lacks faith, one must not speak [of such things] to them; this is called the bodhisattva’s precept of benefiting sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra, Scroll Four;
The Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kapiśā during the Song Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve: Patience, from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*. Chapter Twelve on Patience:
"What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience by nature (*prakṛti-kṣānti*)?
By the power of wisdom, he is able to endure various matters such as suffering and affliction; he endures all things, he endures everything."
All forms of patience arise because of compassion and the attainment of a mind of loving-kindness.
There are two types of natural patience:
first, that of the renunciant; [and second, that of the householder].
The second is the householder.
Both householders and renunciants have three types [of patience]:
first, being able to endure such things as being struck or reviled by sentient beings;
Second, being able to personally endure all forms of suffering;
third, delighting in the endurance of wholesome dharmas.
Regarding the ability to endure the beating and reviling of sentient beings: when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is beaten or reviled by sentient beings, they reflect as follows:
"Since it is due to this self that I have committed evil karma and now receive its retribution, why should I give rise to anger toward others?
I did not seek this suffering and affliction; if I do not endure it now, it will increase further in the future."
One who is unable to endure insults is said to have suffering and afflictions as their cause.
This body I have received and these various afflictions are not the fault of other sentient beings; they are my own transgression.
If there is an evil matter, one truly does not wish to undergo it.
If one now lacks forbearance, this is precisely what one creates oneself; having created it oneself, one must further undergo the inherent suffering of birth and death.
If my body undergoes suffering, why should I not practice patience?
Even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cultivate patience for their own benefit; how much more so should I now, who desire to benefit all sentient beings, fail to practice patience?
"If I do not practice patience, I shall not be able to fulfill the bodhisattva precepts, cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, and attain the Unsurpassed Way.
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates in this way, he cultivates five kinds of patience:
first, he practices patience toward enemies, toward friends, and toward those who are neither enemy nor friend;
Second, cultivating and accumulating patience toward superior, middling, and inferior persons;
third, cultivating and accumulating patience toward those experiencing suffering, those experiencing pleasure, and those experiencing neither suffering nor pleasure;
fourth, cultivating and accumulating patience toward those with merit, those without merit, and those who possess neither merit nor lack merit.
Fifth, one cultivates patience toward all evil persons.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these five kinds of patience, they cultivate five perceptions:
first, the perception of sentient beings; [and so forth].
Second, the perception of phenomena;
third, the perception of impermanence;
fourth, the perception of suffering;
Fifth, there is no notion of "self" or "what belongs to self.
When a bodhisattva is struck by such an evil person, how can they maintain the perception of them as a friend?

The bodhisattva observes with clarity that throughout the past, as they transmigrated through birth and death, there has never been a sentient being who was not their parent, teacher, preceptor, relative, or kinsman—none whom they should respect, honor, and provide for.

When one contemplates in this way, the perception of enmity and hatred ceases and the perception of kinship arises; because the perception of kinship arises, one is able to cultivate patience, and at that time, one achieves the perception of sentient beings.

Regarding the perception of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*): the Bodhisattva observes with clarity that what are called "sentient beings" are termed the *dharmadhātu*, termed conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), and termed outflowing phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
If this *dharmadhātu* encounters the *dharmadhātu*, who strikes whom, and who becomes angry?

When one observes with the power of wisdom that there is no self, no "mine," no life-force, and no person, the notion of a sentient being is extinguished and the notion of phenomena (*dharma*) is accomplished.

Regarding the perception of impermanence, the Bodhisattva contemplates that all sentient beings and all conditioned, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) phenomena are entirely impermanent; because they are impermanent, who is there to revile, and who is there to receive [the reviling]?
If the one who reviles and the one who receives the reviling were to remain stationary for even a moment, then one could not say that all phenomena are impermanent.
If they were permanent, who would revile and who would receive the reviling?

Within both the permanent and the impermanent, neither of these two exists; there is neither agent nor recipient. One should not even give rise to a slight thought of ill-will, much less resort to striking or reviling. Therefore, a bodhisattva destroys the perception of permanence and cultivates the perception of impermanence. By being able to cultivate and accumulate the perception of impermanence, they achieve a mind of patience (*kṣānti*). Because they achieve a mind of patience, they cultivate the path to enlightenment (*bodhimārga*), until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
How does a bodhisattva cultivate and collect the perception of suffering?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva observes in this way: "If even those beings in the desire realm who have attained great mastery and possess vast wealth like that of a wheel-turning king still experience the three kinds of suffering, how much more so for others?"
Regarding the three types of suffering— namely, the suffering of change, the suffering of birth and death, and the suffering of suffering—
when one contemplates in this way, even if sentient beings possess these three sufferings, I should not feel anger toward them.
If I were to harbor anger, how could I possibly rescue those sentient beings from these three kinds of suffering?
If I were to harbor anger, I would instead increase the three kinds of suffering for sentient beings.
When one contemplates in this way, the perception of pleasure ceases and the perception of suffering arises.
Because one is able to cultivate and accumulate the causes and conditions for the perception of suffering, one practices the Eightfold Noble Path and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
How does a bodhisattva cultivate the perception of non-self and non-belonging-to-self?
The bodhisattva observes with discernment that there are certain non-Buddhists who claim, "The self is eternal.
If the self were eternal, then sentient beings would be without a self.

Why is this? Sentient beings are precisely the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Since the five aggregates are impermanent, if there is no self (*ātman*), how could there be "what belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*)?
Therefore, there is neither self nor what belongs to the self.
The Bodhisattva further contemplates in this way: "I" is precisely the bodhicitta.
When a Bodhisattva first gives rise to the bodhicitta, they attain toward all sentient beings the mind of a sole child; this is called "mine."
If I harbored a mind of anger toward them, how could I be said to possess a self or what belongs to a self?
If I were to increase my mind of hatred, I would be unable to deliver all sentient beings.

When practicing this contemplation, one achieves patience (*kṣānti*), increases the mind that is free from "self" and "what belongs to self," and attains the perception of non-self. By these causes and conditions, one cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
How is it that a bodhisattva is able to endure the sufferings of being struck or reviled by sentient beings?

At that time, the bodhisattva further reflects: "In the past, for the sake of the five desires, I underwent all manner of suffering. While living as a householder, I performed labor such as plowing fields and planting crops, undergoing various forms of hardship; I drew near to rulers and engaged in buying and selling, enduring much suffering. Although I underwent such diverse great sufferings at those times, I gained no benefit.
If I now undergo these various pains and afflictions for the sake of delivering sentient beings, I shall surely attain benefit."
"If I am to attain great benefit, I should endure immeasurable and incalculable suffering.
When making this vow, the bodhisattva is then able to endure all forms of suffering.
Those who experience suffering are said to possess all suffering; all suffering is of eight kinds:
first, suffering based on [the body];
second, suffering through worldly conditions (*lokadharma*);...
Third is the suffering of deportment;
fourth is the suffering of upholding the Dharma;
fifth is the suffering of begging for food.
Sixth is the suffering of diligence;
seventh is the suffering for the sake of benefiting sentient beings;
eighth is the suffering of managing affairs.
Regarding "relying on suffering," this refers to the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*) that involve suffering.
If a bhikṣu, having accepted these four reliances, attains the going-forth and receives the precepts, he is called a fully ordained bhikṣu.

If one obtains little clothing, little food, bedding, or medicine for the sick, yet does not give rise to sorrow or distress and remains free from regret in the mind—because one is able to cultivate and accumulate the mind that overcomes suffering—and through the cultivation of the Eightfold Noble Path attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this is called "relying on suffering."
There are nine kinds of suffering pertaining to worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*):
first, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
second, the suffering of ill repute; [and so forth].
Third is the suffering of encountering adverse phenomena;
fourth is the suffering of suffering itself;
fifth is the suffering of loss.
Sixth is the suffering of the exhaustion of possessions;
seventh is the suffering of old age;
eighth is the suffering of illness.
Ninth is the suffering of death; this is called the suffering of worldly phenomena (*lokadharma*).

When a bodhisattva undergoes these nine kinds of suffering, he does not give rise to grief or affliction, nor does his mind feel regret or remorse. He does not abandon the aspiration for unsurpassed bodhi (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*); because he feels no regret, his bodhi increases, and because his bodhi increases, he attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding the suffering of deportment, it refers to the four modes of physical deportment:
first, walking; second, standing;
[third, sitting; fourth, lying down].
Third is sitting;
fourth is lying down.

Whether walking or sitting, the Bodhisattva constantly disciplines the mind of evil karma throughout day and night, enduring the hardships of standing and sitting. He does not lie down at improper times, nor does he remain stationary at improper times.

Whether staying indoors or outdoors—whether on a bed, on the ground, on grass, or on leaves—in these four places, one should constantly keep in mind making offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; praise the sutras and the Dharma; receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts; maintain the unsurpassed Dharma and explain it extensively for others; correctly contemplate its meaning and abide in accordance with the Dharma; and discern the dharma-realm while cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā.
When a bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates such dharmas, if they are able to endure and accept whatever sufferings may arise, this is called the suffering of deportment (*īryāpatha*).
There are seven kinds of suffering involved in gathering the Dharma (*dharmasaṃgraha*):
first, the physical relinquishing of ornaments and finery;
Second, shaving off the beard and hair;
third, wearing cut-and-sewn robes;
fourth, having no mastery over any worldly affairs and one's life depending upon others.
Fifth, sustaining one's life by begging;
sixth, distancing oneself from worldly occupations while possessing few desires and being content;
seventh, relinquishing kin and the pleasures of the five senses.
This is called the suffering of gathering requisites. Regarding the suffering of begging:

one relies entirely upon others for all things necessary to sustain the body—clothing, food and drink, housing, bedding, and medicine for illness and weakness. One must not feel resentment when receiving nothing, and one must know contentment when receiving something; even to the end of one’s life, one is barred from experiencing the five desires, music, and playful laughter. To endure such suffering is called the suffering of begging for alms.

Regarding the suffering of diligent effort: a bodhisattva diligently makes offerings to the Triple Gem, upholds, recites, and studies the Bodhisattva-piṭaka sūtras, copies them, explains them, and contemplates their meaning. Day and night, they do not cease their efforts but apply themselves with even greater vigor to cultivate and accumulate the Noble Path. Because of this diligence, they are able to endure all manner of sufferings; this is called the suffering of diligence.

"Suffering for the sake of benefiting sentient beings" is as explained above in the section on the eleven matters of benefiting those internal and external; this is called suffering for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.

"Suffering of managing affairs" refers to polishing bowls, sewing robes, dyeing and washing them, performing services for the Sangha, providing for one's teachers and elders, or making offerings such as plastering and sweeping Buddha stupas. For the sake of the wholesome Dharma, one never rests; for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one endures various kinds of suffering. This is called the suffering of managing affairs.
Regarding those who endure and delight in the suffering of wholesome dharmas, there are eight kinds of endurance (*kṣānti*):
endurance regarding all the merits possessed by the Triple Gem;
and endurance regarding the inconceivability of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Patience as cause;
patience as fruit;
and patience through skillful means.
Furthermore, the nature of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possesses two kinds of patience:
first, ultimate patience;
second, the patience of pure wisdom, which is called the patience regarding dharmas (dharmakṣānti).
What is the bodhisattva’s endurance of what is difficult to endure?
There are three kinds of such endurance:
first, when immeasurable sentient beings strike or revile the bodhisattva, the bodhisattva is able to endure it.
Second, the bodhisattva possesses the power of mastery, such that when struck or reviled, they endure it without retaliation;
third, although the bodhisattva is born into a noble and wealthy lineage, they are able to endure being treated with lowliness.
What is patience toward all things?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices patience toward enemies, toward friends, and toward those who are neither enemies nor friends—whether it be lower patience, middling patience, or superior patience—this is called patience toward all things.
A person of good character who practices patience possesses five kinds of knowledge regarding the merits of patience:
first, they do not harbor malicious or angry thoughts;
second, their mind is difficult to discourage or destroy.
Third, the mind is free from sorrow and affliction;
fourth, there is no regret at the time of death;
fifth, after death, one experiences the bliss of devas and humans.

The Bodhisattva contemplates that patience possesses such merits; he teaches and transforms sentient beings to practice patience, so that his own cultivation of patience also increases. He praises forbearance, and upon seeing those who practice patience, he honors, respects, praises, and prostrates before them. This is called the patience of a virtuous person.
Regarding the patience toward all conditioned phenomena (*sarvasaṃskāra-kṣānti*), the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates the faults and evils inherent in impatience.
What is meant by "evil retribution"?
It is that which leads one to obtain rebirth in the three evil destinies.

One should practice patience because of the fear of the evil realms; one practices patience out of compassion; one practices patience for the sake of cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*); one practices patience for the sake of a gentle mind; one practices patience out of love for sentient beings; one practices patience with a sincere mind for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; one practices patience for the sake of fulfilling the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); one practices patience for the sake of leaving the household life; one practices patience for the sake of receiving the precepts; one practices patience for the sake of fulfilling one's nature; one practices patience for the desire to cultivate and accumulate patience throughout immeasurable lifetimes; one practices patience for the sake of attaining the nature of patience; one practices patience for the sake of attaining freedom from attachment and freedom from hatred; one practices patience for the sake of seeing the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); one practices patience for the sake of seeing the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*). Patience at all times, patience in all lands, and patience in all states of mind—this is called "patience in all practices."

Regarding the patience of removal (*apanayanakṣānti*): if there are impoverished people who repeatedly beg from a bodhisattva for their necessities, and furthermore, if wicked people also come to beg, and even those who have broken the precepts come to beg, one should cultivate a mind of patience by destroying evil intentions; for the sake of destroying suffering, one bestows pleasant things upon them—this is called the patience of removal.

The bodhisattva who practices patience for the sake of self-benefit and the benefit of others remains ever-vigilant, enduring hunger, thirst, cold, heat, wind, rain, and wild beasts; though suffering within the cycle of birth and death, they maintain compassion for all sentient beings.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain such patiences as these, they increase all wholesome dharmas in the present life and remain far removed from afflictions;

in future lives, they obtain immeasurable wholesome fruits. They are fully able to subdue the evil minds of sentient beings; because evil minds are subdued, all afflictions find no opportunity. There is peace and happiness in the present, and wholesome fruits are obtained hereafter. This is called the patience that benefits both oneself and others.

Regarding the patience of tranquility: if a bodhisattva is struck or reviled by wicked sentient beings, they ultimately do not give rise to an evil mind toward them; they do not conceive thoughts of enmity, but instead regard them as virtuous friends, thinking:
"If there were no such wicked people, how could my wholesome dharmas increase?"
Seeing those who revile him, he responds with gentle words and consolation; by cultivating a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, he is able to destroy all afflictions within the desire realm.
A Bodhisattva who is fully endowed with these ten kinds of patience can cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Chapter Thirteen: On Diligence, from the Bodhisattvabhūmi What is the bodhisattva’s natural diligence (*prakṛti-vīrya*)?

Natural diligence refers to the mind’s diligent application of effort for the sake of gathering wholesome dharmas, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain the unsurpassed path, and for the sake of destroying perversions. Because of this natural diligence, one attains excellence in the actions of body, speech, and mind; this is called natural diligence.
All forms of diligence are of two kinds:
first, mundane; second, supramundane.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, those who live at home;
second, those who have left the home life.
Furthermore, there are three kinds: first, adornment;
second, the gathering of wholesome dharmas.
Third is the adornment for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. Regarding this adornment:

when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first resolves their mind [on enlightenment], they diligently apply themselves with vigor as an adornment, thinking, "If I can cause even a single person to attain liberation, I shall undergo great suffering in the hells for immeasurable kalpas; having undergone that great suffering, I will thereafter attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Once I have attained bodhi, even if I must cause only one person to attain liberation, I shall continue to endure the suffering of the hells without ceasing. This is called adornment.
The Bodhisattva’s perfection of adorned diligence surpasses the merit attained by all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas beyond measure. Why is this?

Because one undergoes great suffering for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, even if one undergoes great pain and affliction for the sake of a single person, one still attains immeasurable and boundless merit; how much more so when it is for the sake of all sentient beings? This is called the bodhisattva’s adornment of diligence.

Regarding those who apply diligent effort in embracing wholesome dharmas: if one applies diligent effort for the sake of practicing the *dāna-pāramitā*, *śīla-pāramitā*, *kṣānti-pāramitā*, *dhyāna-pāramitā*, and *prajñā-pāramitā*, this is called "immovable," because one is not shaken by any afflictions, any evil karma, any wrong views, or any suffering;
it is also called "firm," because of being valiantly adorned;
and it is further called "all-encompassing," because of knowing both worldly arts and crafts as well as supramundane dharmas.
It is further named "Endowed with Skillful Means," because it is the path cultivated through the accumulation of true causes and conditions;
it is further named "Reality," because one attains the meaning of reality;
it is further named "Vast," because it is without rest at all times.
It is also called "subduing," because through the diligent cultivation of vigor, one does not give rise to arrogance.
These seven matters increase wholesome dharmas; this is called the vigor of embracing wholesome dharmas.

Because of diligent exertion, one fulfills the dharma of diligent exertion through the six *pāramitās*. Among all dharmas directed toward enlightenment, this is the proximate cause, unsurpassed and peerless. Therefore, the Tathāgata said in a sutra: "Ānanda!..."
"Those who apply themselves with diligent effort will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
There are eleven kinds of diligent effort for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, as explained in the section on the precepts.

Regarding "difficult diligence," it means that a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not form the notion of clothing, does not form the notion of food, does not form the notion of bedding, does not form the notion of self, does not form the notion of "mine," does not form the notion of dharmas, does not form the notion of the path, and does not form the notion of bodhi; yet, for the sake of bodhi, they diligently cultivate diligence—this is called difficult diligence.
To diligently cultivate vigor at all times, in all lands, and with all states of mind is also called difficult.
To practice with neither haste nor laxity, but in the middle way, is called difficult vigor.
There are two causes for difficult diligence:
first, compassion;
second, wisdom.
There are four kinds of those who exert personal diligence:
first, abandoning unwholesome dharmas;
second, increasing wholesome dharmas.
Third, polishing and refining wholesome dharmas;
fourth, increasing wisdom.

Regarding the abandonment of unwholesome dharmas, it is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s diligent cultivation of vigor, because they diligently apply skillful means to ensure that unwholesome dharmas not yet arisen do not arise.
To increase wholesome dharmas means to employ skillful means so that wholesome dharmas already arisen may expand and broaden.

To polish and refine wholesome dharmas means to diligently cultivate the causal conditions of bodily, vocal, and mental actions, and with a sincere mind, maintain mindfulness while upholding wholesome dharmas.

Regarding the increase of wisdom: if a bodhisattva diligently practices vigor, because they increase wisdom through extensive learning and the cultivation of meditative concentration, this is called "all self-vigor."

Regarding the diligence of virtuous people: when a bodhisattva exerts diligent effort for the sake of wholesome dharmas, even if their body and head were to be burned, they would not consider it heat.
When a bodhisattva cultivates wholesome dharmas and practices diligent effort, they do not even perceive the heat of the fires of hell, let alone the fires of the mundane world.
The bodhisattva practices diligence with neither excess nor deficiency, acting with equanimity because he increases his diligence through skillful self-mastery.
Why is this? Because his mind is pure;

because his mind does not weary or cease and is free from regret; because he attains great benefit without error; and because he will ultimately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is called the diligence of a virtuous person.

Regarding the diligence of all practices: it is constant diligence, wholehearted diligence, wisdom diligence, uninterrupted diligence, adorned diligence, endurance-of-suffering diligence, immovable diligence, untimely diligence, and insatiable diligence. When a bodhisattva accomplishes this diligence of all practices, it is called "great power."
