Always diligent and energetic, dwelling securely in wholesome states with steadfast adornment, they attain wholesome dharmas without ceasing or resting.
This is because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who desires the mind of diligence seeks Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva who exerts diligence with a sincere heart does so for the sake of increasing the bodhicitta.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva who exerts diligence with a skillful mind is not defiled in his heart by the stains of the various afflictions, for he takes this body as a vessel to accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Supreme Diligence does so because he would rather not save his own body or head from a fire for the sake of wholesome dharmas.
In this way, such a bodhisattva surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who seeks diligence does so for the sake of seeking all the various arts and skills of both worldly and world-transcending dharmas.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who trains in diligence swiftly attains both worldly and world-transcending dharmas.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s diligence for the benefit of others has eleven types, as explained in the section on morality: not forming the intention to transgress, and having transgressed, repenting;
excluding [the specific types of] diligence and those for one's own benefit and the benefit of others, it is as explained in the section on patience.
There are ten kinds of those who practice tranquility with diligence:
first, suitability;
second, cultivation and accumulation.
Third, non-fluctuation;
fourth, firm persistence;
fifth, at all times.
Sixth is focusing on the three characteristics;
seventh is equanimity;
eighth is non-distraction.
Ninth is self-mastery; tenth is the orientation toward bodhi.

If a bodhisattva gives rise to any afflictions, they apply the appropriate antidote to eliminate those ailments: when desire arises, they contemplate the sign of impurity; when anger arises, they cultivate a mind of loving-kindness; when ignorance arises, they contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination; when discursive thoughts arise, they contemplate *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing); and to destroy pride, they contemplate the realm of sentient beings. This is called "appropriate diligence."
The diligence of a bodhisattva has neither beginning nor end; having been constantly accomplished throughout immeasurable lifetimes, it is called the cultivation and accumulation of diligence.
The diligence of a bodhisattva is always practiced with constant effort as if it were first attained; this is called unshakable diligence.
Because one exerts diligent effort at all times, this is called "the immovable.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is constantly able to draw near to teachers, elders, and those of virtuous merit to study and cultivate extensive learning; and when, while practicing samādhi and contemplating its meaning, they apply themselves with diligent effort and listen to and receive the teachings in accordance with them, this is called "firmly maintaining diligence."

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is free from inverted views in his mind; when it is appropriate to cultivate śamatha, he cultivates śamatha; when it is appropriate to cultivate vipaśyanā, he cultivates vipaśyanā; and when it is appropriate to cultivate upekṣā, he practices upekṣā. This is called diligence at all times.

The bodhisattva skillfully understands concentration, wisdom, and equanimity, and from time to time cultivates and accumulates these three characteristics: the characteristic of entry, the characteristic of abiding, and the characteristic of emergence. Without losing right mindfulness, he applies himself with a sincere and diligent mind; this is called the diligence that takes the three characteristics as its object.

If a bodhisattva hears that the diligent exertion of all buddhas and bodhisattvas is inconceivable, and having heard this, their mind does not disparage itself, does not feel distress, and knows no satiety—this is called the relinquishment of diligence.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva from time to time disciplines the sense faculties and the sense bases, practices moderation in eating, reduces sleep during the first and last watches of the night, maintains an undistracted mind free from negligence, seeks out adornments by exerting diligent effort, and cultivates the true meaning with a mind free from inversion while following the path of cultivation—this is called non-distracted diligence.
The bodhisattva’s diligence is neither too hurried nor too slack; he engages in all undertakings with moderation. This is called "disciplined diligence.

All the bodhisattva’s diligence is dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Whether it be the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s diligence of nature up to his diligence of tranquility, it is entirely for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is called "all-encompassing diligence."
Dedicating it all toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: the vigor maintained by all bodhisattvas of the past was entirely for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
the vigor maintained by all bodhisattvas of the future will also be for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;

and the vigor maintained by all bodhisattvas of the present, who practice with sincere minds and without negligence, is likewise for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is called the vigor directed toward enlightenment.
Chapter 14: Dhyāna, from the Bodhisattvabhūmi, Chapter Fourteen on Dhyāna. "What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s *prakṛti-dhyāna* (natural dhyāna)?

If a bodhisattva hears the Dharma-treasury of the bodhisattvas, or contemplates its meaning, or practices both mundane and supramundane dhyānas, binding the mind to a single point with the equalization of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) while cultivating the Path—this is called *prakṛti-dhyāna*."
All practitioners of dhyāna are of two kinds:
first, those of the mundane world;
second, those of the supramundane.
These two types further comprise three kinds:
first, entering meditative absorption and experiencing happiness in the present;
second, entering meditative absorption to increase bodhi.
Third, entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) to benefit sentient beings.

Regarding "experiencing happiness in the present": when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas shatter the web of all doubts, their body and mind become tranquil; they experience the joy of seclusion, destroy all arrogance, do not crave the flavor [of concentration], and remain detached from all marks (*nimitta*). This is called entering meditative absorption to experience happiness in the present.

Regarding "entering dhyāna to increase bodhi": the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva have various conditions that are inconceivable, incalculable, and limitless. By encompassing the nature of the ten powers (*daśabala*), they attain various *samādhis*. Such *samādhis* are such that even all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not even know their names, let alone be able to cultivate and accumulate them.

Furthermore, there are shared dharmas, namely: the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*), the ten totalities (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*), the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*), the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇājñāna*), and the knowledge of the summit (*mūrdhajñāna*). Because one increases such shared dharmas, this is called "entering dhyāna to increase bodhi."
Regarding entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to benefit sentient beings, there are eleven kinds, as explained in the section on the precepts.

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate these eleven kinds of dhyāna, they are able to transform sentient beings, destroy suffering and afflictions, cultivate and accumulate various wholesome dharmas and wisdoms, recognize kindness and repay it, rescue sentient beings from their manifold sufferings and distresses, bestow all necessary things, skillfully understand expedient means (*upāya*) to nurture disciples, and enable disciples to receive and practice according to their inclinations. Such dhyānas are called "all-encompassing dhyānas" (*sarvadhyāna*).
There are three kinds of those who find meditation difficult:

first, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter meditative absorption, the bliss they experience surpasses all worldly pleasures as well as supramundane pleasures; yet for the sake of sentient beings, they relinquish the bliss of meditative absorption to take on bodies within the desire realm.

Second, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates and accumulates meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), as well as immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, inconceivable, and inestimable samādhis; no Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas can know the realm into which they enter.
Third, because of the causal conditions of dhyāna, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is called "difficult dhyāna.
There are four kinds of all self-dhyāna: first, that which is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra; [the others follow].
Second is shared joy;
third is shared happiness;
fourth is shared equanimity; these are called all self-meditations.
There are five kinds of virtuous practitioners of dhyāna:
first, those free from craving;
second, those who share in loving-kindness.
Third is sympathetic joy;
fourth is sympathetic joy;
fifth is equanimity—these are called the meditations of a virtuous person.
There are thirteen types of practitioners of all meditative practices (*sarva-caryā-dhyāyin*):
first, those who are wholesome or indeterminate (*kuśala-avyākṛta*);
second, those with the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Third, tending toward śamatha;
fourth, tending toward vipaśyanā;
fifth, self-benefit;
Sixth is benefiting others;
seventh is attaining the meditative concentration of the merit of the five supernormal powers;
eighth is the analysis of causal conditions.
Ninth, the causal condition of meaning;
tenth, the causal condition of the characteristics of śamatha;
eleventh, the causal condition of the characteristics of vipaśyanā.
Twelfth is the causal condition for relinquishing signs;
thirteenth is the causal condition for the practice of experiencing happiness in the present—these are called all-encompassing meditative practices (*sarva-caryā-dhyāna*).
There are eight types of those who exclude meditative concentration (*dhyāna-vivarjita*):

First, when a bodhisattva enters samādhi, they are able to eliminate the various kinds of suffering and poison for sentient beings—namely, violent winds, hail, rain, feverish diseases, and demonic illnesses; this is called dhyāna.
Second, if one enters samādhi and can cure the suffering of the four great elements within the bodies of sentient beings when they are out of harmony, this is called dhyāna.
Third, if one enters samādhi and can bring down sweet rain during times of drought and famine, this is called dhyāna.
Fourth, if one enters samādhi and can cause sentient beings to be free from various fears—namely, fear of humans, fear of ghosts, fear of water, and fear of land—this is called dhyāna.

Fifth, if upon entering samādhi one is able to bestow upon sentient beings suffering from hunger and thirst in the wilderness whatever they require, such as water, grain, and food, this is called dhyāna.
Sixth, if upon entering samādhi one is able to bestow upon those who are poor and afflicted by hardship all manner of necessities, this is called dhyāna.
Seventh, if one enters samādhi and is able to destroy the negligence of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, this is called dhyāna.
Eighth, if one enters samādhi and is able to shatter the various nets of doubt of sentient beings, this is called dhyāna.
This is called the meditation that eliminates [defilements].
Regarding the meditation that benefits both oneself and others, there are nine types:
first, entering meditative absorption through the supernormal power of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) in order to subdue sentient beings;
Second, entering dhyāna by means of the knowledge of others' minds to subdue sentient beings;
third, entering dhyāna by means of speaking the truth to subdue sentient beings;
fourth, entering dhyāna to manifest the sufferings of hell for evil sentient beings.
Fifth, entering meditative concentration to cause those who have lost their speech to speak;
sixth, entering meditative concentration to cause those who have lost mindfulness to regain it;

seventh, entering meditative concentration to accord with and explain the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas, and the Bodhisattva-vinaya, so that the Dharma may abide for a long time.

Eighth, having entered dhyāna, they are able to teach sentient beings various worldly affairs, such as calligraphy, correspondence, arithmetic, recitation, writing, and the crafts of metalwork, carpentry, and pottery;
ninth, having entered dhyāna, they emit great radiance to shatter the suffering and affliction of sentient beings in the three evil realms.
This is called the dhyāna that benefits both oneself and others.
There are ten kinds of dhyāna of tranquility:
first, the purity of tranquility regarding worldly phenomena;
Second is the purity of quiescence regarding supramundane dharmas;
third is the purity of quiescence regarding skillful means;
fourth is the purity of quiescence regarding the fundamental.
Fifth is the purity of supreme tranquility;
sixth is the purity of entering tranquility;
seventh is the purity of abiding in tranquility.
Eighth is the purity of the arising of tranquility;
ninth is the purity of mastery over tranquility;
tenth is the purity of the tranquility of the two obscurations of afflictions and wisdom.
These ten kinds of tranquil purity are called the pure dhyānas.
By cultivating and accumulating these ten, the bodhisattva accomplishes immeasurable and boundless merit for the sake of attaining the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi.
Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present all cultivate this dhyāna and thereby attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Chapter Fifteen: The Chapter on Wisdom (*Prajñā-varga*) of the Bodhisattva-bhūmi. "What is the innate wisdom (*prakṛti-prajñā*) of a bodhisattva?"
To discern the dharma-dhātu for the sake of omniscience is called innate wisdom (*prakṛti-prajñā*).

Furthermore, to skillfully study the five types of arts and sciences—namely, internal arts and sciences, logic (*hetu-vidyā*), grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*), and all worldly affairs—is called innate wisdom.
There are two kinds of all-encompassing wisdom:
first, worldly; second, supramundane.

These two types further comprise three kinds: first, knowing reality as it is (*yathābhūta*). This consists of knowing the five arts as they truly are; knowing the three categories of sentient beings; knowing the skillful means for benefiting sentient beings; knowing that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is ineffable; and knowing the four noble truths to be without self (*anātman*) and without what belongs to a self (*anātmiya*). Regarding all dharma-realms, there is no discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); one contemplates the dharma-realms with a mind of equanimity. Without abandoning or clinging, and neither eternalizing nor annihilating, one speaks of the Middle Way—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
Second, knowing worldly affairs as well as supramundane dharmas for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is called wisdom.
Third, contemplating the profound realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*) and explaining it through discernment for the benefit of sentient beings is called wisdom.
This is called all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*).
There are eleven kinds of difficult wisdom, as explained in the section on the precepts.
To skillfully know the minds of sentient beings for the purpose of taming them is called difficult wisdom.
To know that the entire dharma-realm is without obstruction is called difficult wisdom.
To expound the profound dharma-realm for the sake of all sentient beings is called difficult wisdom.
To skillfully understand non-self and that which belongs to no self is called difficult wisdom.

Regarding "all self-knowledge" (*sarva-svaprajñā*): if one is able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, one thereby attains the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*). Because of this wisdom of cultivation, one attains the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*). By means of the power of wisdom, one knows what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated, what is to be done and what is not to be done, and contemplates immeasurable matters with a sincere mind; this is called all self-knowledge.
There are five kinds of wisdom for virtuous persons:
first, that which is obtained through hearing the true Dharma;
second, that which is obtained through reflecting upon the true Dharma.
Third, it is attained because of benefiting oneself and others;
fourth, it is attained because of not having perverted views regarding the locus of phenomena;
fifth, it is attained because of destroying afflictions.
Furthermore, there are five kinds:
first, because one is able to know subtle and profound meanings;
second, because through the cultivation and accumulation of meditative concentration, one knows the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Third, it is the adornment of shared wisdom because one attains insight;
fourth, it is so called because it originates from Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
fifth, it is so called because one fully attains a mind of tranquility up to the ultimate mind—this is termed the wisdom of a virtuous person.
There are thirteen kinds of wisdom regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*):
first, the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*);
second, the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*).
Third is the knowledge of cessation;
fourth is the knowledge of the path;
fifth is the knowledge of exhaustion.
Sixth is the knowledge of non-arising;
seventh is the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna);
eighth is inferential knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
Ninth is mundane knowledge;
tenth is the knowledge of supernormal powers;
eleventh is the knowledge of causes.
The twelfth is the wisdom of power;
the thirteenth is the wisdom of the initial resolve—these are called the wisdom of all practices.

As for "wisdom that removes," this refers to the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and mundane and supramundane wisdoms; because they shatter all darkness, they are called "wisdom that removes."

Regarding the wisdom that benefits oneself and others: as explained in the first five arts, it is by means of these five arts as causes and conditions that one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is called the wisdom that benefits oneself and others.

One of tranquil wisdom cultivates and accumulates for the sake of reality; cultivates and accumulates for the sake of sentient beings; cultivates and accumulates for the sake of attaining the meaning; cultivates and accumulates for the sake of knowing cause and effect; cultivates and accumulates for the sake of destroying perversions; cultivates and accumulates for the sake of skillfully knowing means; cultivates and accumulates for the sake of knowing what should and should not be done; cultivates and accumulates for the sake of knowing the afflictions; and cultivates and accumulates for the sake of ultimate attainment. This is called tranquil wisdom.

When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these ten kinds of wisdom, it is called knowledge, it is called wisdom, it is also called ultimate, it is also called reality, and it is also called immeasurable wisdom.
By virtue of these causes and conditions of immeasurable wisdom, the bodhisattva fulfills the perfection of prajñā; because he fulfills the perfection of prajñā, he attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

As stated in the Buddha’s sūtras, there are those who possess prajñā in its entirety and those who do not; one should know that this applies to the ten types, from nature (dhātu) up to tranquility (śānti).
Sometimes one pāramitā is taught, sometimes two, three, four, five, or six. If one is taught, it subsumes all six; likewise, even when six are taught, they also subsume all six.

If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing these ten names within each [of the categories], believe and accept them, uphold, read, recite, copy, analyze, and explain them extensively to teach and transform other sentient beings, they will ultimately attain the complete fulfillment and accomplishment of the six pāramitās.
Chapter 16: Gentle Speech, from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*. Chapter Sixteen on Gentle Speech. "What is the bodhisattva’s natural gentleness of speech?

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva speaks with joy, speaks words that are pleasant to hear, speaks truthfully, speaks according to the Dharma, speaks according to the meaning, and speaks for the benefit of sentient beings; this is called natural gentleness of speech."

Regarding "using all gentle speech": when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees someone with whom they have no prior acquaintance, upon seeing them, they first engage in conversation with gentle words and a friendly disposition. If they see that the person before them is upright, virtuous, and superior to themselves, they harbor no jealousy; rather, they abandon pride and respectfully inquire after their well-being:
"Are your four elements at ease?"
"Are you not exhausted from the road?
Are you not suffering?
Welcome to see us."
He provides seats and bedding and offers drinks and water for the sake of practicing worldly conventions and in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings.

A bodhisattva never speaks harsh or evil words to sentient beings—such as speaking of death, killing, destruction, plundering, or the loss of property—but speaks only wholesome words, such as: "Your children have grown up and are now married; your wealth has increased, your grain is abundant, your wisdom is perfected, and your faith, precepts, generosity, diligence, and extensive learning are vast."
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with such speech of the Dharma for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, this is called "all gentle speech.
There are two ways to analyze gentle speech: first, that which conforms to the world; [second, that which conforms to the Dharma].
The second is following the supramundane.
There are two kinds of "world": first, the inferior world; [the second is the superior world].
The second is the superior world.
Regarding the supramundane, there are two types:
first, the supramundane through the correct Dharma for one's own benefit; [and second, the supramundane for the benefit of others].
Second, there is the supramundane soft speech for the benefit of others through the True Dharma.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva employs gentle words for the sake of both inferior and superior mundane dharmas, as well as for the sake of self-benefit and the benefit of others regarding supramundane dharmas, this is called the analytical soft speech.

Regarding those who speak with difficult or harsh words: if there are sentient beings who come to harm the Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva conceives of them as his own children and addresses those who strike, revile, or plunder him with sincere and gentle speech.

Furthermore, regarding "difficult gentle speech": a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva constantly speaks with gentle words to those who are deluded when teaching the Dharma; yet his physical, verbal, and mental actions involve undergoing much suffering.

Although he undergoes great suffering, he continues to instruct and admonish them, saying: "You should study diligently; later you shall become like me, or perhaps even surpass me. This is called difficult gentle speech.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva encounters those who are angry, envious, or stingy; those who do not accept the teacher’s instruction; those who deceive their teachers, elders, parents, or those of long-standing virtue; or those who are malicious, hold wrong views, or are thieves and caṇḍālas—he speaks gently to them without giving rise to ill will. This is called "difficult gentle speech."
There are four kinds of gentle speech directed toward oneself:
first, gentle speech for the purpose of destroying the causes and conditions of afflictions;
second, gentle speech for the purpose of producing the causes and conditions for rebirth among humans and devas.
Third, gentle speech for the sake of increasing the causes and conditions for wholesome dharmas;
fourth, gentle speech for the sake of explaining the causes and conditions that adorn enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are four kinds:
First, it is because they explain the Four Noble Truths to bring about understanding;
second, because they destroy the four inversions;
and third, because they destroy negligence.
Fourth, it is for the purpose of destroying doubt. This is called "all gentle speech of oneself.

Regarding the "gentle speech of a virtuous person," when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva teaches and transforms sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma for specific causes and conditions. That is to say, he preaches the Dharma to explain causes and conditions; he preaches the Dharma to adorn the causes and conditions of Bodhi; he preaches the Dharma for the sake of the causes and conditions of the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*); and he preaches the Dharma for the sake of the causes and conditions of upholding the precepts. Therefore, all phenomena arise from conditions and cease from conditions; this is called the "gentle speech of a virtuous person."

Regarding "acting with gentleness in all ways": when preaching the Dharma, there may be those who should be encouraged to listen and those who should be restrained; one speaks in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) using gentle words, ensuring that the syllables are not inverted. For those who are terrified, one can use gentle words to remove their fear; for those who come seeking, one likewise uses gentle words to grant them what they request. This is called acting with gentleness in all ways.

To eliminate harsh speech means to abandon the four evils of the mouth: lying, divisive speech, abusive language, and idle chatter. To see one says "I see," to hear one says "I hear," to know one says "I know," and to perceive one says "I perceive. Likewise, if one has not seen, heard, perceived, or known, one likewise says so. This is called eliminating harsh speech.

Regarding gentle speech for the benefit of oneself and others: if one speaks with gentle words upon seeing those who are suffering; if one teaches sentient beings through gentle words; or if one instructs sentient beings with gentle words; or if one teaches them to hold right view with gentle words; or if one teaches them to practice giving with gentle words; or if one teaches them to maintain right livelihood with gentle words; or if one expounds the True Dharma with gentle words—this is called gentle speech for the benefit of oneself and others.
There are twenty kinds of serene and gentle speech, as explained in the first chapter, the "Chapter on Innate Power" (*Gotrabala*). Regarding innate altruism:

if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, for the sake of instructing others, discriminates the meaning of the precepts and explains the meaning of dwelling in accordance with the Dharma; if, out of compassion for sentient beings, they cultivate and accumulate a heart of pity, and with a sincere mind teaches and subdues sentient beings—this is called innate altruism.

Regarding all those who benefit others: because they cause immature sentient beings to attain liberation, they provide them with instruction for attaining happiness in the present life and happiness in future lives; this instruction for going forth is called "happiness in future lives."
To teach the Dharma and command the breaking of the fetters of the desire realm is called happiness in the present life and in future lives.

Because one has destroyed the afflictions of the desire realm, body and mind are tranquil; because body and mind are tranquil, one experiences peace and bliss—this is called benefiting others in every way.
There are three kinds of those who are difficult to benefit:

first, if there are sentient beings who have not yet planted roots of goodness and lack virtuous causes, making them difficult to transform and teach, this is called "benefiting others who are difficult to benefit."
Second, if there are sentient beings who possess abundant wealth and treasures and exercise sovereign power, yet are greedy, stingy, and difficult to transform— why is this?
Because they are negligent.
This is called "difficulty in benefiting others.
Third, there are those with heterodox views who are difficult to transform. Why is this?
Because they are deluded or insane,
yet are able to manifest such transformations to bring about benefit, this is called "benefiting others with difficulty.
There are four kinds of all-encompassing self-benefit and benefit for others:
First, to teach those who have no faith so that they may develop it;
second, to teach those who have no precepts so that they may uphold them;
third, to teach stingy and greedy people so that they may practice giving.
Fourth, to instruct ignorant people so that they may attain wisdom is called benefiting both oneself and others in every respect.

As for the altruism of virtuous people, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to know reality, to know the proper time, to know the meaning, and to know gentle speech, and teaching them to cultivate loving-kindness—this is called the altruism of virtuous people.

Regarding all those who act for the benefit of others: when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas see sentient beings who are worthy of praise, they praise them with pleasant words; when they see those who are worthy of censure, they censure them with harsh words.

If there are sentient beings who have destroyed their faith in the Buddha’s True Dharma, he is able to subdue them; those who have not yet entered the Buddha-dharma, he teaches so that they may enter it; and for those who have already entered, he expounds the True Dharma so that their roots of goodness may increase, thereby subduing and establishing them within the Three Vehicles.

For those whose faculties are already matured, he teaches liberation; for those who delight in the vehicle of the śrāvaka, he instructs them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; for those who lack virtuous adornment, he teaches them how to adorn themselves; and for those who lack a fixed nature, he teaches them a mind of fixed nature.
This is called benefiting others through all practices. As for "excluding [certain forms of] benefiting others":

if there are sentient beings who lack a sense of shame and remorse, one teaches them to develop shame and remorse; for those who are coarse and violent, one teaches them to cultivate their minds; for those who are envious and jealous, one eliminates and destroys their envy; for those who are stingy and greedy, one eradicates and cuts off their stinginess; for those with doubting minds, one tears apart and removes their web of doubt. This is called excluding [certain forms of] benefiting others.

Regarding benefiting oneself and others: when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas constantly teach and transform sentient beings through the ten wholesome paths of action, this is called benefiting oneself and others.
Regarding the benefit of others through tranquility, there are ten kinds of goodness: five kinds of internal tranquility and five kinds of external tranquility.
The five internal [qualities] are: first, purity;
second, non-retrogression.
Third, sequential order;
fourth, universal presence;
fifth, conformity with wholesome dharmas.
Regarding "purity": it means that a bodhisattva does not use unwholesome dharmas, impure dharmas, or unvirtuous dharmas to teach sentient beings;

this is called purity. Regarding "non-reversal": it means that within liberation, a bodhisattva does not speak of non-liberation; within pure dharmas, he does not speak of impurity; and within non-perversion, he does not speak of perversion; this is called non-reversal.

To not speak of liberation regarding that which is not liberation, to not speak of purity within impure phenomena, and to not speak of non-perversion regarding perverted phenomena—this is called "non-reversal."

Regarding the sequence: when a bodhisattva perceives someone who is deluded, he teaches them shallow and easy meanings to subdue them; for those of medium faculties, he teaches the middle dharma; and for those of sharp faculties, he teaches the superior dharma.
First generosity is taught, next ethical discipline, and finally wisdom; this is called "sequential order.

Regarding "universal presence": when a bodhisattva teaches the Dharma, they do not consider the caste, lineage, poverty, or wealth of sentient beings, but rather teach the Dharma according to their capacity and wisdom so that those beings may attain peace and happiness; this is called "universal presence."

Regarding "conforming to wholesome dharmas": observing all sentient beings and teaching them according to the lower, middle, or superior dharmas they should attain is called conforming to wholesome dharmas.
Regarding the "five matters of external tranquility":
first, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates and accumulates immeasurable loving-kindness for the sake of sentient beings.
Second, undergoing immeasurable suffering for the sake of sentient beings;
third, attaining great joy upon seeing that sentient beings have obtained benefit;
fourth, attaining great mastery while remaining subject to sentient beings like a servant.
Fifth, there are bodhisattvas who possess great majestic power yet remain humble like the son of a candāla;
this is called benefiting others through inner and outer tranquility.
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s sharing of benefits?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has personally accomplished and perfected wholesome dharmas, and further exhorts and encourages sentient beings to do the same, this is called the bodhisattva’s sharing of benefits.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva teaches and transforms sentient beings for the sake of practicing together with them; once sentient beings have received these teachings, their minds become firm in wholesome dharmas and are difficult to incline or move. Why is this?
Sentient beings truly know that after the Bodhisattva has accomplished these wholesome dharmas, he turns them to exhort me, desiring to bring me peace and happiness.
If practicing wholesome dharmas were to result in evil matters, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva would never practice them himself nor exhort me to do so.

When a bodhisattva exhorts and transforms immeasurable sentient beings so that they share in their own benefit, there is not a single person who can say that the bodhisattva has not achieved it themselves yet exhorts others; nor is there anyone who says:
"You yourself are not good, so how can you exhort others to practice the wholesome Dharma?"

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who have achieved it themselves but cannot encourage others; those who have not achieved it themselves but can encourage others; those who have achieved it themselves and can encourage others; and those who have neither achieved it themselves nor can encourage others.

"To achieve it oneself and not exhort others" means that when one shares the same teacher, the same studies, the same Dharma, and the same virtues as others, one does not manifest one's own merit; this is called achieving it oneself and not exhorting others.

Regarding "being unable to achieve it oneself yet being able to exhort others": if a bodhisattva sees various evil sentient beings practicing unwholesome dharmas—ranging from outcastes (*caṇḍāla*) to animals—and for the sake of subduing them, takes on a body similar to theirs and engages in activities identical to theirs in order to destroy their evil karma, this is called "being unable to achieve it oneself yet being able to exhort others."

Regarding those who have achieved self-perfection and are able to exhort others: the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva personally accomplishes wholesome dharmas and also exhorts others to accomplish wholesome dharmas, thereby destroying arrogance, contemptuousness, and biased minds. This is called having achieved self-perfection and being able to exhort others.

There are those who do not achieve it themselves nor encourage others to do so: this refers to when a bodhisattva, due to their own negligence, is unable to teach, transform, and subdue sentient beings. A bodhisattva-mahāsattva adorns their own body with the six *pāramitās* and adorns sentient beings with the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). A bodhisattva-mahāsattva disciplines their own mind with the six *pāramitās* and disciplines the minds of sentient beings with the four methods of attraction. Because their body, speech, and mind are pure, the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) are pure; because their own person is pure, the minds of sentient beings are pure. Because they have accomplished a virtuous body and mind, it is called unsurpassed, peerless, and without equal.
To teach and transform sentient beings through this unsurpassed, peerless, and uncommon [teaching] is called "common benefit.
Regarding all sentient beings, time, and material things, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva makes no distinctions whatsoever.

Regarding those who are without discrimination among sentient beings: for the sake of sentient beings, the bodhisattva practices the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, seeking all wholesome dharmas.
Regarding "at that time, being without discrimination," it means that at all times, for the sake of sentient beings, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva diligently and vigorously seeks wholesome dharmas.
Regarding non-discrimination toward things: although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accept and store various items for the sake of sentient beings, their minds harbor no greedy attachment to these objects.
By virtue of these three causes and conditions of non-discrimination, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva joyfully delights in practicing and accumulating all wholesome deeds with a mind free from regret or retreat; through the causes and conditions of such practice and accumulation, he is able to destroy the false dharmas and false views of sentient beings, while his own roots of goodness cultivated through study increase. With a sincere heart, he contemplates the merit of wholesome conduct, which no false views can obstruct or destroy. He never seeks the body of a Wheel-Turning King, nor the bodies of Śakra, Māra, or Brahmā; he does not seek gratitude, profit, offerings, fame, long life, or physical pleasure.
When a bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates such dharmas as these, they then attain the fulfillment of the dāna-pāramitā up to the prajñā-pāramitā; this is called "common benefit."
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate the practice of common benefit, their minds remain unshakable and indestructible—pure, tranquil, brilliantly luminous, and free from obscuration.
Abiding in the Ground of Pure Mind, these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas fully accomplish the light of unsurpassed wholesome dharmas and virtuous dharmas.
Regarding the "wholesome dharmas of radiance," these are the wholesome dharmas practiced by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, which no one at all can disparage or destroy.
When the mind of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is unmoving, the wholesome dharmas they cultivate do not waver; they increase day and night like the crescent moon at its birth.
Regarding the "quiescent wholesome dharmas," the samādhi attained by the bodhisattva is as quiescent as that of a Tathāgata, and he is close to attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Because of the causes and conditions of all giving and precepts and all four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the vajra-body and the fruit of the dharma-body.
Because of the causes and conditions of giving and precepts that are difficult to practice, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva obtains the wondrous fruit of the inconceivable merit of the Tathāgata.
By virtue of the causes and conditions of one’s own practice of giving and precepts, one obtains the fruit of being honored and provided with offerings by all humans and devas.
By virtue of the causes and conditions of a virtuous person’s practice of giving and precepts, they become unsurpassed among all sentient beings.
By virtue of the causes and conditions of practicing all forms of giving and morality, one obtains the Tathāgata’s thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics.
By virtue of the causes and conditions of transcending both giving and morality, one attains the seat of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, such that the hosts of Māra cannot shake it.
By virtue of the causes and conditions of giving and precepts for the benefit of oneself and others, one attains the eternal bliss of liberation of the Tathāgata.

By virtue of the causes and conditions of the tranquility of giving and precepts, one attains the four fruits of tranquility, namely: tranquility of body, tranquility of objects, tranquility of mind, and tranquility of wisdom. For the sake of sentient beings, there are eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), such as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, the three foundations of mindfulness, the five knowledges, and samādhi. For the sake of benefiting wisdom, there are immeasurable numbers of unique qualities.
*Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, Scroll Five;
*Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kapiśā during the Song Dynasty.
Chapter 17: The Chapter on Making Offerings to the Triple Gem, from the Bodhisattvabhūmi.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva making offerings to the Tathāgata?
There are ten kinds of making offerings to the Tathāgata:
first, making offerings to the physical body;
second, making offerings to stūpas.
Third is worship through direct perception;
fourth is worship through non-direct perception;
fifth is personal worship.
Sixth, the offering of others;
seventh, the offering of benefit;
eighth, the supreme offering.
Ninth is the offering of purity;
tenth is the offering of upholding.
Regarding the offering to the form-body (*rūpakāya*): if a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the Buddha’s form-body and makes an offering to it, this is called making an offering to the form-body.

Regarding the offering to a stūpa: if a bodhisattva mahāsattva constructs stūpas, temples, images, or cave sanctuaries for the sake of the Tathāgata; repairs ruined, decayed, or ancient stūpas; or, upon seeing a new stūpa, makes offerings of flowers and incense—this is called making an offering to a stūpa.

Regarding "making offerings through direct perception": when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees an image of the Tathāgata, they regard it as seeing this very Buddha; seeing the Buddhas of the ten directions is likewise so. This is called making offerings through direct perception.

Regarding offerings made without direct perception: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes offerings to the Buddhas currently present or to their stūpas and shrines, they attain a mind of faith and understanding, thinking:
"I am now making these offerings while seeing them directly; by this, I also make offerings to the Buddhas of the past and the future."
Why is this? Because all Tathāgatas share the same single dharmatā; for this reason, one thereby makes offerings to the Buddhas of the past and the future.
If I make offerings to the stūpas of the present Buddhas, I likewise make offerings to the stūpas of the Buddhas of the past and the future.

Why is this? Because all such stupas share the same single *dharmatā*; if one makes offerings to a single Buddha, one has already made offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions, and if one makes offerings to a single stupa, one has already made offerings to the stupas of all Buddhas of the ten directions.
Constructing shrines and caves, repairing old stupas, and making offerings to stupas are likewise like this; these are called "offerings not witnessed.
Furthermore, regarding offerings not witnessed: if one does not see the Buddha or the Buddha-stupa, one forms a mental image and thinks, "This is the Tathāgata; this is the Buddha-stupa."
It is the same for all Buddhas, all stūpas, all caves, and all images; this is called "invisible worship. Furthermore, regarding invisible worship:

if, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, a bodhisattva establishes stūpas and temples or constructs shrines and caves for the sake of the Tathāgata—whether one, two, or even an immeasurable number according to their capacity—this is called "invisible worship."
Through such immeasurable fruits of merit, one gathers the immeasurable fruits of Brahma-merit.
By these causes and conditions, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not fall into the evil realms for immeasurable kalpas, and is also able to adorn the path to enlightenment.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva makes offerings without seeing the Three Jewels before their eyes, it surpasses the offerings made by those who see them; it is immeasurable and incomparable, and the resulting retribution cannot be fully described.

Ignorant people offer worship after having seen [the object] with their own eyes; wise people, although they do not see it directly, are nevertheless able to offer worship—this is called "worship of that which is not seen."

Regarding "making offerings by one's own hand": when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva makes offerings to the Buddha or to a stūpa, they manage the affairs personally and do not have others perform them; this is called making offerings by oneself.
Regarding "offering by others": when one wishes to make an offering to either a Buddha or a stūpa, one gathers many people and performs it collectively rather than acting alone.

These "many people" include parents, wives, children, kinsmen, relatives, and servants; kings, ministers, brahmins, and elders; neighbors, friends, intimates, and outsiders; men and women, the poor and the wealthy, those experiencing suffering and those experiencing pleasure; as well as teachers and preceptors, those with the same teacher or the same preceptor, those who dwell together, share the Dharma, study together, live in the same country, or have the same name and surname—even including those with wrong views and caṇḍālas. This is called "offering by others."

Furthermore, regarding others who provide offerings: if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses wealth and mastery, they bestow gifts upon sentient beings with a heart of compassion. At the time of giving, they make this vow: "Sentient beings are impoverished and suffering, lacking in merit.

Now that they have received these gifts, I shall exhort them to make offerings to the Triple Gem. By means of these causes and conditions of offering to the Triple Gem, they shall destroy their poverty and acquire great merit."

Having made this vow, he bestows gifts upon sentient beings; having bestowed them, he instructs them to make offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha—this is called "offering by means of others. Regarding "beneficial offering":

if a bodhisattva, with respect to the Buddha or a stūpa of the Buddha, offers robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and dwellings, and performs prostrations and reverent worship; furthermore, if he makes offerings of various kinds of mixed flowers, unguents, powdered incense, scattered incense, music, banners, canopies, and lamps; and again, if he praises the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata, prostrates himself on the ground, circumambulates to the right three times or even up to immeasurable times; and additionally, if he presents gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, conch shells, *kaustubha* stone, musaragalva, agate, as well as personal necklaces, bells, and chimes—even down to a single coin, a single thread, or a single grain of rice—this is called the bodhisattva’s beneficial offering.

Regarding the supreme offering: if a bodhisattva, with respect to the Buddha or a stūpa of the Buddha, performs offerings of benefit, constant offerings, offerings of excellent things, visible offerings, invisible offerings, personal offerings, offerings made by others, offerings made with a sincere heart, offerings made with a joyful heart, and offerings made with sincere patience and delight toward the Triple Gem—and dedicates such offerings toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—this is called the supreme offering.

Regarding pure offerings: when a bodhisattva makes offerings to the Buddha or a stūpa, they do so with their own hands, not by causing others to perform the task out of a mind of pride or contempt. They are free from negligence, acting with diligence, vigor, sincerity, and a pure heart. They do not offer out of a desire to inspire faith and respect in a sovereign, nor for the sake of receiving future offerings from kings, ministers, elders, or householders, nor to manifest their own personal merit. Furthermore, they do not smear the ground with yellow orpiment, egg yolk, lac, resin, oil, or ghee when fashioning images; they do not burn resin incense or aromatic incense as offerings, nor do they offer *pōkā* flowers or the like. They do not offer any foul-smelling flowers, even if they possess beautiful colors, nor do they offer any kind of putrid or filthy substance.
To be free from such forms of offering is called pure offering. Regarding the practice of receiving and maintaining offerings:

if a bodhisattva, with respect to the Buddha or a stūpa of the Buddha, either provides wealth from their own resources or seeks it from others, whether creating an image or constructing a stūpa—be it one, two, or even hundreds of thousands of immeasurable tens of billions of them—and before each stūpa and each image, they reverently prostrate and make offerings of exquisite flowers, incense, music, lamps, garlands, banners, and canopies; yet they do not, by reason of these offerings, seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor do they seek the path of the Buddha.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the stage of non-retrogression.
Having abided in this stage of non-retrogression, Bodhisattvas receive bodies in all Buddha-lands without obstruction.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not expend his own wealth nor seek the wealth of others, but makes this vow:

"If there are sentient beings in Jambudvīpa who are able to make offerings to the Triple Gem—the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha—and likewise all sentient beings from the four continents up to the trichiliocosm and throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions who offer to the Triple Gem with superior, middling, or inferior gifts, I shall follow their joy with a sincere heart."
He further made this vow:
"By these causes and conditions, may all sentient beings fully achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
This is called the Bodhisattva’s adornment of the path to unsurpassed bodhi; this is called making offerings in accordance with the Dharma.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates and accumulates the mind of loving-kindness for even the duration of a cow’s suckling, it is the same for the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. They deeply contemplate that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, selfless, without pleasure, and impure, while observing the subtle and wondrous merits of Nirvāṇa. They remain mindful of the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, generosity, precepts, and the devas, and so forth, until they do not perceive within the Dharmadhātu even a minute fraction of a characteristic that can be described. With a sincere heart, they practice the six pāramitās and gather in sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); this is called making offerings in accordance with the Dharma.

If there is a bhikṣu who always delights in seeing and reverently making offerings to stupas and images made of gold or silver, or to stupas and images made of crystal, pearl, musāragalva, agate, or jade, yet does not delight in seeing or reverently making offerings to stupas and images made of clay or wood, it should be known that this person’s practice of making offerings is not in accordance with the Dharma.
This is making an offering in accordance with the Dharma; it is called the unsurpassed offering, the peerless offering, and the supreme offering.
Such an offering excels all other offerings and can attain immeasurable and peerless fruits.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas make offerings to the Triple Gem for six reasons: first, because there is no field of merit superior to it;
second, because they recognize and repay kindness;
third, because it surpasses all beings—whether one-footed, two-footed, many-footed, or footless.
Fourth, because it is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower;
fifth, because one naturally attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without a teacher or preceptor;
sixth, because it enables sentient beings to obtain the causes for both worldly happiness and supramundane happiness.
The same applies to the Dharma and the Saṃgha.
When a bodhisattva wishes to receive the bodhisattva precepts, they should examine the preceptor; if the preceptor possesses eight qualities, one may then receive the precepts from them.
First, they must be fully endowed with the upāsaka precepts, the śrāmaṇera precepts, and the mahābhikṣu precepts.
Second, they are able to bring about offerings;
third, they are well able to observe the characteristics of those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them;
fourth, they attain śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Fifth, to possess a compassionate heart that takes pity on all;
sixth, to be able to relinquish one's own pleasure to bestow it upon sentient beings;
seventh, to be fearless.
Eighth, he does not preach what is contrary to the Dharma nor listen to what is contrary to the Dharma.

Toward those who preach what is contrary to the Dharma, he rebukes, admonishes, and provides analogies. He is able to endure all forms of suffering, including censure, destruction, beating, verbal abuse, and harassment. Regarding those who violate the precepts out of greed, hatred, or delusion, as well as those who are indolent, he expounds the Dharma in the midst of the assembly without declining the fatigue. He does not erroneously interpret the meaning, nor does he speak with error.
His speech is gentle and never coarse; he constantly keeps sentient beings in mind, desiring to bring them peace and happiness.
Whenever he has doubts, he immediately requests clarification without harboring any sense of shame.
He is skilled in knowing the expedient means for teaching and transforming sentient beings.
Knowing the remedies for the afflictions of all sentient beings, his mind is impartial toward them all, without distinction between the noble and the base or the high and the low.
His six sense faculties are complete, and his deportment is composed and orderly.
Do not believe slanderous words; maintain pure conduct and do not be self-conceited or look down upon others. Do not manifest flattery or crookedness for the sake of gain and support.
Abandon greed, envy, and stinginess; if you obtain benefit yourself, first offer it to others.
His mind was always single-minded and free from negligence; seeing others obtain benefit, he rejoiced as if it were his own.
Contented and possessing few desires, he kept only six articles; beyond these six articles, whatever he obtained, he gave away immediately.
He constantly exhorts others to confess their transgressions as soon as they occur, demonstrating to them the method for mindfulness and knowing how to repent.
He is skilled at caring for those suffering from illness.
He never proclaims the faults of the Śrāvaka-piṭaka or the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
If there is one who is fully endowed with such qualities, they may serve as an upādhyāya.
Once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has received the precepts, if the upādhyāya is ill, he should serve him; if he is not ill, he should act according to his instructions.

One should give rise to a mind of profound reverence and respect, welcoming [the teacher] and prostrating, attending to them at their side, and offering clothing, food, bedding, and medicine. One should comply with their Dharma-exhortations, acting in accordance with the Dharma without wavering, and confessing whatever transgressions have been committed with complete sincerity.

When listening to the Dharma, if one forms the perception of the Buddha, the perception of the Saṃgha of bhikṣus, the perception of it being difficult to encounter, the perception of the eye of wisdom, the perception of it being the cause of great knowledge, the perception of it being a great radiance, the perception of attaining a great fruit and retribution, the perception of it being the cause for the unsurpassed path of Great Nirvāṇa, and the perception of attaining permanence, bliss, tranquility (śamatha), and insight (vipaśyanā)—one who forms such perceptions possesses the true perception of the Dharma; this is called being fully endowed with the merit of listening to the Dharma.
Furthermore, when listening to the Dharma, one should listen with a focused mind and with faith; one should not think to oneself:
"I should not now inquire about the Dharma from one who has broken the precepts, who is of low birth, whose faculties are incomplete, who speaks improperly, or who is of a wicked nature."
"Free from such thoughts, one listens to the Dharma with a sincere mind.
There are two kinds of bodhisattva precepts received by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva:
the first is wisdom;"
Second is delusion.
If one engages in the aforementioned contemplation and reflection, this is called ignorance; it does not increase wholesome dharmas nor does one attain great wisdom.
A bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates the four immeasurable minds: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
The four immeasurable minds are of three kinds:
first, those with sentient beings as their object; second, those with phenomena as their object; [and third, those with no object].
Third is the objectless [compassion].

Regarding the object of sentient beings, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates and accumulates a mind of loving-kindness, clearly observing all sentient beings of the three categories: first, those experiencing pleasure; second, those experiencing suffering; and third, those experiencing neither suffering nor pleasure.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate and accumulate a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they contemplate those experiencing pleasure so that it may increase; they contemplate suffering sentient beings so that their suffering may be extinguished and joy may arise; and they contemplate those who experience neither suffering nor pleasure so that they may eliminate both suffering and pleasure and attain *nirvāṇa*. This is called the "object-condition of sentient beings" (*sattvālambana*).
Regarding the object of phenomena (*dharmālambana*): the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates only the characteristics of phenomena and does not form the notion of sentient beings. [He reflects:
"If I cultivate loving-kindness without sentient beings, who is it that attains liberation from suffering?"
Who is it that attains the experience of bliss?

This is called "having dharmas as an object" (*dharmālambana*). As for "having no object" (*anālambana*), it means relinquishing the perception of sentient beings and the perception of dharmas to increase the mind of loving-kindness; this is called "having no object."
As it is with loving-kindness, so it is with the other three immeasurables.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates these immeasurable minds because of sentient beings, one should know that such minds are no different from those of non-Buddhists, and are shared in common with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
When the four immeasurable minds of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva are integrated, they constitute compassion; therefore, a bodhisattva is called "one of great compassion" (mahākaruṇā).

The bodhisattva observes that there are one hundred and ten ways in which sentient beings undergo suffering, and for the sake of eliminating this suffering, he cultivates and accumulates great compassion.
What are these one hundred and ten?
First is the suffering of birth.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
First is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
second is the suffering of losing what has been obtained.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
First is the suffering of suffering;
second is the suffering of conditioned existence;
third is the suffering of change.
Furthermore, there are four kinds:
first, the suffering of separation from what is loved;
second, the suffering of encountering what is hated.
Third is the suffering of death;
fourth is the suffering of the non-extinction of the five aggregates.
Furthermore, there are five kinds:
First, suffering caused by desire;
second, suffering caused by hatred;
third, suffering caused by sleep.
Fourth is the suffering caused by restlessness and regret;
fifth is the suffering caused by doubt.
Furthermore, there are six kinds:
First, the suffering of the causes of the evil realms;
second, the suffering of the results of the evil realms;
third, the suffering of excessive seeking.
Fourth is the suffering of guarding;
fifth is the suffering of insatiable acquisition;
sixth is the suffering of loss.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds:
first, the suffering of birth;
second, the suffering of old age; [and so forth].
Third, the suffering of illness;
fourth, the suffering of death;
fifth, the suffering of separation from what is loved;
Sixth is the suffering of association with the disliked;
seventh is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds:
First, the suffering of cold;
second, the suffering of heat;
third, the suffering of hunger.
Fourth is the suffering of thirst;
fifth is the suffering of lacking self-mastery;
sixth is the suffering of one's own making, such as that of the Nirgranthas.
Seventh is suffering caused by others, such as royal service and the like;
eighth is the suffering of long-term postures.
Furthermore, there are nine kinds:
First, the suffering of one's own poverty;
second, the suffering of others' poverty;
third, the suffering of the loss of loved ones.
Fourth is the suffering of losing wealth and property;
fifth is the suffering of illness;
sixth is the suffering of breaking the precepts.
Seventh is the suffering of wrong views;
eighth is present suffering;
ninth is the suffering of future lives.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds:
first, the suffering of having food but no vessel;
second, the suffering of traveling on foot without a vehicle.
Third, the suffering of not obtaining necklaces, flowers, or incense when seeking them;
fourth, the suffering of not obtaining music, entertainment, or play when searching for them;
fifth, the suffering of not obtaining light when seeking it.
Sixth, not suffering when seeking servants;
seventh, not suffering when seeking drink;
eighth, not suffering when seeking clothing.
Ninth, obtaining what is not desired;
tenth, seeing those who come seeking [what they desire].
Furthermore, there are nine kinds:
First, all suffering; second, great suffering;
third, all self-inflicted suffering.
Fourth is the suffering of not abiding in accordance with the Dharma;
fifth is the suffering of transformation;
sixth is the suffering of lack of autonomy.
Seventh is the suffering of harm;
eighth is the suffering of pursuit;
ninth is the suffering of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
"All suffering" refers to obtaining present suffering due to causes from the past.
"Great suffering" refers to how sentient beings undergo the sufferings of the hells throughout immeasurable lifetimes.
All forms of self-inflicted suffering include the sufferings found among hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas.

Suffering from dwelling unrighteously includes: the calamity one suffers when, having plotted to harm another, the scheme fails and one instead meets with disaster; the great suffering one undergoes after craving food and drink; the suffering of contemplating desire, hatred, and delusion; the suffering endured due to evil karma of body, speech, and mind; and the sorrowful suffering incurred by violating the precepts.

Regarding the transformation of suffering: it is like the present body of a king transforming in another world into the suffering of a slave; it is like present parents, brothers, wives, and children transforming in another world into the suffering of enemies and those one hates; it is like being immensely wealthy in the present transforming in another world into the suffering of poverty.

The suffering of lacking mastery refers to the distress of not obtaining one's desires, such as wishing for long life, wishing for physical beauty, wishing for birth in a noble family, wishing for wealth and status, wishing for physical strength, wishing for wisdom, or wishing to eliminate enemies.

Regarding the suffering of harm: it is like people in the world who seek to overcome poverty but cannot overcome the suffering [of its persistence]; or like those who have left the household life and seek to destroy their afflictions but cannot destroy the suffering [of their persistence]. It is also like the suffering of difficult tasks, the suffering of the outbreak of war, the suffering of traveling on a desolate road, the suffering of having one's hands and feet cut off, the suffering of being imprisoned, beaten, and bound, and the suffering of being driven out and banished.

"All conditioned phenomena are suffering" means: suffering due to the cause of suffering; suffering due to the departure from pleasure; suffering because all sensations have not been severed; suffering of being unable to leave the household life; suffering of being unable to attain tranquility; suffering of not attaining bodhi; suffering of the proliferation of discursive thoughts; the suffering of ordinary worldlings; the suffering of the four great elements; the suffering of the three realms; and the suffering of the afflictions.
These are called the one hundred and ten sufferings.
When a bodhisattva contemplates such sufferings as these, great compassion increases.
Such great suffering grows by means of eighteen kinds of causes.
What are the eighteen?
First is the suffering of ignorance;
second is the suffering of experiencing the retribution of karma.
Third is the suffering of conditioned existence;
fourth is the suffering of permanence;
fifth is the suffering of birth.
Sixth, suffering created by oneself;
seventh, suffering created by others;
eighth, suffering resulting from the breaking of precepts.
Ninth, the suffering of wrong views;
tenth, the suffering of the past world;
eleventh, great suffering.
Twelfth is the suffering of the hells;
thirteenth is the suffering of humans and devas;
fourteenth is the suffering of transmigration.
Fifteenth is the suffering of experiencing pain;
sixteenth is the ignorance of suffering;
seventeenth is the increase of suffering.

Eighteenth is the suffering of indolence. A bodhisattva is said to possess great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) by virtue of four causes and conditions: first, to contemplate with precision that the causes and conditions for sentient beings' suffering are profound and difficult to understand; [the other three are as follows: second, to contemplate with precision that the duration of sentient beings' suffering is long and difficult to exhaust; third, to contemplate with precision that the nature of sentient beings' suffering is subtle and difficult to perceive; and fourth, to contemplate with precision that the remedy for sentient beings' suffering is difficult to apply. Because they contemplate these four matters with such depth, bodhisattvas are called those of great compassion. Furthermore, because they do not abandon sentient beings who suffer due to these four causes and conditions, they are called those of great compassion. Moreover, because they generate the thought of supreme, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) for the sake of liberating sentient beings from these four causes and conditions of suffering, they are called those of great compassion. Furthermore, because they endure all manner of suffering for the sake of liberating sentient beings from these four causes and conditions of suffering, they are called those of great compassion. Furthermore, because they seek the Dharma for the sake of liberating sentient beings from these four causes and conditions of suffering, they are called those of great compassion. Furthermore, because they manifest the power of the Buddha’s wisdom for the sake of liberating sentient beings from these four causes and conditions of suffering, they are called those of great compassion. Furthermore, because they manifest the power of the Buddha’s liberation for the sake of liberating sentient beings from these four causes and conditions of suffering, they are called those of great compassion. Furthermore, because they manifest the power of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision of liberation for the sake of liberating sentient beings from these four causes and conditions of suffering, they are called those of great compassion. Furthermore, because they manifest the power of the Buddha’s ten powers (*daśa-bala*) for the sake of liberating sentient beings from these four causes and conditions of suffering, they are called those of great compassion. Furthermore, because they manifest the power of the Buddha’s immeasurable and boundless light for the sake of liberating sentient beings from these four causes and conditions of suffering, they are called those of great compassion. Furthermore, because they manifest the power of the Buddha’s immeasurable and boundless life-span for the sake of liberating sentient beings from these four causes and conditions of suffering, they are called those of great compassion. Furthermore, because they manifest the power of the Buddha’s immeasurable and boundless assemblies for the sake of liberating sentient beings from these four causes and conditions
Second, they have been cultivated and accumulated over immeasurable lifetimes;
third, they have been cultivated and accumulated with a sincere mind;
fourth, because of that sincere mind, one does not begrudge even body or life for the sake of sentient beings.

By virtue of these four causes and conditions, one is able to labor with humility for the sake of sentient beings, enduring suffering and accepting a body of suffering; therefore, the bodhisattva is called "Pure Great Compassion," and Pure Great Compassion is termed the stage of the Tathāgata.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates these one hundred and ten matters, which all Bodhisattvas collectively cultivate and assemble; for the sake of sentient beings, he increases his great compassion.

In this way, while a bodhisattva can give rise to great compassion by observing sentient beings and the characteristics of phenomena, they cannot give rise to great compassion by observing the characteristic of the objectless; therefore, it cannot be called "great compassion.
Because the Tathāgata is fully endowed with these three types [of observation], it is called "great compassion."

Because the Bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he attains tranquility of body and tranquility of mind. By virtue of these causes and conditions of physical and mental tranquility, he is able to destroy all the afflictions of sentient beings; he dwells on the Pure Grounds and the Ground of the Only Son, loving all sentient beings as if they were his own children.

By virtue of the causal conditions of great compassion, one diligently practices asceticism for the sake of all sentient beings with a mind free from regret or retreat; just as one experiences untainted bliss when awakening to the Four Noble Truths through the path of the śrāvaka, so too is it for a bodhisattva cultivating compassion.
When a bodhisattva cultivates compassion, it is solely for the sake of sentient beings and not for the sake of their own person; this is the causal condition for cultivating compassion.

For the causal conditions of cultivating compassion, the bodhisattva does not begrudge even their own body and life, nor external wealth and possessions. Through the causal conditions of cultivating compassion, they undergo the relinquishing of one body and the taking up of another, yet they never violate or lose the prohibitive precepts of the Tathāgata. They are able to attain samādhis that are difficult to obtain, and they are able to attain wisdom that is difficult to obtain.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has said in the sūtras:
"In what does the bodhisattva’s anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi abide?
It should be said that it abides in great compassion."
Because it is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable, it is called "Great Compassion.

When Bodhisattvas cultivate and accumulate this immeasurable mind, they attain happiness in the present life, enable sentient beings to distance themselves from suffering and affliction, and acquire an immeasurable, unsurpassed mass of merit that adorns *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

18. Chapter Eighteen: The Thirty-Seven Factors of Enlightenment in the Bodhisattva-bhūmi. "What is meant by the sense of shame (*hrī*) and the dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
There are two kinds of shame and remorse:
first, that which is innate;
second, that which arises from causes and conditions.

Regarding "nature" (prakṛti): it is when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, knowing for himself that what he has done is contrary to the Dharma, gives rise to shame and remorse out of fear of its evil retribution.
Regarding "condition" (pratyaya): it is when a bodhisattva, regarding an evil deed committed by himself, gives rise to shame and remorse because he fears others might find out.
Those whose nature is shame and remorse obtain it not through causes and conditions, as is the case with the nature of a bodhisattva.
Those who cultivate shame and remorse obtain them through causes and conditions, as is the case with the eightfold noble path.
There are four kinds of shame and remorse:
first, the arising of shame and remorse for having done what should not have been done;
second, the arising of shame and remorse for not having done what should have been done.
Third, one gives rise to shame and remorse because doubt arises within one's own mind;
fourth, one gives rise to shame and remorse because one fears others will discover the concealed transgressions.
What is meant by the term "bodhisattva"?
"Sattva" means being courageous, valiant, and fearless. The nature of a bodhisattva inherently possesses vigorous strength;

because this nature is valiant, they are able to subdue afflictions and not follow their whims. They can endure various sufferings and manifold terrors; even when faced with fear, they cannot be shaken from the adornments of all the bodhisattva's wholesome dharmas. This is called the power of innate valor, and for this reason, one is named a Bodhisattva.
There are five causes and conditions for the courageous and robust power of a bodhisattva:
first, the various sufferings of birth and death;
second, the various evil karmas committed by sentient beings.
Third, to benefit sentient beings throughout immeasurable lifetimes and undergo immeasurable suffering;
fourth, to wholeheartedly uphold the bodhisattva precepts;
and fifth, to wholeheartedly listen to and receive the profound Dharma.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have five causes and conditions by which they undergo great and piercing suffering for the sake of all sentient beings, yet their minds remain free from sorrow and affliction.
First, because they possess great courage and strength;
second, because they have cultivated and accumulated freedom from sorrow.
Third, because of being vigorous and diligent through skillful means;
fourth, because of the vigor of the power of wisdom;
and fifth, because of cultivating a compassionate mind with single-minded mindfulness.
How does a bodhisattva understand worldly books? A bodhisattva skillfully knows the arts and techniques of the world;

they know the characters, the phrases, the terminology, and the meanings. With mind and speech in harmony, they single-mindedly contemplate, receive, and uphold them. This is called the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the teachings (*dharma*) and their meanings (*artha*).

Because they know the teachings and their meanings, they are able to explain them to others. Through the causes and conditions of such explanation, their knowledge of the teachings and knowledge of the meanings increase. This is called the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
By means of these causes and conditions of the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection, the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣa-dharma) increase.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the world?
There are two kinds of worlds:
The first is the world of sentient beings;
the second is the receptacle world.
Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the world of sentient beings, the sūtra says:
"Worldly asceticism is experienced within birth and death; because one does not understand birth and death, one cannot attain liberation.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands the world of sentient beings; therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Sentient beings have five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya):"
First is the impurity of lifespan;
second is the impurity of sentient beings;
third is the impurity of afflictions.
"Fourth is the defilement of views;
fifth is the defilement of the eon.
As the human lifespan today does not exceed one hundred years, this is called the defilement of life."

Nowadays, sentient beings are unable to practice filial piety toward their parents, teachers, preceptors, śramaṇas, and brahmins; they do not act in accordance with righteousness, they have no fear of the present or future worlds, they do not delight in giving, they do not rejoice in merit, and they do not take pleasure in observing the fasts, maintaining the precepts, or practicing diligence—this is called the defilement of sentient beings.

Nowadays, because of their afflictions (*kleśa*), sentient beings kill their parents; they commit unlawful acts against their mothers, sisters, and other relatives; and for the sake of creating evil conditions for sentient beings, they take up bows, arrows, swords, staves, and spears. Many sentient beings engage in lying, divisive speech, harsh words, and idle chatter. When such immeasurable evils, unwholesome states, and afflictions arise, this is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśakaṣāya*).

Nowadays, sentient beings view what is not the Dharma as the Dharma and view the Dharma as not the Dharma; they preach what is not the Dharma as the Dharma and preach the Dharma as not the Dharma. Because of these views and teachings, they destroy the True Dharma and increase false dharmas, causing immeasurable sentient beings to cultivate and accumulate wrong views. This is called the turbidity of views (dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya).
