second, the inner skin.
Third is the bone.

When one attains the practice of joy (*prīti-caryā*), the obstruction of the skin is severed; when one attains the practice of signlessness (*animitta-caryā*), the obstruction of the flesh is severed; and when one attains the practice of the Tathāgata, the obstruction of the bone is severed.

By being fully endowed with such practices as these, one attains eleven purities: through the first practice, one attains purity of nature; through the second, purity of liberation; through the third, purity of mind; through the fourth, purity of precepts; through the fifth, purity of vows; through the sixth, seventh, and eighth, purity of the adornment of wisdom; through the ninth, purity of the adornment of bodhi; through the tenth, purity of true wisdom; through the eleventh, purity of unimpeded wisdom; through the twelfth, purity of all-knowledge; and through the thirteenth, purity of habitual tendencies.

In the first and second stages, upon hearing the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, one attains faith; in the third stage, one establishes the vow with a sincere mind to cultivate and accumulate the remaining practices; in the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, one thoroughly understands the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); and from the seventh through the thirteenth stages, one perfects all practices regarding the causes and effects of tranquility.

The Śrāvakas also have twelve kinds of practice: possessing the nature of a Śrāvaka is called the first practice; attaining the supreme worldly dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is called the second practice; attaining the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*) is called the third practice; attaining the fourfold faith and the purity of precepts is called the fourth practice; abiding in the Dharma according to the precepts so that it increases is called the fifth practice; contemplating the Four Noble Truths is called the sixth, seventh, and eighth practices; cultivating and accumulating the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*) is called the ninth practice; being fully accomplished in the three samādhis is called the tenth practice; attaining liberation is called the eleventh practice; and the fruit of Arhatship is called the twelfth practice.

Chapter One: The Arising of the Ultimate Ground The arising of a bodhisattva possesses five kinds of "all-encompassing" qualities; all practices and all purities of a bodhisattva are for the sake of establishing sentient beings in peace and happiness.
First, existence for the sake of leaving suffering;
second, existence that follows the movement of the mind;
third, superior existence.
Fourth is the existence of mastery;
fifth is the subsequent existence of a bodhisattva.

Regarding the "existence remote from suffering": if a bodhisattva sees sentient beings afflicted by the suffering of hunger and thirst during a time of famine and high grain prices, the bodhisattva, through the power of their vows, assumes the body of a great fish many *yojanas* in length to give to those beings. Once the beings have eaten and their hunger and thirst are removed, the bodhisattva’s body continues to grow larger through the power of their vows.

If, in an evil age, all sentient beings should simultaneously be afflicted by the four hundred and four diseases, the Bodhisattva at that time, through the power of his great vows, acts as a great king of physicians, able to cause sentient beings to be far removed from the suffering of illness.

If there is an evil age when weapons and armor arise in competition and sentient beings are terrified, and when lords of the earth contend for kingdoms without knowing contentment, at that time the Bodhisattva becomes a Great Dharma King of great power and influence. Through skillful means, he reconciles the two adversaries; by means of gentle speech, he destroys their malevolent intentions. He does not strike them, nor punish them, nor confine them, nor bind them; he does not take their lives or seize their wealth and treasures. He regards all sentient beings equally as if they were his only child, feeling compassion for them.

If there are those with wrong views who perform perverse deeds to make offerings to celestial deities, the Bodhisattva manifests in the form of a ghost to destroy such wrong views, appearing in their dreams to instruct them, saying:
"You should not now slaughter sheep for sacrificial offerings."

Therefore, for the sake of destroying the various sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings, the Bodhisattva manifests the acceptance of various states of existence; this is called "existence apart from suffering.

Regarding "existence that follows the movement of the mind," because of their power of vows, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas manifest the acceptance of various bodies among animals in order to destroy the various evil karmas of animals. They manifest as the bodies of evil ghosts or evil humans, or again as the bodies of Brahmins with false views, or they may manifest as those who crave the five desires. First, they follow the inclinations of others' minds to manifest the acceptance of various existences, in order to cause sentient beings to leave behind evil karma.

Although they assume a physical body, they do not commit evil deeds; even when others are committing them, they never do so themselves, and when sentient beings see this, they likewise refrain from doing so.
By means of skillful expedients, they destroy all the evil karma of sentient beings; this is called "existence according to the movement of the mind."

Regarding "superior existence": when a bodhisattva is born, they surpass all other sentient beings in terms of lineage, physical appearance, lifespan, and karmic fruition. As for this karmic fruition, it is as explained in the "Chapter on Benefiting Self and Others. This is called having mastery over superior existence.

When the Bodhisattva cultivates the first stage of joy up to the twelfth stage of practice, the body he manifests at that time is called "sovereign"; this sovereignty is precisely the power of his vows.

From the stage of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā-bhūmi) up to the twelve practices, they assume the bodies of universal monarchs (cakravartin), the bodies of the sovereign gods (Īśvara), and even the bodies of the Akaniṣṭha gods, as well as all states of existence beyond the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Within all states of existence, one attains the supreme body by means of the power of vows and the power of karma; this is called sovereign existence (*vaśitā-bhava*).
As for the "subsequent existence" of a bodhisattva, the final body of a bodhisattva is termed the "bodhisattva existence."

Fully accomplishing the adornment of bodhi, whether born into the Brahmin caste or the Kṣatriya caste, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and performs all the works of a Buddha; this is called the "subsequent existence" of a bodhisattva.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past also underwent these five kinds of existence, and those of the present and future will likewise do so; by means of these five existences, they attain the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If there is a bodhisattva who practices and manifests the acceptance of these five forms of existence, they shall immediately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
*Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, Scroll Eight;
*Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇavarman of Kapiśī during the Song Dynasty.
Chapter Two: On Gathering. Chapter Two: On Gathering in the Ultimate Stage.

"When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices all deeds, there are six matters through which he skillfully gathers sentient beings: [1] giving material gifts; [2] speaking with gentle words; [3] acting for the benefit of others; [4] practicing concordant conduct; [5] teaching the Dharma according to their faculties; and [6] establishing them in the ultimate fruit."
First, grasping with a sincere mind;
second, grasping through augmentation;
third, grasping by way of taking up.
Fourth is ultimate appropriation;
fifth is non-ultimate appropriation;
sixth is subsequent appropriation.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first resolves to attain enlightenment, they embrace sentient beings as their own parents, brothers, wives, children, and kinsmen; with a sincere mind and focused mindfulness, they employ skillful means to embrace them, thinking: "How can I bestow peace and happiness upon these sentient beings?"
When making such a vow, one gives according to one's ability; this is called a bodhisattva’s wholehearted gathering [of beings].
Although a bodhisattva-mahāsattva may excel over their parents, brothers, wife, children, and kinsmen, they harbor no pride in their heart, but rather increase their offerings to them.
If one acts as a king, the treatment of his retinue is likewise. As for those who increase [his virtue]:

he destroys evil dharmas and instructs them in wholesome dharmas; he pays them homage, praises them, and makes offerings to them at the appropriate times; he bestows upon them clothing, food, and all necessary items; he recognizes their kindness and repays it by attending to them when ill and providing medicine; he does not regard his servants as lowly but regards them as brothers; if he sees them commit a transgression, he endures and accepts it with patience, and his speech is always gentle and never harsh.

If one acts as a sovereign of a nation, refraining from inflicting suffering upon his kinsmen and not taking their lives, remaining far removed from punishments and ruling the country with the True Dharma;

if he does not give rise to greed or seizure regarding the territories belonging to other nations according to the boundaries of his ancestral lineage; if he nurtures the people according to his power, regarding them as his only son; if he shares all possessions with his kinsmen; if his speech is truthful, gentle, and not coarse, and is free from stinginess and greed—this is called the Bodhisattva’s gathering through increase.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas embrace all sentient beings through two causes and conditions:
first, the giving of material wealth;
second, the giving of the Dharma.
Through the gift of material wealth, one destroys poverty; through the gift of the Dharma, one destroys wrong views.

One maintains an impartial mind toward all sentient beings, refraining from stinginess regarding the Dharma and avoiding the conceit of thinking oneself a teacher. One does not seek gratitude nor do one seek offerings; yet, if there are those who come to offer gifts seeking merit, one does not refuse them, so as to cause their adornment of merit to increase.

If there are those who cultivate and accumulate wholesome dharmas, uphold the precepts, and practice diligence, he regards them with care, makes offerings to them, and personally serves as their attendant.

To those who do not understand the meaning, he explains the meaning for them; to those who already understand the meaning, he speaks so as to cause it to increase. If there are those caught in the net of doubt, he explains the profound meaning for them, enabling them to sever and eliminate it. Whether in suffering or joy, he shares equally with them, his mind remaining without increase or decrease.
When there are those who have committed offenses, they teach them through skillful means to repent; at times they reprove them, and at other times they praise them.
Seeing those afflicted by illness and suffering, they attend to them without abandoning them, skillfully employing expedient means to eliminate their ailments.

If there are sentient beings who possess inferior appearance, inferior diligence, inferior mindfulness, and inferior wisdom, he does not treat them with contempt, but preaches the causes and conditions for a correct mind to them at the appropriate time.
Seeing those who are distressed and suffering, he preaches the Dharma to comfort and console them.
Reflect well upon this yourself; do not rely on the words of others, for none shall be able to move you.
If you obtain what is bestowed, share it equally with the assembly.
Cultivate and gather compassion until it is fully perfected.

Or they may see one who maintains a right livelihood, who first greets others with kind inquiry, who stays far removed from evil thoughts and constantly cultivates wholesome dharmas, and who never indulges in negligence or succumbs to indolence.
Such a person always makes this vow:
"How may my merit and virtue be made equal to those of all beings?"
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not practice grasping or taking up at all times; rather, they take up [things] only when it is beneficial. This is called the bodhisattva’s grasping and taking up.
If sentient beings have dull faculties and their roots of goodness are difficult to ripen, then they are gathered for a long duration. Why is this?
Because they will ultimately possess a pure mind.
If those of middling faculties reach maturity at a middling level, it will not take long. Why is this?
Because they will attain a pure mind before long.
If there are those with sharp faculties who are easily ripened, thoroughly ripened, easily purified, and easily disciplined, this is called the bodhisattva’s subsequent appropriation.
This is called the bodhisattva’s sixfold appropriation, which is the appropriation of the true Dharma.

By means of these six means of attraction, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas gather in all sentient beings of the three periods of time; the Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present who gather in sentient beings do so entirely without departing from these six means of attraction.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas gather in sentient beings, there are twelve difficult matters.

That Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, knowing there is no self and nothing belonging to a self, and that there are no sentient beings, yet practice and accumulate ascetic austerities for the sake of sentient beings—this is called the first difficulty.
To administer reprimands for the sake of disciplining others, while also protecting one’s own precepts so as not to let them be violated or damaged—this is called the second difficulty.
To have few possessions while beggars are very numerous—this is called the third difficulty.
That a bodhisattva’s single body is bound to many people, serving them by running about and attending to their needs, is called the fourth difficulty.
That devas who are heedless take on bodies similar to theirs, yet within their own minds they are never at all heedless, is called the fifth difficulty.
Constantly acting as a servant for all sentient beings, yet personally never violating or losing one’s own prohibitive precepts—this is called the sixth difficulty.
Constantly dwelling together with those who are greedy, hateful, deluded, stingy, deceitful, crooked, treacherous, and wicked, yet not following their conduct—this is called the seventh difficulty.
To fully understand that birth and death are fraught with many faults and afflictions, yet not renounce them, is called the eighth difficulty.

All afflictions and births and deaths abound in faults; at the time of casting off one's life, the mind is not yet pure. Although it is not yet pure, one does not lose right mindfulness—this is called the ninth difficulty.
To be able to give away to others one's own beloved possessions, wife, children, and kinsmen before having attained a pure mind—this is called the tenth difficulty.

Sentient beings have diverse minds and different spheres of experience; at times one must speak with gentle words, and at times one must practice relinquishment—this is called the eleventh difficulty.
To never be free from negligence and to never sever the afflictions is called the twelfth difficulty.

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not treat all sentient beings as either light or heavy; at times he treats them lightly, and at times he treats them heavily. At times he contemplates their objective realms, or cultivates a resolute mind; at times he establishes vows, or practices non-negligence; at times he cultivates wisdom, or cultivates gentleness; at times he practices self-reproach, or at times he practices equanimity; at times he exerts diligent effort, or at times he is indolent, or he employs skillful means.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas train in this manner, their minds feel no sorrow or regret regarding the twelve difficult places; they are thus able to protect themselves and also benefit others.

Chapter Three: The Ultimate Stage (Niṣṭhā-bhūmi) "Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate twelve practices across seven stages: six are the stages of Bodhisattvas alone, while the remaining one stage is shared by Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas."
First, the stage of the nature;
second, the stage of understanding;
third, the stage of the pure mind.
Fourth is the stage of maintaining the ground;
fifth is the stage of concentration;
sixth is the stage of the practice of concentration.

Seventh is the stage of ultimate consummation (*atyanta-bhūmi*); this is called the seventh stage. The stage of natural conduct (*prakṛti-carita*) and the stage of conduct through understanding (*adhimukti-carita*) each constitute one stage. The stage of joyful conduct (*pramudita-carita*) is named the Stage of the Pure Mind (*śuddha-citta-bhūmi*). The stages of ethical conduct (*śīla-carita*), wisdom conduct (*prajñā-carita*), and signless conduct (*animitta-carita*) together constitute the Stage of Sustenance (*dhāraṇī-bhūmi*). The stage of non-action and signless conduct is named the Stage of Concentration (*samādhi-bhūmi*). The stage of unimpeded wisdom conduct is named the Stage of the Practice of Concentration (*samādhi-carita-bhūmi*). The stage of Tathāgata conduct is named the Stage of Ultimate Consummation; this Stage of Ultimate Consummation shall be explained in detail hereafter.
When a bodhisattva enters the Ground of Pure Mind from a lower ground, how is it that they are able to sever the suffering of the three evil realms?

The bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates mundane *sāsrava* dhyāna; having cultivated *sāsrava* dhyāna, they attain mundane pure (*anāsrava*) dhyāna; having cultivated pure dhyāna, they immediately attain the Ground of Liberation.

Adorning bodhi by cultivating and accumulating one hundred and ten kinds of compassion; because of cultivating compassion, one attains a compassionate heart toward sentient beings, and because of attaining a compassionate heart, one regards the three evil realms with joy as if they were one’s own home.

When a bodhisattva observes for themselves that they abide in the three evil realms as an adornment of enlightenment, they undergo great suffering and affliction for the sake of sentient beings, thinking: "If my pure mind possesses power, I vow that all the sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings shall gather entirely within my own body."

"Having well established great vows, because of the power of those virtuous vows and through world-purifying dhyāna, one distances oneself from the afflictions and habitual tendencies of body and mind. Because these habitual tendencies are abandoned, the body composed of the four great elements is transformed; since the four great elements are thus transformed by means of world-purifying dhyāna, one does not fall into the three evil realms. Therefore, the Bodhisattva cuts off the suffering of the three evil paths."

Having transcended the stage of understanding (*adhimukti-bhūmi*), one enters the pure stage (*śuddha-bhūmi*). The remaining virtues are as explained in the "Chapter on Practice" (*Caryā-paṭala*) regarding the ten pure minds.

These ten pure dharmas have ten corresponding antidotes: the mind that does not act, the mind that does not resolve [to attain enlightenment], the non-reception of the bodhisattva precepts, lack of faith, an evil mind, the failure to cultivate compassion, a mind of anger, a mind of regret and remorse, a lack of loving-kindness, and a mind of negligence; furthermore, speaking harshly, being stingy with one's body and life, not following the world, indolence and laziness, lack of shame and lack of dread of blame, being oppressed by physical suffering, the net of doubt and cowardice, and being unable to make offerings to the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
These and others are the remedies for impurity.
Among these ten purities, the first three dharmas purify the mind, while the latter seven dharmas purify adornment.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva has faith in awakening and the path to awakening; because of this faith in the path to awakening, they perceive suffering sentient beings and give rise to great compassion. Because they have given rise to a compassionate mind, they immediately form this vow:
"May I rescue and deliver such suffering beings as these."

Out of compassion, he gives away his body in charity without any greed or regret; for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, his mind is free from sorrow or remorse. Because his mind has no remorse, he understands the worldly arts and techniques (*laukika-vidyā*). Because he understands these worldly arts, he skillfully knows the proper seasons and accords with the minds of sentient beings; because he knows the seasons, he is said to "know the world. By virtue of this power of wisdom, when adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*) arise, he feels deep shame and remorse. Because of this shame and remorse, those afflictions are rendered powerless; this is called "courageous vigor" (*vīryavān*). Because of this courageous vigor, he is without negligence (*pramāda*); because he is not negligent, he cultivates and accumulates wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*); because he accumulates wholesome dharmas, he receives the Bodhisattva precepts; because he receives the Bodhisattva precepts, he makes offerings to the Triple Gem; because he makes offerings to the Triple Gem, his mind becomes pure—this is called the "Pure Ground" (*śuddhabhūmi*).
Chapter Four: The Practice of the Ultimate Ground. "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling from the Ground of Understanding up to the Bodhisattva Ground have four practices:
first, the practice of the pāramitās;
second, the practice of awakening."
Third is the practice of supernormal powers;
fourth is the practice of maturing sentient beings.

Regarding the practice of the *pāramitās*: the six *pāramitās* are as previously explained, along with the *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya*), the *pāramitā* of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), the *pāramitā* of power (*bala*), and the *pāramitā* of knowledge (*jñāna*). These ten *pāramitās* are called the practice of the *pāramitās*.
There are twelve kinds of skillful means as previously explained; these are called the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).
There are five kinds of vows as previously explained; these are called the perfection of vows (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).
The purification through the adornment of the ten powers is called the power-pāramitā.
Knowing all dharmas as being either possible or impossible is called the knowledge-pāramitā.
Because it knows the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), it is called the knowledge-pāramitā; because it knows the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), it is called the prajñā-pāramitā.

Furthermore, immeasurable wisdom is called the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā); seeking ever-superior wisdom is called the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā); being unobstructed by the four māras is called the perfection of power (bala-pāramitā); and being able to know the true nature of all phenomena is called the perfection of knowledge (jñāna-pāramitā).

The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, the four searches, and the four true knowledges are as previously explained; these are called the practices of enlightenment (*bodhicaryā*).
The supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are as explained in the "Inconceivable Chapter."
The six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), as previously explained, are called the practice of spiritual power (rddhiprātihārya).

The two immeasurables—the immeasurable of subduing (vinaya-apramāṇa) and the immeasurable of skillful means (upāya-apramāṇa), as previously explained—are called the practice of ripening (paripācana-pratipatti).
These four practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva encompass all practices.

Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, ultimately fulfill and purify all wholesome dharmas, surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and because they ultimately grasp the fruit of the path to enlightenment and are ultimately able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, these are called the ten pāramitās.
If one speaks of their sequence, there are three matters:
first, because of their function as antidotes;
second, because of their arising.
Third, because of attaining the fruit.
Regarding wholesome dharmas, there are six matters:
first, stinginess and greed;
Second is evil karma;
third is a mind of malice;
fourth is indolence.
Fifth is a distracted mind;
sixth is ignorance.
Due to these six factors, one does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
In order to destroy the six dharmas, the six pāramitās—from dānapāramitā up to prajñāpāramitā—are taught.
These six pāramitās encompass the four pāramitās; this is called the counteractive (pratipakṣa).
Regarding "arising": when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva relinquishes all worldly things to leave the household life and study the Way, this is called dānapāramitā.
Having left the household life, they receive the bodhisattva precepts; this is called śīlapāramitā.
Because of guarding the precepts, one silently endures abuse and physical assault without retaliation; this is called kṣānti-pāramitā.
When the precepts are thus pure, one diligently cultivates wholesome dharmas; this is called vīrya-pāramitā.
Because of diligence, the five faculties are subdued; this is called the dhyāna-pāramitā.
Once the five faculties are subdued, one knows the true dharma-dhātu; this is called the prajñā-pāramitā.
This is called "arising.

As for the "fruition," it means that when a bodhisattva practices wholesome dharmas such as generosity in the present life, after relinquishing the body, they obtain great external wealth and internally attain the five perfections.
The fivefold endowment consists of obtaining longevity, beauty, strength, happiness, and eloquence when born among humans or devas; this is called the fruit of giving.

By means of the causal conditions of giving, one cultivates and accumulates wholesome dharmas, with a mind free from envy and patient toward all faults and transgressions; this is called the second complete retribution.
Due to the causal conditions of giving, when performing worldly or world-transcending activities, the mind is free from weariness or regret; this is called the third retribution.
Due to the causal conditions of giving, the mind becomes supple and free from confusion; this is called the fourth retribution.

By means of the causal conditions of giving, one clearly discerns what constitutes a field of merit and what does not; one knows what may be given and what may not be given; and one skillfully understands the expedient means for seeking and acquiring wealth. This is called the fifth fruition of retribution.
The four pāramitās encompass the six pāramitās and consist of three types of precepts:
first, the precept of following the rules;
second, the precept of following the mind.
Third is the precept that accords with wisdom.
The Bodhisattva’s *śīlapāramitā* is called the precept that accords with the precepts;
the *dhyānapāramitā* is called the precept that accords with the mind.
The Prajñāpāramitā is called the precept that accords with wisdom.
Apart from these three precepts, there is no bodhisattva precept; the three precepts of the bodhisattva encompass all precepts.
There are four matters by which a bodhisattva is able to benefit sentient beings.
What are the four? First, to cultivate and accumulate wholesome dharmas for the sake of bodhi;
second, to first know the meaning of all dharmas through true wisdom.
Third, increasing wholesome dharmas;
fourth, ripening the faculties of sentient beings.
Through these four matters, the bodhisattva is able to bring great benefit to sentient beings.
If anyone were to say that there is a way to benefit sentient beings apart from these four matters, such a thing is impossible.
Chapter Five: The Thirty-two Marks and Eighty Minor Characteristics of the Ultimate Ground The thirteen practices of a Tathāgata are called the ultimate ground of Buddhahood.
Regarding the ultimate stage of Buddhahood, there are one hundred and forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).

These are: the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, the four purities of all conduct, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three foundations of mindfulness, the three ways in which he needs no protection, great compassion, constant non-forgetfulness, the severance of the habitual tendencies of afflictions, and omniscience. These are called the one hundred and forty unique qualities.
Regarding the thirty-two marks: first, the soles of the feet are level;
second, there are thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of the feet;
third, the fingers are slender and long.
Fourth, his heels are full and elevated;
fifth, his fingers and toes are joined by a web;
sixth, his hands and feet are soft and supple.
Seventh, his calves are like those of the king of the eneya deer;
eighth, his ankle bones are not visible;
ninth, standing upright, his hands reach his knees.
Tenth, his limbs are well-tucked away like those of an elephant or a horse king;
eleventh, his body is perfectly rounded and full like a nyagrodha tree;
twelfth, the hairs on his body point upward.
Thirteenth, each hair curls to the right;
fourteenth, his body is the color of pure gold;
fifteenth, his constant radiance extends one fathom on all sides.
Sixteenth, his skin is fine and soft, such that dust and grime do not adhere to it;
seventeenth, he is full in seven places;
eighteenth, his upper body is like that of a lion.
Nineteenth, his arms and elbows are rounded and well-proportioned;
twentieth, his collarbone is flat and full;
twenty-first, he possesses the mark of a well-rounded body.
Twenty-second, he has forty teeth;
twenty-third, his teeth are closely set without gaps;
twenty-fourth, the color of his teeth is white.
Twenty-fifth, his jaw is square like that of a lion;
twenty-sixth, he attains the supreme taste among all tastes;
twenty-seventh, he possesses the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa* (the cranial protuberance).
Twenty-eighth, a broad and long tongue;
twenty-ninth, a Brahma-like voice;
thirtieth, deep blue eyes.
The thirty-first is eyes like those of a bull king; the thirty-second is the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows.

Regarding the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*): the twenty fingers are called the twenty marks; the eight surfaces of the hands and feet are flat and full; the six areas of the ankles, knees, and thighs are exquisitely beautiful; the hands have three clusters; the six areas of the shoulders, elbows, and wrists are full; the waist and the center of the navel are called two marks; the hips and the two buttocks are called three marks; the horse-like sheath and the two upper arms are three marks; the waist, navel, both flanks, both armpits, and both breasts are called eight; and the abdomen, chest, spine, and neck are called sixty.

The upper and lower teeth; the upper and lower lips and palate; the two cheeks and two jaws; the two eyes and two shoulders; the two nostrils; the two tufts of hair on the forehead; the two ears; and the head being perfectly rounded—these are called the eighty [minor marks].

“When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the Pure Ground (śuddhabhūmi), although they attain these eighty minor marks (aśīty-anuvyañjana) by the power of their karma, they are not yet brilliantly pure. It is only when they arise at the tree of enlightenment (bodhidruma) that they become brilliantly pure. When they are not yet brilliantly pure, this is called the practice of the Bodhisattva grounds.”
There are two kinds of adornment for bodhi:
first, the proximate;
second, the remote.
That which is distant refers to not yet having attained the retribution of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
if one has attained them, it is called "near.
The teaching of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics is for the purpose of causing sentient beings to perform wholesome karma.

Sentient beings perform various kinds of unwholesome karma; because of this unwholesome karma, they obtain various kinds of unwholesome fruits. For this reason, the Tathāgata speaks of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, which are the various kinds of wholesome karma and the various kinds of wholesome fruits.
Upon hearing this, sentient beings immediately eliminate and destroy their various evil karmas.
Because the Bodhisattva wholeheartedly cultivates and maintains pure precepts, his soles become level.
By making offerings to his parents, preceptors, teachers, elders, and those of virtuous character, through these causal conditions, he obtains the mark of wheels on the soles of his feet.

One does not give rise to thoughts of harm toward sentient beings nor harbor intentions to plunder them; when seeing one's parents, preceptors, teachers, elders, or those of virtuous character, one goes out from afar to welcome them, provides them with seats, and pays them respectful homage while abandoning arrogance. By these causes and conditions, one obtains long, slender fingers.
By possessing the three aforementioned practices, one obtains full and rounded heels.
By gathering sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), one obtains webbed fingers and toes as a result of these causes and conditions.
By massaging and washing one’s parents, preceptors, teachers, elders, and virtuous persons with fine ghee and oil, one obtains soft hands and feet as a result of these causes and conditions.
Cultivating and accumulating wholesome dharmas without ever knowing satiety—by this causal condition, one obtains the mark of the calves being like those of an antelope (*ajinapāda*).

Hearing the Dharma with joy and delighting in explaining it for others, acting as a servant for the sake of the Dharma—by this causal condition, one obtains the mark of the ankle bones being inconspicuous (*anavanata-gulpha*).

By purifying the three karmas, nursing the sick and bestowing medicine, and by eliminating arrogance while practicing contentment with food and drink, through these causes and conditions, one attains the mark of standing upright with the hands reaching to the knees.

Seeing those who were separated, he skillfully spoke words of reconciliation; he personally cultivated a sense of shame and remorse (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*) and also taught others to do so. By these causes and conditions, he obtained the mark of the horse’s sheath (*aśvakośa*). He purified his own three karmas and also taught others to purify them;

if there were sentient beings whose four great elements (*mahābhūta*) were unbalanced, he was able to provide medical treatment for them. By these causes and conditions, he obtained the mark of the body being perfectly rounded (*vṛtta-kāya*).
Hearing the Dharma with joy and delighting in explaining it for others, by these causes and conditions, one obtains the mark of body hairs curling upward.

Contemplating the profound meaning of all dharmas and delighting in the cultivation of wholesome qualities, making offerings to one's parents, preceptors, teachers, elders, and virtuous persons, and while traveling on a road, clearing away bricks, stones, thorns, and impurities from stupas and monasteries—by these causes and conditions, one obtains the mark of body hairs.
If one gives food, drink, and ornaments to others and thereby eliminates anger, by these causes and conditions one obtains two marks:
first, a golden complexion;
second, a constant radiance.
By what karmic conditions is the mark of each individual hair obtained?
It is by these very same karmic conditions that the body becomes fine, soft, and free from the adherence of dust or grime.
By constantly bestowing upon sentient beings whatever things they require, one obtains the mark of the seven places being full through these causal conditions.

Having personally destroyed pride and made his nature supple and gentle, he acts in accordance with the Dharma according to the minds of sentient beings; to eliminate unwholesomeness, he teaches them wholesome dharmas. By these causes and conditions, he attains the mark of the upper body being like that of a lion, the mark of rounded shoulders, and the mark of the collarbone being flat and full.
By what karmic conditions does one obtain the mark of slender fingers?
It is by these very same karmic conditions that one obtains the mark of smooth limbs.

By refraining from double-tongued speech and reconciling those who are at strife, through these causes and conditions, one obtains the marks of having forty teeth, teeth that are closely set without gaps, and teeth that are even and level.
By practicing loving-kindness toward those in the desire realm, through these causes and conditions, he attained the mark of white teeth.
By joyfully welcoming and seeing off those who come seeking him, through these causes and conditions, he attained the mark of full and square jaws.
Regarding all sentient beings with equal regard as if they were one's only child, by this causal condition, one attains the mark of the supreme flavor.

Constantly bestowing the unsurpassed flavor of the Dharma upon sentient beings, providing them with mindfulness whenever one sees someone who has forgotten it, personally upholding the five precepts and teaching them to others, and cultivating compassion to perform the great gift of the Dharma—by these causal conditions, one attains the mark of the uṣṇīṣa (the protuberance on the crown of the head) and the mark of the broad and long tongue.
By speaking truthful words, joyful words, Dharma words, gentle words, and by not speaking at improper times—for these causes and conditions, one attains the mark of the Brahma-voice.
By cultivating and accumulating a heart of compassion and regarding all sentient beings as one would one's own parents—for these causes and conditions, one obtains two marks:
first, eyes of deep blue color; [second, eyelashes like those of a cow].
Second, his eyes are like those of a bull king.
When he sees those with virtue, he praises them truthfully; by this causal condition, he attains the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*).
Although the causal conditions for each of the thirty-two marks are explained individually, the true causal condition is the observance of the precepts and diligent effort.
Why is this? If one who does not uphold the precepts were able to practice with diligence, they would not even attain a human body, let alone the thirty-two marks.
This applies equally and without distinction to the mark of the invisible crown and the mark of the fleshly protuberance.
Furthermore, when one performs any action with a concentrated mind and without regret, by this causal condition one obtains the mark of level soles.

If one acts with a sincere heart, by this causal condition one obtains the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel, the second and third marks of webbed fingers and toes, the mark of the seven parts being full, the fine and soft shoulders, the full collarbone, the straight body, and the mark of the broad and long tongue.

If one constantly practices these deeds, by these causes and conditions one attains the mark of long fingers, the mark of standing upright with hands reaching the knees, the mark of a constant radiance extending one fathom, and the mark of teeth that are closely set without gaps.
If one performs pure deeds, by this causal condition one obtains other marks.

Furthermore, if one gives rise to a mind of pure goodness toward sentient beings, by this causal condition one obtains hands and feet that are soft and supple, with skin so fine and smooth that dust and grime do not adhere to it.
By practicing and accumulating [merit] in successive stages and at the proper times, through these causes and conditions, one obtains the second, third, and fourth marks.

By delighting in the cultivation of wholesome dharmas and having a mind free from regret or retreat, through these causes and conditions, one obtains a golden-colored body, a constant radiance, white teeth, and the tuft of hair between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*).

If, upon hearing praise, one does not give rise to arrogance, and conceals one's wholesome dharmas so as not to let others know of them, by these causes and conditions one obtains the mark of the horse’s sheath.

If the wholesome dharmas one cultivates are dedicated toward Bodhi, by these causes and conditions one obtains the marks of having a single hair in each pore, body hairs that curl upward, forty teeth in the mouth, and the mark of the supreme sense of taste.
Because of diligent and energetic effort, through these causes and conditions, he attains the marks of having full, square jaws and an upper body like that of a lion.

Because he cherished all sentient beings with a sincere heart as if looking upon an only son, through these causes and conditions, he attains the marks of even, level teeth, deep blue eyes, and eyes like those of a bull king.
Cultivating and accumulating wholesome dharmas without ever knowing satiety, by these causes and conditions, he obtains the remaining marks.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the practice of his nature, he cultivates the karma for the thirty-two marks; yet while dwelling in pure conduct, although he possesses these thirty-two marks, they are not yet complete and have not attained clarity and purity. Only when he dwells in the thirteen practices does he clearly perceive them, manifesting and fully perfecting all Buddha-dharmas.

Although sentient beings possess immeasurable characteristics that differ from one another—being inconceivably categorized as inferior, middling, or superior—the Buddha therefore taught the thirty-two marks.
If all the merits possessed by every sentient being were combined and gathered together, they would exactly equal the merit of a single pore of the Tathāgata.
The combined merit of all the pores, gathered and accumulated, constitutes a single secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*).

The merit of all these secondary marks, further multiplied a hundredfold, constitutes a single primary mark (*lakṣaṇa*), with the exception of the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*) and the invisible crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*).
Combining all other remaining marks and increasing them a thousandfold, these two marks are formed.

By harmonizing and gathering together all the merits of the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, and increasing them by a factor of a thousand million billion, the Tathāgata’s profound and far-reaching conch-like voice is produced; its sound is heard throughout immeasurable and boundless Buddha-worlds.

The Tathāgata has accomplished such immeasurable and boundless merits; for this reason, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, is called "Unsurpassed," and the Dharma he practices is called the "Unsurpassed Practice."
The thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics possess three kinds of immeasurability:
first, the immeasurability of three kalpas;
second, the immeasurability of cultivating wholesome deeds.
Third, the benefit of sentient beings is immeasurable.
For this reason, it is said that the Tathāgata has accomplished immeasurable merit.
Chapter Six: The Stage of Ultimate Abiding. Regarding the four purities of a Bodhisattva: first, purity of body; [and so forth].
Second is purity of objects;
third is purity of mind;
fourth is purity of wisdom.

Having eternally severed habitual tendencies and attained the vessel of purity, one realizes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; with mastery over the body and freedom in birth and cessation, this is called the purity of the body.
Mastery over supernormal powers is called purity of conditions.
Cultivating and accumulating wholesome dharmas so that the mind is free from afflictions is called purity of mind.
Knowing all dharmas without obstruction and attaining sovereign wisdom to know the practice of all dharmas is called purity of wisdom.
By means of these four dharmas of purity, the bodhisattva attains the ten powers (*daśabala*).
What are the ten? First is the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).
Second, knowing the power of all karmas;
third, knowing the power of all dhyānas, samādhis, and liberations;
fourth, knowing the power of the sharpness or dullness of all faculties.
Fifth, knowing the power of the various inclinations and understandings of sentient beings;
sixth, knowing the power of the realms of sentient beings;
seventh, knowing the power of the paths leading to all destinations.
Eighth is the power of knowing past lives;
ninth is the power of the divine eye;
tenth is the power of the exhaustion of outflows.
That which the Tathāgata has spoken is true and non-dual; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.

If he speaks of the true causes and conditions, the true essence, the true nature, the true abiding, and the true arising of wholesome and unwholesome fruits, this is called "the possible" (*sthāna*). To claim that wholesome and unwholesome fruits arise from what is not their cause—that is called "the impossible" (*asthāna*).
The wisdom that destroys pride is called true wisdom, called all-encompassing wisdom, called unimpeded wisdom, called pure wisdom, and called the wisdom that is free from arrogance.
Because it follows the numerical sequence, it is called the "first power.
Because there is nothing superior to it, it is called "all-encompassing practice.
Because it benefits sentient beings and destroys all Māras, it is called "power."
Because one attains mastery through the adornment of reality, it is called "endowment.
Because it can shatter all terrors, it is called "nirvāṇa.
Because it relies on the eightfold noble path to destroy all sufferings, it is called "unsurpassed."
Because it abides in accordance with the Dharma, it is called "the real.
Because one has personally attained the pure Dharma and compassionately expounds it for the sake of sentient beings, it is called the "Brahma-wheel.
That which is the Brahma-wheel is called the Tathāgata; that which is the Tathāgata is called "coolness"; that which is coolness is called "precept" (śīla).

To uphold the pure precepts and speak in accordance with those precepts is called pure and correct speech, truthful speech, beneficial speech, extensive speech, unimpeded speech, all-encompassing speech, ultimate speech, unsurpassed speech, untainted speech, unconditioned speech, external speech, and manifest speech; therefore, it is called the Great Lion’s Roar.

It is taught that through the skillful means of wholesome power one explains the true cause; by means of these true causes and conditions, one attains the true fruit—namely, the fruits of humans, devas, and the unsurpassed fruit. Because it is the unsurpassed fruit, it is called "unsurpassed."
If an action has already been performed and its fruit has increased and been obtained, it is called "past.
If an action has already been performed but its retribution has not yet been received, it is also called "past.
An action not yet performed that one intends to perform, or a fruit not yet obtained that one intends to obtain, is called "future."
Karma already performed that has not yet yielded its fruit, and karma that has been experienced as fruit and has already ceased in the past—this is called the present.
Past, future, and present karma are of three types, namely: the fruits of body, speech, and mind.
Regarding the fruits of body, speech, and mind: where one performs wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, and where one obtains their fruit;
where one performs unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, and where one obtains their fruit—this is called "the place."
That pure and wholesome karma does not yield an evil fruit is called an impossibility (*asthāna*).
That unwholesome and evil karma does not yield a wholesome fruit is called an impossibility.
That human karma does not receive the retribution of the hells is called an impossibility.
Karmic actions of the hells do not receive retribution among humans; this is called an "impossible case" (*asthāna*).

However, except for those who are able to cultivate bodily discipline, precepts, mind, and wisdom, causing the retribution of the hells to be experienced lightly as a human, it is called "hellish retribution" because it resembles [the original] and "human fruit" because it is experienced lightly as a human.
This is called the possible and the impossible.
Having attained mastery in the cultivation of such dharmas as the four dhyānas and the eight liberations, and because of this mastery, the Tathāgata is constantly in samādhi.
When the Dharma is being preached, Brahmā, the King of Devas, and others hear only the sound but do not see the physical form.

In such states of meditative concentration and liberation, there are two kinds of afflictions: namely, the sorrow of desiring to attain what has not yet been attained, and the sorrow of losing what has already been attained.
The Tathāgata has already severed these two kinds of sorrow and attained great mastery.

He knows all the thoughts and mental activities of sentient beings; although he fully understands their minds, he does not become attached to them nor give rise to worldly joy. Having cultivated and perfected this, he attains it whenever he wishes, attains it greatly and with ease, and once attained, he never regresses. This is called the third power of meditative concentration and liberation.

To know that the five faculties, such as faith and so forth, have superior, middling, and inferior degrees—whether they arise from hearing or from right reflection—is called the power of the faculties (*indriya-bala*).
To know the superior, middling, and inferior levels of aspiration (*chanda*) is called the power of resolve (*adhimukti-bala*).

To know the various dispositions—the disposition of śrāvakas, the disposition of pratyekabuddhas, the disposition of tathāgatas, and the dispositions of sentient beings ranging from greed to the eighty-four thousand afflictions—is called the fifth power.
Knowing that various bodies in the world-worlds are obtained due to afflictions is called the sixth power.

Knowing that each affliction has its own specific antidote, knowing that all states of existence likewise have their own specific counterparts, and knowing the antidotes that destroy all evil and false views—this is called the power of the path leading to the destination.
He thoroughly understands the various names of the diverse sentient beings in the four directions; he knows that past sentient beings were mindful of eight things:
first, their name;
second, their birth; and so forth.
Third, the three castes;
fourth, the four kinds of nutriment;
fifth, the experiencing of suffering and pleasure.
Sixth, longevity;
seventh, dwelling;
eighth, the end of life.
Furthermore, one contemplates six matters: first, the name;
second, the clan, such as Kṣatriya and so forth.
Third, kinsmen and parents;
fourth, food and drink;
fifth, poverty and wealth.
Sixth is longevity and premature death;
this is called the eighth power.

The practice of the heavens is termed the four dhyānas; because one attains the fruit of the four dhyānas, it is called the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*). Because it fully obtains the fruit of pure goodness, it is called "pure. Because its clarity is peerless, it is called the "supernormal eye" (*atīndriyacakṣus*).
There are those in the desire realm who possess the divine eye; although the name is the same, because it is impure, it is not called the "divine eye.
Those who know with the divine eye see sentient beings falling; those who fall are called "devas" (heavenly ones).
Furthermore, there are those who fall [into rebirth], which is called human death;
birth is called the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
There are two kinds of intermediate states:
The first is wholesome;
the second is unwholesome.

The color of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the unwholesome is like that of a black coarse cloth; it is seen by the pure eye during the darkness of night, and the vision of the intermediate state’s color by the pure divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is likewise.

The color of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for those of merit is like the garment of a woman from Vārāṇasī; it is seen by the pure eye during the time of the bright moon, and the vision of the intermediate state by the purified divine eye is likewise so.
Those who are black are called beings of downward movement; those who are white are called beings of upward movement.

Because of the causes and conditions of evil karma of body, speech, and mind, they are called downward-moving; because of the causes and conditions of wholesome karma of body, speech, and mind, they are called upward-moving.
Evil karma is termed wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
There are two kinds of wrong view:
the first is that which can be transformed;
The second is "irreversible.
To slander cause and effect by claiming that there are no noble ones (ārya) is called irreversible.
To perceive what is not a cause as a cause, or what is not a fruit as a fruit, is called reversible.
Therefore, unwholesome karma is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), while wholesome karma is called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Not slandering the Four Noble Truths and believing in the true retribution of wholesome and unwholesome karma—therefore, wholesome karma is called right view.

Due to the causal conditions of evil karma, one dies and passes into hell; because one does not delight in receiving the fruits [of such actions], it is called "hell" (niraya). With heedlessness and evil karma acting as its wings, one will inevitably reach hell.
Because one clearly perceives cause and effect, it is called the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

Due to the conditions of wholesome karma, one passes beyond death through evil and receives the retribution of pleasant feelings by attaining a human or celestial body; because of right view, one is born into a favorable existence (*sugati*). One who is born into a favorable existence is termed a human or a deva; because one sees with clarity and precision, it is called the divine eye.
What is wholesome existence?
Obtaining a wholesome fruit by means of wholesome causes and conditions is called wholesome existence.
This is called the ninth power.

By means of the causes and conditions of cultivating bodily discipline, morality, mind, and wisdom, one cuts off all outflows (*āsrava*); because of cutting off the outflows, one attains the untainted (*anāsrava*) body, morality, mind, and wisdom.
This untainted body, morality, mind, and wisdom is of two kinds: that of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and that of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
By means of these two paths, the mind attains liberation and wisdom attains liberation.
Because of this attainment of liberation through both mind and wisdom, one is able to manifest supernatural powers to teach and transform sentient beings; this is called the tenth power.

The Bodhisattva Daśabala knows natures, knows distinctions, knows specific characteristics, common characteristics, and unique characteristics; he knows equality, knows karma, knows sequence, and knows what is superior and what is not.
A bodhisattva is able to know these seven matters.

Regarding the knowledge of nature: the nature of the ten powers is identical to the nature of the five faculties; because wisdom (*prajñā*) predominates, it is termed the "nature of knowledge. Therefore, it is said that one knows what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), rather than saying one knows the possibility and impossibility of faith.
This applies likewise up to the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
There are three kinds of discrimination:
first, discrimination by time; [and so forth].
Second is the discrimination of conduct;
third is the discrimination of specific and general characteristics.
The Ten Powers can know all times—namely, the past, future, and present—and this is called the discrimination of time.
The Ten Powers are able to know the immeasurable antidotes to afflictions throughout all worlds in the ten directions; this is called the discernment of activities (*carita-vibhāga*).
The Ten Powers are able to know all forms and characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*); this is called their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
To know that form is impermanent, and so on, up to the fact that all phenomena are impermanent—this is called the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
This is what is meant by "discriminating between specific and common characteristics.
As for the uncommon [characteristics], the ten powers (*daśabala*) are not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddhas of the ten directions equally attain the ten powers; this is called equality.
Regarding the knowledge of karma: it is the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).
Truly knowing causes as causes and truly knowing effects as effects is the second power.

The Tathāgata fully understands the karmic retribution of his own actions and likewise knows all the karmic fruits of sentient beings; by virtue of the power of meditative concentration and liberation, the Tathāgata attains three kinds of manifestations through which he is able to discipline sentient beings.

By means of the power of knowing faculties, the Tathāgata thoroughly understands the inferior, middling, and superior faculties of sentient beings; because he knows their faculties, he teaches the Dharma in accordance with those faculties.

By means of the power of understanding, the Tathāgata thoroughly knows the virtuous and non-virtuous natures of all sentient beings; to eliminate non-virtuous natures, he instructs them in virtuous natures.
By means of the power of knowing worlds, the Tathāgata constantly engages in the ways of the world, yet remains unstained by worldly phenomena.

Because he knows the world, he knows the realm of sentient beings; because he knows the realm of sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma according to their faculties, their minds, and their afflictions.
How does the Tathāgata first instruct sentient beings to lead them into the Buddha-dharma?
If the Tathāgata were to instruct śrāvakas and bodhisattvas who have newly entered the Buddha-dharma, he would speak thus:
"Good sons! You should cultivate and gather deep delight in solitude, quietude, and dwelling alone."
The name given to you by your parents at the time of your birth, and even the names assigned by your teachers and preceptors—you should contemplate these with a sincere mind:
"Do these names, which were created for me by my parents, teachers, and preceptors, exist within or without the six internal and external sense bases?"

"Good son! If you are free from the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*) and do not perceive them as existing, at that time you will attain true wisdom and know that these names are provisional and not real."
The Dharma is not real, and names are not real either.
Since both names and dharmas are unreal, how could one give rise to arrogance on this basis? Good son!
At that time, you should further contemplate the eye and the name "eye.
There are two kinds of eyes:
first, the name; [second, the substance].
Second is dissemination:
the eye is called "non-eye," and the characteristic of the eye is "non-eye.
If there were any entity named "eye," that entity would likewise not exist.
If the eye truly existed, its name should also be real.
If it were real, sentient beings would naturally recognize it at birth without requiring instruction;
yet we have never seen anyone who could know something without being taught.
For this reason, one knows that names are not real and things are not real.
As it is with the eye, so it is with consciousness.

When one contemplates in this way, one eliminates attachment to all internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*). Because one eliminates internal and external attachment, one eliminates the marks of all phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*); because one eliminates the marks of all phenomena, one truly knows the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The nature of all phenomena means that they are unreal and devoid of characteristics.
Son of good family!

When one contemplates in this way, if one wishes to attain omniscience, wishes to attain great loving-kindness and great compassion, wishes to attain the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, wishes to attain the conduct of nature up to the conduct of a Tathāgata, or wishes to attain the bodhisattva stages, the six supernormal powers, up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—one shall be able to attain them all.
This is called the sixth power.
By means of the power of knowing the paths leading to various destinations, he discerns the true path from the untrue path; having destroyed the untrue path, he reveals the true path.

By the power of his past lives, he knows the experience of manifold sufferings; knowing for himself that he finds no delight in birth and death, he also teaches sentient beings not to take pleasure in birth and death, thereby destroying their view of permanence.
By means of the power of the divine eye, he bestows predictions upon others, thereby severing the view of nihilism.

By means of the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), the Tathāgata knows for himself that he has attained liberation; he is able to destroy the views of sentient beings who mistake one who is not a Tathāgata for a true Tathāgata, those who mistake one who is not a śramaṇa for a real śramaṇa, and those who mistake one who is not a brāhmaṇa for a real brāhmaṇa.
When the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he attained these ten powers all at once.
Why, then, do you speak of them as having a sequential order?

When the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he first contemplated cause and effect; therefore, this initial [power] is called the power of the possible and the impossible (sthānāsthāna-bala).
By whom, then, are such causes and effects experienced and produced?
This is called the power of karma.

Because one has destroyed [the bonds of] karma, one cultivates and accumulates meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). In order to know which sentient beings are capable of cultivating and accumulating it and which are not, one observes their faculties (*indriya*).
The faculties are of three kinds: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
This is called the nature of sentient beings; this is called the fifth power.
Because one knows their nature, one knows whether the mind is pure or impure; this is called the world.

Because one wishes to know the causes and conditions of pure and impure minds, one knows the path leading to their destination; such a path severs the views of eternalism and nihilism, and this is called the power of the divine eye of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-divyacakṣus-bala*).

Because the two views have been abandoned, all outflows (*āsrava*) are forever exhausted; this is called the power of the exhaustion of outflows. This is the sequential order. Furthermore, there is another sequence:

when the Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he first contemplates what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*); next, he contemplates worldly karma; because he seeks to destroy worldly karma, he contemplates the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*), as well as whether sentient beings are able or unable to cultivate and accumulate the Path. Next, with the divine eye, he perceives the sharpness or dullness of the faculties (*indriya*) of all sentient beings for the purpose of knowing them; the rest is as previously explained.

Furthermore, there is a sequential order: when the Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) as what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*).
Since the twelve links arise from karma, he therefore contemplates karma.

Because the various karmas of sentient beings may either result in retribution or not, he observes with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) what is appropriate for them; for the sake of sentient beings, he contemplates the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is called "liberation."
The dharma-realm and the world are without distinction; yet, because he wishes to know those who are difficult to discipline and those who are easy to discipline, he knows his past lives.
Because he wishes to know who will receive the teaching and who will not, he knows the sharpness or dullness of their faculties.
Having known this, he teaches them the eightfold path, which is called the "path leading to the destination."
By means of the power of the Path, one severs all afflictions; this is called the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*).
What is the difference between the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*) and the power of karma (*karma-bala*)?
To thoroughly know good and evil karmas, as well as their respective good and evil fruits, is called the power of the possible and the impossible.
That the doer certainly experiences [the result] and the non-doer does not experience it is called knowing the power of karma.
One cultivates and accumulates meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) for the purpose of subduing unwholesome karma.
There are two kinds of subduing:
First is faith;
second is lack of faith; therefore, one observes the faculties (*indriya*).
There are two kinds of faithful mind:
First is faith in the Three Jewels;
second is faith in Maheśvara—this is called liberation.
It is of three kinds, namely inferior, middling, and superior; this is called worldly power.

Having known the worlds, he teaches the worldly path, the path of the śrāvakas, the path of the pratyekabuddhas, the path of the bodhisattvas, and the path of the buddhas; this is called the power of knowing the paths leading to various destinations.
To observe the good and evil causes, as well as the heavy and light karmic retributions, of all sentient beings is called the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñānabala*).
Because of this knowledge, one abandons the views of eternalism and nihilism; this is called the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Because one sees reality as it truly is, all outflows are forever exhausted; this is called the power of the exhaustion of outflows.
The nature of the ten powers is entirely the nature of wisdom and is without distinction; it is only because of the conditions of their respective objects that distinctions are spoken of.
The four fearlessnesses are as previously explained.
The Tathāgata teaches sentient beings four matters:
first, the liberation of the unique dharmas not shared with the śrāvakas;
Second, the liberation common to śrāvakas;
third, the liberation from the suffering of sentient beings;
fourth, teaching the remedies for sentient beings to sever their suffering and attain liberation.

Regarding what is not shared with the śrāvakas: that which I have awakened to and known—if you were to say there is any dharma that I do not know, I do not see any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, human, deva, Māra, or Brahmā who could speak in accordance with the Dharma, saying that I do not know or do not see it; because I do not see such a thing, I feel no shame or fear.

My outflows are already exhausted; if one were to say they are not exhausted, I would not see that person—whether a śramaṇa or even a Māra or Brahmā—to speak of them as they truly are, saying, "Your outflows are not yet exhausted. Because I do not see such a person, I feel no shame or fear.

I have already attained the Way; if one were to say that this Way is not ultimate, I do not see any śramaṇas, nor even Māras or Brahmās, who could speak truthfully, saying, "You have not attained the Way, and it is not ultimate. Because I see no such person, I feel no shame or fear.

I have declared what obstructs the path; if one were to say that it does not obstruct, I do not see any śramaṇas, up to and including Māra or Brahmā, who speak of obstruction or non-obstruction in accordance with reality. Because I do not see such persons, I feel no shame or fear.

The path taught by the Buddha was intended for both bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. When the collections were compiled after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the name "bodhisattva" was removed from the Śrāvaka Piṭaka and the name "bodhisattva" was established within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka; therefore, the Vaipulya is called the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
That which is not shared with the śrāvakas refers to the Tathāgata’s three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma and [the disciples] listen and receive it with a sincere heart, their minds attain joy and they experience various forms of peace and happiness; yet even as they abide according to the Dharma and do not contravene the Buddha's teaching, the Buddha does not feel delight, but cultivates and maintains a mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), never losing right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) nor being negligent.

When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma and there are those who do not believe or accept it, or who act contrary to what has been taught, the Buddha likewise feels no anger and has no sorrow or distress, but cultivates and maintains a mind of equanimity, never losing right mindfulness nor being negligent.

When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, there may be those who listen and those who do not; the listeners feel no joy, and those who do not listen feel no sorrow. They cultivate and accumulate a mind of equanimity, neither losing right mindfulness nor falling into negligence.
These are called the three foundations of mindfulness.
Furthermore, there are qualities not shared with the śrāvakas, namely the three ways in which the Tathāgata has nothing to guard:
the Tathāgata does not need to guard his body, his speech, or his livelihood.
There are Arhats who give rise to indeterminate karma due to a lapse in mindfulness.
Such indeterminate karma is termed *duṣkṛta*.
The Tathāgata has already severed all indeterminate karma.
Why is this? Because he constantly cultivates right mindfulness.
Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks according to the mind and reprimands his retinue; that is to say, he drives them away with harsh words, yet his mind remains free from fear or distress.
Why is this? Because body, speech, and livelihood are pure.
Furthermore, there is that which is not shared with the śrāvakas, namely, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), as previously explained.
What does the Tathāgata do? Where does he do it? By what causes and conditions does he do it?
"What is being done?
When was it done? To be able to know such matters as these according to reality is called mindfulness.
What the Tathāgata knows is all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Where is it? In all worlds.
By what causes and conditions? For the sake of disciplining sentient beings.
What is the agent? It is skillful means.
At what time does the agent act? At all times.
For this reason, the Tathāgata constantly cultivates the mind of right mindfulness.

Whether the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, moves or blinks, speaks or walks, stands or acts, at all times he is free from the habitual tendencies of afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*). For this reason, it is said that the Tathāgata has eternally severed the habitual tendencies of afflictions; the Arhats and others are not like this, and therefore this is not shared with the Śrāvakas.
The Tathāgata fully awakens to three categories of phenomena:
first, the category of meanings that bring benefit; second, the category of meanings that do not bring benefit; and [third, the category of meanings that are neither].
Third is the category of things that are neither beneficial nor non-beneficial.
The Tathāgata knows these three categories with perfect clarity; therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata has attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
These one hundred and forty such unique qualities are not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; therefore, they are called the "unshared [qualities] of the śrāvakas."

When a bodhisattva practices, they attain the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; however, these are not yet clear and pure. Only when sitting beneath the Bodhi tree and practicing and cultivating the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without a teacher do they become clear and pure.

Once a Bodhisattva on the stage of training has attained the Vajra-samādhi, in the very next moment they attain the ten powers, all Buddha-dharmas, and even all pure wisdom; because these are all fully obtained, it is called omniscience, unimpeded wisdom, unobstructed wisdom, pure wisdom, tranquil wisdom, purified wisdom, and perfect wisdom. This is called the Ultimate Stage (niṣṭhā-bhūmi), which transcends all bodhisattva practices and all bodhisattva stages, enters the Tathāgata stage and the Tathāgata practice, attains the supreme body, transforms the bodhisattva body, eternally severs habitual tendencies, and dwells in the Ultimate Stage.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas behold the Buddha-dharma, it is as if looking through thin silk; for the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, there is no such thing at all, and for this reason it is called "pure.
Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stage of ultimate perfection see the Buddha-dharma as one sees forms from a distance, whereas the Buddhas see dharmas as if seeing forms from nearby.
Ultimately, a bodhisattva perceives the Buddha-dharma as one sees forms in the dark, whereas the Buddhas perceive phenomena as one sees forms in the light of day.
Ultimately, a bodhisattva is like one who has not yet emerged from the womb, while the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like those who have already emerged.
Ultimately, the bodhisattva is like something seen in a dream, while the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like objects seen upon waking.
Ultimately, the bodhisattva is like a lamp that does not shine brightly, while the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like a fully blazing lamp.
Once the Bodhisattva has attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he is able to perform the Buddha-work in all Buddha-worlds.
There are nine kinds of such Buddha-work, and each kind of Buddha-work can greatly benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
What are the nine? First, he performs the deeds of a great man himself and is able to cause sentient beings to believe in the deeds of a great man.
Second, he adorns his body with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, thereby benefiting sentient beings by tearing apart their web of doubt.
Third, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the ten powers; being fully endowed with the ten powers, he is able to benefit sentient beings.
If someone should ask, "What are these powers?
he is then able to explain them well and dispel their doubts, thereby subduing sentient beings and destroying their false views.

Fourth, the Tathāgata is endowed with the four fearlessnesses: for the sake of inspiring faith in the Triple Gem, for the sake of subduing sentient beings, for the sake of destroying false views, and for the sake of the great lion’s roar.

Fifth, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the three foundations of mindfulness; he acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts, destroying all afflictions, able to sustain a retinue of disciples and able to transform sentient beings.

Sixth, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the three qualities of non-protection; for the sake of benefiting sentient beings and for the sake of disciplining sentient beings, he constantly observes all sentient beings day and night with his Buddha-eye.

Seventh, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with great compassion; for the sake of fulfilling the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), and in order to cause sentient beings to be free from all suffering and to bestow upon them peace and happiness.

Eighth, the Tathāgata is endowed with a mind free from error and non-forgetfulness; therefore, without a teacher, he acts in accordance with the Dharma and abides in accordance with the Dharma, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings and bringing them to subdual, and for the sake of destroying the various forms of negligence among sentient beings.

Ninth, the Tathāgata has eternally severed the habitual tendencies of afflictions; he knows dharmas that accord with meaning, dharmas that do not accord with meaning, and dharmas that neither accord nor do not accord with meaning. For this reason, the Tathāgata speaks of dharmas that accord with meaning, remaining detached from dharmas that do not accord with meaning and from those that neither accord nor do not accord with meaning.

The Tathāgata is endowed with one hundred and forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). These nine matters are able to perform the Buddha-work; this is called the practice of the Tathāgata, this is called the stage of the Tathāgata, and this is called the ultimate stage of the Tathāgata.

Why is this? Because for the sake of the conduct of a Tathāgata, the stage of a Tathāgata, and the ultimate stage of a Tathāgata, they have received the bodhisattva precepts and cultivated the practices of enlightenment for immeasurable billions of nayutas of kalpas.

Ultimately, a bodhisattva is able to instruct immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to abide in the stage of ultimate reality; all the Buddha-dharmas of a Tathāgata are for the sake of sentient beings and not for his own sake.
All dharmas possessed by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are merely for their own benefit and provide little benefit to others.
Therefore, the two vehicles have no dharmas that are not shared [with ordinary beings], and the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma is ultimately not similar to the dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Great compassion is unerring and severs the habitual tendencies; it is the samādhi of all-knowledge and the five wisdoms. The Tathāgata is fully endowed with all the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma); therefore, he is called "Unsurpassed."

"This sutra expounds upon the bodhisattva precepts, the bodhisattva path, the fruits of the bodhisattva precepts, all bodhisattva practices, and all practices for the fruits of the bodhisattva precepts; therefore, it is called the Bodhisattvabhūmi, the Bodhisattvapitaka, and the Bodhisattvavinaya, which encompasses all Mahāyāna sūtras and the Sutra of Unobstructed Wisdom."

Whether they be devas, humans, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas, those who believe in this sutra, receive and uphold it, listen to it, expound it, read and recite it, copy it, extensively explain it, cultivate and collect its meaning, and analyze its significance; and those who, seeing one who upholds it, provide offerings, show respect, honor, and praise, making offerings of lamps, incense, flowers, and music—it should be known that such persons are constantly protected and remembered by the Buddhas of the ten directions, who proclaim their names, and they shall obtain an immeasurable mass of merit.

Why is this? Because through the causes and conditions of the bodhisattva precepts, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; by upholding, reciting, copying, and explaining the bodhisattva precepts, the True Dharma of the Tathāgata will abide for a long time without perishing, and all evil bhikṣus will gradually diminish.
"If there are no bodhisattva precepts, evil bhikṣus will gradually increase in number, and the True Dharma of the Tathāgata will soon perish.
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What shall this sutra be named? "Upāli!

It shall be named 'Excellent Precepts,' named 'The Bodhisattva Grounds,' named 'The Bodhisattva Vinaya-mātṛkā,' named 'The Tathāgatagarbha,' named 'The Root of All Wholesome Dharmas,' named 'The Cause of Peace and Bliss,' and named 'The Collection of All Pāramitās.'"
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Upāli rejoiced, prostrated, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
*The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Good Precepts*, Fascicle Nine.
